"Clayface," the third theatrical DCU film, is out in the world.
So, is it any good?
If you listen to critics, the answer is: 'Yeah! Pretty good!'
Of course, while "Clayface" is the third film in an all-new DC cinematic universe, it's far from one of the first movies to be based on DC Comics. That honor goes all the way back to 1966's "Batman."
Over the last 60 years, there have been 57 movies based on characters introduced in the pages of DC Comics and its imprints Vertigo Comics, WildStorm, and Paradox Press.
We used Rotten Tomatoes to determine how each DC film has rated with critics, from the universally panned to the beloved classics.
Here's how each DC Comics film stacks up, including "Superman," "Supergirl," and "Clayface."
57. "Steel" (1997)
Steel, aka John Henry Irons, is one of Superman's most famous allies — but you'd never know it from this film, which invents a new backstory for Steel (played, we'll say, woodenly, by Shaquille O'Neal), that sees him don an iron suit to get revenge on his nemesis Nathaniel Burke, played by Judd Nelson of all people.
"Shaq isn't much of an actor, of course, but as with his first starring effort, 'Kazaam,' he's used more for his screen 'presence.' And casting Nelson in the picture helps, since he's always pretty awful," wrote Chris Hicks for Deseret News.
56. "Catwoman" (2004)
"Catwoman" stars Halle Berry as Patience Phillips, aka Catwoman, in an all-new take on the character. Really, her only resemblance to the comics character is that she, well, likes cats.
In this film, Patience gets her powers (which are new from the comics) from the Egyptian goddess Bast, and decides to take down her evil boss, Laurel (Sharon Stone), who has created an antiaging cream with dangerous side effects. It's as silly as it sounds.
Christy Lemire of the Associated Press called the movie a "soulless amalgamation of quick edits, computer images and swooping, nausea-inducing dolly shots."
55. "Jonah Hex" (2010)
"Jonah Hex" stars Josh Brolin as the titular character, a former Confederate soldier who was left for dead and healed by a Native American tribe, leaving him with the ability to communicate with the dead.
It also stars Megan Fox as Lilah, Jonah's gun-toting love interest, John Malkovich as Jonah's nemesis, Quentin Turnbull, and Michael Fassbender as Turnbull's maniacal right-hand man, Burke.
"It's a loud and subtle-as-a-sledgehammer assault on the senses, though, at 81 minutes, mercifully short," wrote Marc Lee for The Telegraph.
54. "Batman & Robin" (1997)
"Batman & Robin" is known to some as a campy classic filled with neon lighting, a suit with Bat-Nipples, and a pun-loving Mr. Freeze played by Arnold Schwarzenegger.
However, we can't cosign George Clooney's performance as Bruce Wayne or Batman. He just doesn't have it.
"Of all modern Batmans, George Clooney bears the closest physical resemblance to the comic-book hero, but there isn't much to say about his performance because there isn't much performance to discuss," wrote The Wall Street Journal's Joe Morgenstern.
52 (tie). "The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen" (2003)
"The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen" is based on the WildStorm/America's Best Comics series of the same name — originally, these were independent brands from DC Comics, but they were acquired in 1998 by the comics giant, angering "League" creator Alan Moore.
He should've waited until 2003 to see how director Stephen Norrington would butcher his source material to get truly angry, though.
This film takes place in a universe where some of the most iconic characters in fiction (think Dorian Gray, Allan Quatermain, Captain Nemo, and Tom Sawyer) are part of a team of agents that take down threats such as Professor Moriarty of "Sherlock" fame.
"Destined to go down in the history books as the 'Heaven's Gate' of superhero flicks, this is nothing more and nothing less than an extraordinary waste of time and money," wrote Jamie Russell for the BBC.
52 (tie). "Superman IV: The Quest for Peace" (1987)
By the time Christopher Reeve was suiting up for his fourth (and final) go-around as Superman, it was clear that it was time to move on from this version of the character.
The actors seemed somewhat checked out, the effects weren't improving, and the choice to deviate from the comics by pitting Superman against a new villain called Nuclear Man was unwise.
"In many sequences, Reeve looks as if he's pink-faced from embarrassment as he flies through the air looking like a cardboard cut-out," wrote The Boston Globe's Michael Blowen.
51. "Supergirl" (1984)
Helen Slater stars as Kara Zor-El, the cousin of Kal-El (you might know him better as Superman), who had a very different upbringing than her cousin — instead of being raised on Earth by kindly farmers, she grew up among the remnants of Krypton. After a mishap with a wizard played by Peter O'Toole (!), Kara is sent to Earth and becomes Supergirl.
However, the cheesiness of this movie and Faye Dunaway's performance as the main villain, Selena, make it a tough watch in 2026.
Anna Maria Dell'oso of The Sydney Morning Herald called the film a "disappointingly bland and twitty movie."
50. "The Kitchen" (2019)
Did you even know a comic-book movie starring Melissa McCarthy, Tiffany Haddish, Elisabeth Moss, Domhnall Gleeson, Common, and Margo Martindale was released in 2019?
If you didn't, you're not alone. It made just $16 million on a $38 million budget, per Box Office Mojo.
The film is based on the Vertigo Comics series of the same name. In it, McCarthy, Haddish, and Moss play three mob wives who are suddenly put in a position of power after their husbands are sent to jail, giving them freedom for the first time.
"Moss, somehow, retains her dignity but McCarthy and Haddish are made to look like amateurs. I'm a fan of both women. Get me outta this kitchen," wrote Charlotte O'Sullivan for the London Evening Standard.
48. "Green Lantern" (2011)
What can we say about the quality of "Green Lantern" that Ryan Reynolds hasn't already said in the post-credit scene of "Deadpool 2"?
For those not familiar, Reynolds plays Hal Jordan, a test pilot who discovers a ring and becomes endowed with the powers of the Green Lantern Corps, an alien police force.
There's a lot wrong with this movie, from the underwhelming villain to the cheesy special effects. Thankfully, James Gunn, Kyle Chandler, and the DCU finally got Hal right in "Lanterns" this year.
"Even by the standards of the current run of mediocre comic-book movies, this one stands out for its egregious shoddiness," wrote Slate's Dana Stevens.
48. "Suicide Squad" (2016)
When the first teaser for "Suicide Squad" came out, people were excited. And then the cast proudly chatted to the press about their matching tattoos and the camaraderie they built on set (Jared Leto's method-acting as the Joker notwithstanding).
Unfortunately, the finished product didn't live up to the hype. In a word, this team-up of some of the most iconic comic villains of all time (Harley Quinn played by Margot Robbie, Deadshot played by Will Smith, Adewale Akinnuoye-Agbaje as Killer Croc, etc.) is cringe.
"For all its cast and crew's inglorious chest-thumping, 'Suicide Squad' is a failed, forced exercise in — of all things! You had one job! —ensemble chemistry," wrote K. Austin Collins for The Ringer.
47. "Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice" (2016)
For all that's been written about the DC Extended Universe and its failures, "Batman v Superman" is really where the wheels started falling off.
Instead of making the "Man of Steel" sequel that fans wanted, or introducing a new Batman, as played by Ben Affleck, in his own stand-alone film, the studio chose to smush those two stories together in a nonsensical story that hinges on Batman and Superman's moms having the same name.
"If a filmmaker attempted to combine everything casual moviegoers don't like about superhero franchises, they couldn't come up with a picture as execrable as this one," wrote Jason Bailey for Flavorwire.
45 (tie). "Joker: Folie à Deux" (2024)
The first "Joker," which stars Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur Fleck, a mentally unstable wannabe comedian who just wants to be loved, made over $1 billion at the box office, was nominated for best picture at the Academy Awards, and Phoenix even won for best actor.
Its long-awaited sequel, which added Lady Gaga as Harley Quinn? Not so much.
It was a bomb, making just $207 million worldwide, and got such negative reviews from critics that it essentially disappeared from culture altogether.
"'Folie à Deux' is a punishingly dull affair. It's a pointless sequel with very little plot. It wastes the talent on screen, and it squanders the genuinely intriguing conceit of its characters breaking into song," wrote Esther Zuckerman for Bloomberg.
45 (tie). "Superman III" (1983)
A classic move in "Superman" storytelling is to explore the possibility of Superman having a bad day — what would happen if the most powerful being on the planet decided he wasn't so good after all?
That's a compelling concept, if it's done right. In "Superman III," which sees our favorite Kryptonian corrupted by synthetic Kryptonite, it's not.
David Denby of The New Yorker called the film "tedious, labored, and feeble beyond belief."
44. "Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom" (2023)
The last film in the DCEU made before James Gunn and Co. took over went out with a whimper, not a bang. While its predecessor made over $1 billion, this film topped out at $439 million.
In "Lost Kingdom," Aquaman (Jason Momoa) now rules the seven seas with his wife, Mera (Amber Heard, in a much reduced role compared to the first film). But when an old enemy (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) gets hold of a powerful magical weapon, Aquaman must team up with his formerly villainous half-brother Orm (Patrick Wilson) to stop him.
"Where 'Aquaman' felt original, 'Lost Kingdom' is stale, void of all originality," wrote Jenny Nulf at the Austin Chronicle.
42 (tie). "Black Adam" (2022)
Infamously, while promoting this movie, Dwayne Johnson warned fans that the hierarchy of power in the DC Universe was about to change.
In a way, he was right — just two months after this film's post-credit scene reintroduced Henry Cavill's Superman to the big screen for the first time in years, James Gunn announced he'd be starting from scratch with a new actor playing Superman in his revamped DCU.
But "Black Adam" itself is pretty boring. Johnson stars as Teth-Adam (aka Black Adam), an anti-hero who was bestowed superpowers by ancient Egyptian gods. After he's awakened from a centuries-long slumber, he goes on a mission to stand up for his home country, Kahndaq.
"'Black Adam' is two hours of cinematic soup, the ultimate statement from the god-king of movies that everyone sees but no one remembers," wrote Dylan Roth for the Observer.
42 (tie). "Justice League" (2017)
This is the first version of "Justice League" released, to be clear — the one directed by Zack Snyder that was then taken over by Joss Whedon, starring Ben Affleck as Batman, Henry Cavill as Superman, Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman, Jason Momoa as Aquaman, Ezra Miller as the Flash, and Ray Fisher as Cyborg.
The biggest problems with this movie, which sees the most powerful metahumans on Earth unite to defeat an alien called Steppenwolf, are that there's too much going on and the tone is all over the place.
Also, Henry Cavill's CGI-ed out mustache.
"Perhaps the new Superman is closer to what the fans wanted. But he doesn't really feel like a character anymore. He, like the rest of his movie, feels like a focus group-approved concept," wrote Mashable's Angie Han.
41. "Batman Forever" (1995)
"Batman Forever" was the third installment of WB's first attempt at a "Batman" franchise and the first (and only) outing of Val Kilmer's take on the Caped Crusader.
In this film, Bruce Wayne teams up with Robin (Chris O'Donnell) to take down the new team of the Riddler (Jim Carrey) and Two-Face (Tommy Lee Jones). Both Carrey and Jones are absolutely going for it in these roles, and for that alone, it's worth the watch.
"'Batman Forever' is in and out but wins in the end by staying true to its unbridled comic spirit," wrote Peter Travers for Rolling Stone.
40. "Red 2" (2013)
"Red 2" is the sequel to 2010's "Red" (coming later on this list). Once again, the film stars Bruce Willis as Frank Moses, a "retired and extremely dangerous" former CIA agent. He gets pulled into another scheme when he's framed for an operation back in the Cold War that involved smuggling bombs into the USSR.
"While we applaud the minds behind 'Red 2' for making a film for adults in a sea of movies for kids and teenage boys, they didn't actually make a good film for adults," wrote IndieWire's Kimber Myers.
38 (tie). "Constantine" (2005)
Based on the comic character of the same name, Keanu Reeves stars in "Constantine" as the titular exorcist and demon hunter, John Constantine, as he searches for the archangel Gabriel (Tilda Swinton).
Though this film wasn't very beloved by critics or a huge financial success, it certainly has its fans — so much so that, per Deadline, a sequel was announced to be in development in 2022.
"Keanu Reeves is — let me just get this off my chest — very good," wrote Salon's Andrew O'Hehir.
38 (tie). "The Losers" (2010)
In 2010, the year before Chris Evans would join the MCU as Captain America, he starred in a different comic-book movie — this one based on the Vertigo Comics series "The Losers."
The titular Losers are a group of black-ops soldiers who are sent on the most dangerous missions in the world. In this film, they're sent on a mission to Bolivia to destroy a drug trafficking compound, but are double-crossed by their evil boss, Max (Jason Patric).
"'The Losers' is a ho-hum scraping of the comic-book barrel, which feels particularly needless with both 'The A-Team' and 'The Expendables' on their way," wrote Tim Robey for The Telegraph.
37. "Shazam! Fury of the Gods" (2023)
"Shazam! Fury of the Gods" was one of the DCEU movies released after the announcement that an entire universe rehaul was imminent, rendering the events of this movie irrelevant.
It's a sequel to the perfectly lovely 2019 film "Shazam!," but this movie seemingly forgot what was charming about the first one. Zachary Levi (who plays the adult Billy) and Asher Angel (teen Billy) don't seem to be playing characters who have any knowledge of each other.
"The original film left nothing of substance for this superhero sequel," wrote Adam Mullins-Khatib for Chicago Reader.
36. "Supergirl" (2026)
The second theatrical DCU film in James Gunn's new cinematic universe was unable to reach the heights of 2025's "Superman," but even middling reviews praised Milly Alcock's performance as Kara Zor-El, aka Supergirl, Superman's cousin.
In the film, she goes on a quest to find the antidote to the poison that's killing her beloved dog Krypto. She also deals with lingering trauma from her upbringing on an offshoot of Krypton, where she watched her entire family die due to Kryptonite poisoning.
"I left 'Supergirl,' however, thinking only of Kara and wanting more of this striving, imperfect heroine, intrigued by what her role in this universe might next be," wrote Moira Macdonald for the Seattle Times.
35. "The Return of Swamp Thing" (1989)
The sequel to 1982's "Swamp Thing," "The Return of Swamp Thing," leans into every schlocky, campy quality of the original and turns it up to 11.
This time, Swamp Thing (Dick Durock) must rescue a young botanist, Abby Arcane (Heather Locklear), from her evil stepfather Anton (Louis Jourdan), who wants to steal her youth.
Lindsay Costello of The Stranger called the movie "one of the most precious gifts ever put to celluloid."
33 (tie). "Man of Steel" (2013)
In the 13 years since "Man of Steel" was released, there's been a lot written about what this movie did to the character of Superman, the destruction he wrought (seemingly without a second thought) across both Smallville and Metropolis, Cavill's portrayal of Kal-El, and the controversial characterization of his adopted dad Pa Kent (played in this iteration by Kevin Costner).
In general, we think it's a solid origin story that was hindered by a couple of casting choices, a lack of humor, and an oppressively gray color palette.
"Christliness has always been an element of the Superman myth. But this film's near literal insistence upon it becomes absurd since director Zack Snyder and screenwriter David S. Goyer don't dramatize the analogy, they presume it," wrote Wesley Morris for Grantland.
33 (tie). "Wonder Woman 1984" (2020)
"Wonder Woman 1984" is the highly anticipated follow-up to 2017's "Wonder Woman," moving our heroine (played by Gal Gadot) from WWI-era Europe to 1980s Washington, DC.
The film also stars Pedro Pascal as Maxwell Lord, a would-be billionaire who becomes the living embodiment of a genie's lamp when he gets the ability to grant anyone's wishes just by getting near them.
Diana (aka Wonder Woman) has to choose between getting the love of her life, Steve (Chris Pine), back from the dead or having her powers and the ability to save people.
"It's a refreshingly silly and airy adventure focused on the emotions of one character, Wonder Woman (played by Gal Gadot), and a charming end to a tiring year of cinema," wrote David Sims of The Atlantic.
32. "The Flash" (2023)
A lot was riding on "The Flash" before it hit theaters in 2023 after numerous delays. Apparently, Tom Cruise himself was so taken by it that he called director Andy Muschietti for 15 minutes to rave about it, per Variety.
Instead, it ended up being a somewhat garbled mess. Ezra Miller stars as Barry Allen, a young man struck by lightning who develops superspeed. But that's the least of Barry's concerns; he also has a dad who's been falsely imprisoned for murdering his mom. After the events of "Justice League," Barry figures out he can travel back in time and makes the choice to stop his mom from dying.
That small choice sends things into chaos, with Barry getting catapulted into an alternate universe with no other metahumans and the Michael Keaton version of Batman.
"Mad trippy or catastrophic? This DC superhero epic is actually a mix of both, dragged down by exhausting multiverse hopping but flashy fun on the wings of virtuoso Ezra Miller and the grumpy comic perfection of Michael Keaton as a Batman on the ropes," wrote Peter Travers for ABC.
31. "Watchmen" (2009)
The second-best reviewed Zack Snyder joint on this list is "Watchmen," adapted from the iconic, highly lauded comic of the same name.
In this story, masked crime-fighters have been around for decades (oh, and Richard Nixon is a five-term president at the height of the Cold War) — but they've been outlawed for years.
One such former vigilante, Rorschach (Jackie Earle Haley), becomes convinced that someone is taking out former heroes one by one, and tries to warn his former team, the Watchmen, that someone might be after them. But the conspiracy goes deeper than any of them could've imagined.
"'Watchmen' isn't boring, but as a fragmented sci-fi doomsday noir, it remains as detached from the viewer as it is from the zeitgeist," wrote Entertainment Weekly's Owen Gleiberman.
30. "Swamp Thing" (1982)
"Swamp Thing" was directed by horror legend Wes Craven, and is his love letter to the creature features of the 1950s such as "The Creature from the Black Lagoon."
It's a pretty standard monster movie anchored by performances by Ray Wise, Dick Durock, Adrienne Barbeau, and Louis Jordan. Alec Holland (Wise), a scientist, is turned into a superhuman monster after an experiment gone wrong. Horror ensues.
Roger Ebert called it "one of those movies that fall somewhere between buried treasures and guilty pleasures."
29. "Aquaman" (2018)
"Aquaman" stars Jason Momoa as Arthur Curry, a half-human, half-Atlantean hero who is of both land and sea. Over the course of the film, he must learn to accept his birthright as the king of Atlantis — but first, he must defeat Black Manta (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) and his half-brother Orm (Patrick Wilson).
"Hollywood has given us the greatest, goofiest holiday gift in a long time," wrote Jordan Hoffman for AMNY.
28. "Joker" (2019)
The discourse around "Joker" (Is it about incels? Is it a truly nihilistic piece of art? What is a Joker movie without a Batman?) has almost obfuscated the fact that it's a pretty good movie.
Joaquin Phoenix is almost unrecognizable as Arthur Fleck, a down-on-his-luck wannabe comedian who struggles with telling the difference between reality and delusion. But as his psyche begins to crack, he only becomes more beloved by the disillusioned residents of Gotham.
Wenlei Ma wrote for news.com.au, "'Joker' is a jumble — sometimes brilliant and sometimes trite. Among its flashes of excellence is a self-serious movie that isn't nearly as deep as it thinks it is."
27. "Zack Snyder's Justice League" (2021)
As you might remember, there already was a "Justice League" movie on this list — but it wasn't the director Zack Snyder's complete product, since he had to step away from filming due to personal reasons.
But when fans became aware that Snyder had shot enough footage to make a four-hour cut of the film that was true to his vision, they became obsessed with the #SnyderCut.
Sure, it took years, but "Zack Snyder's Justice League" hit HBO Max in 2021, all 242 minutes of it, after the fans' unrelenting pressure on Warner Bros.
While the general story remains the same, there's much more of every character in Snyder's cut, especially Cyborg (Ray Fisher), who was almost entirely cut out of the theatrical version. And it's a better movie for Fisher's performance, who is the heart of the film.
"It actually succeeds. In more ways than I ever expected," wrote NPR's Eric Deggans.
24 (tie). "DC League of Super-Pets" (2022)
The first (but not last!) animated film on this list is "DC League of Super-Pets," which is essentially the Justice League with cats and dogs (and turtles and guinea pigs and squirrels …).
In the same year he played Black Adam in live-action, Dwayne Johnson also voiced Krypto, Superman's pet dog. Kevin Hart, on the other hand, voiced Ace, Batman's boxer mix, whom the Dark Knight has adopted.
"The Super-Pets aren't the most witty or cutting bunch — and no doubt destined to be plush toys on store shelves soon — but there's little reason to resist the cute," wrote The Guardian's Adrian Horton.
24 (tie). "Red" (2010)
"Red" is a somewhat forgotten movie these days, but it was actually nominated for a Golden Globe in 2010, for best motion picture — musical or comedy.
It's based on the WildStorm comic (a DC imprint) of the same name about a retired CIA agent named Frank Moses (Bruce Willis) who is pulled back into action after another agent, William Cooper (Karl Urban), is tasked with killing him by the vice president, Robert Stanton (Julian McMahon).
"A fast, funny, smart, adult-oriented action-comedy that generates precisely the kind of giddy vibe 'The Expendables' lacked," wrote The Age's Jim Schembri.
24 (tie). "Superman Returns" (2006)
The plot of "Superman Returns" completely ignores the events of "Superman III" and "Superman IV," and is instead a semi-reboot, semi-legacy sequel to "Superman II."
This time, though, our hero is played by Brandon Routh, who we'd maintain never got a fair shake at playing Superman. This movie is pretty good! The airplane sequence that kicks off the movie holds up 20 years later.
"It's all about heart — not that the spectacle falters; this is the finest popular entertainment since the 'Rings' trilogy closed. Superman doesn't fly — he soars," wrote Ian Nathan for Empire.
23. "V for Vendetta" (2005)
"V for Vendetta" is based on the Vertigo Comics series of the same name. It takes place in an alternate version of Great Britain that has been overtaken by a fascist, totalitarian regime. A lone anarchist, known as V (Hugo Weaving), who is never seen without a Guy Fawkes mask, begins planting the seeds of a revolution with the help of a young woman, Evey (Natalie Portman).
Claudia Puig wrote for USA Today, "The dark and stylized 'V for Vendetta' is visually exhilarating, provocative and disturbing."
21 (tie). "Stardust" (2007)
"Stardust" is based on the Neil Gaiman novel of the same name that was published by DC Comics in 1999.
It's an epic romantasy starring Charlie Cox as Tristan, a young man who wants to collect a fallen star to present to his love, Victoria (Sienna Miller) — but when the fallen star turns out to be a young woman named Yvaine (Claire Danes), Tristan finds himself in a love triangle.
"A stern editor with a sense of dramatic timing could have given this film more tension to go with its random bursts of comedy and big, happy fantasy setpieces, but lacking tautness, it'll have to settle for expansive joy," wrote the AV Club's Tasha Robinson.
21 (tie). "Batman" (1989)
Tim Burton's "Batman" took Gotham City's favorite vigilante out of the campy '60s and into the gothic, dark '80s.
The film (which actually isn't really an origin story — it starts off with Bruce Wayne having been Batman for at least six months) stars Michael Keaton as Wayne/Batman and Jack Nicholson as the Joker, in one of the most entertaining performances of his career.
Newsday's Mike McGrady called the film "one of the most interesting comic-book movies ever made, a movie that vividly illustrates where most of the others have gone wrong."
19 (tie). "Blue Beetle" (2023)
"Blue Beetle" is a charming little movie about a recent college grad, Jaime Reyes (Xolo Maridueña), who becomes fused with a piece of alien tech known as the Scarab (voiced by Becky G) and becomes a powerful hero known as the Blue Beetle.
"'Blue Beetle' is both scrappy and tailored, poignant and breezily amusing. Pitched from a new angle and guided by talented hands, 'Blue Beetle' is a rarity in these superhero end-times: a genuine pleasure to watch, reviving tired old formula with brio," wrote Richard Lawson for Vanity Fair.
19 (tie). "Clayface" (2026)
It's an interesting choice for James Gunn and Co. to make DC Studios' third film overall a body-horror origin story for one of Batman's B-list villains, Clayface (Tom Rhys Harries). But sure!
"There are scenes of such inventive gruesomeness that I found myself whimpering pitifully and hiding behind my backpack for much of the feature. That may not sound like fun, but — trust me — it is," wrote The Observer's Wendy Ide.
18. "Birds of Prey" (2020)
Margot Robbie's casting as Harley Quinn was far and away the best choice DC ever made. She shines in this movie as a newly empowered version of the Joker's ex-girlfriend who teams up with a few other local female criminals — The Huntress (Mary Elizabeth Winstead), Black Canary (Jurnee Smollett-Bell), and Cassandra Cain (Ella Jay Basco) — to take down the crime lord Black Mask (Ewan McGregor).
"Kinetic, silly, candy-colored, and hyperviolent, 'Birds of Prey' is a serious treat for fans of comic book films. But it wouldn't work without the equal parts goofy, hilarious, and unhinged performance of its lead," wrote Max Weiss for Baltimore Magazine.
17. "Batman" (1966)
This version of the Caped Crusader is based on the equally campy '60s TV show that aired on ABC for three seasons.
From that iconic theme song, to Adam West's perfectly calibrated performance as an adult man who feels the need to dress up as a bat to fight crime, to all the wild "bat" gadgets (Bat-Shark Repellant, anyone?), this movie is a classic.
"I'd choose Adam West's Batmobile over Michael Keaton's any day," wrote Time Out.
14 (tie). "Batman Returns" (1992)
"Batman Returns" is a weirder, slimier, grimier, and meaner film than its predecessor — and it's a Christmas movie!
Michael Keaton is once again solid as Batman, but this movie belongs to Michelle Pfeiffer as Catwoman and Danny DeVito as the Penguin, two portrayals of the characters that live on 34 years later.
"The strange, ambitious character work that comprises 'Batman Returns' is wrapped in the perfunctory framework of a Tim Burton superhero film," wrote Justin Clark for Slant Magazine.
14 (tie). "Road to Perdition" (2002)
Yup, "Road to Perdition" is a comic movie. The series was published by the DC Comics imprint Paradox Press in the '90s and 2000s.
The Sam Mendes film stars Tom Hanks as Michael Sullivan, an enforcer for the Irish Mob in '30s Illinois. After his family is targeted by a rival mobster, Michael and his son, played by Tyler Hoechlin, are forced to go on the run, killing anyone in their way.
"This is classic albeit somber filmmaking, restrained and all of a piece, by a director who believes film can tell adult stories in an adult manner, who knows the effects he wants and how to get them," wrote the Los Angeles Times' Kenneth Turan.
14 (tie). "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm" (1993)
"Batman: The Animated Series" is one of the most iconic and beloved cartoons of all time, so it stands to reason that a theatrical adaptation of the cartoon would work. And it does! The late, great Kevin Conroy's vocal performance as Batman/Bruce Wayne will live on forever as the definitive portrayal of the character, and the design of Gotham City is timeless.
The story itself is pretty standard Batman fare, but it's compelling to watch Bruce grapple with the choice to stay a vigilante or give it up for love.
"A fantastic-looking back-to-basics telling of the legend, it totally disregards any attempt at nineties reinvention," wrote Ross Jones for The Guardian.
13. "Superman" (2025)
The first feature film under James Gunn's new DC Universe (and it was also written and directed by Gunn himself) was, of course, 2025's "Superman."
It introduced audiences to an all-new version of Superman, this time played to perfection by David Corenswet. He's surrounded by an all-time supporting cast, including Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane, Nicholas Hoult as Lex Luthor, Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Nathan Fillion as Guy Gardner (a Green Lantern), Isabela Merced as Hawkgirl, and Krypto, a really great dog.
"It makes you want to cheer. That's it, that's the secret ingredient that's been missing from so many superhero stories for so long," wrote Glen Weldon of NPR.
11 (tie). "Batman Begins" (2005)
We'd call "Batman Begins" the first Batman movie of the modern era. It's directed by Christopher Nolan, and puts Batman (Christian Bale) into the most realistic version of Gotham City we'd seen to date. Plus, Cillian Murphy's portrayal of the Scarecrow still haunts us.
"The psychological realism and the science-fiction villainy don't always mesh seamlessly. But unlike so many superheroic summer spectacles, this one actually has a soul behind the special effects," wrote David Ansen for Newsweek.
11 (tie). "The Batman" (2022)
Tied with "Batman Begins" is the newest version of the Bat, this time played by Robert Pattinson in one of the most emo roles of his career. Seriously, this Bruce Wayne looks like he's a fully nocturnal animal.
In a change from the rest of his big-screen portrayals, this Batman is equally as much of a detective as he is a brawler — and he certainly does a lot of both.
We also have to pay respects to Zoë Kravitz's Catwoman and Colin Farrell's unrecognizable turn as the Penguin, which led to him getting his own HBO Max show.
"'The Batman' is the Batman movie we deserve, though: overwrought and overlong, but also carefully crafted and exhilarating," wrote Adam Nayman for The Ringer.
9 (tie). "The Dark Knight Rises" (2012)
Christian Bale wrapped up his time as the Dark Knight in 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," which picks up eight years after the events of "The Dark Knight," when Batman was shunned by the people of Gotham after he took the fall for killing Harvey Dent.
This movie's lasting legacy is probably its villain, the hulking mass that is Bane (Tom Hardy) and his, we'll say, unique way of speaking.
But a lot happens in this movie. Batman meets Catwoman (Anne Hathaway), he gets his back broken and fully recovers, the city of Gotham is cut off from civilization via a series of bombings, and Batman fakes his own death. Phew.
"[Christopher] Nolan has turned a preposterous character back into a grave myth, the story of a tortured saviour, reluctantly giving his all," wrote The London Evening Standard's David Sexton.
9 (tie). "Superman: The Movie" (1978)
Arguably, this could be considered the first modern superhero movie, the film that set us down the path we're still taking to the movie theaters to this day. It's cheesy, but not overly so, it has an all-time superhero theme composed by John Williams (that's still being used in "Superman" content now), and the casting of Christopher Reeve as Superman remains the best superhero casting of all time, period.
And we didn't even mention Gene Hackman as Lex Luthor and Margot Kidder as Lois Lane, who complete a trifecta of A-plus performances in this film.
"Reshaping a comic book adaptation into a modern myth told with wonder, sincerity and soul, 'Superman: The Movie' didn't just make you believe a man could fly, it made you want to," wrote Zaki Hasan for the San Francisco Chronicle.
7 (tie). "A History of Violence" (2005)
Not even director David Cronenberg is immune to the comic-book movie craze. In 2005, he adapted the 1997 graphic novel published by Paradox Press (and later Vertigo Comics).
The film stars Viggo Mortensen as Tom, a small-town diner owner with a wife and son. He becomes the center of a media frenzy when he takes out two spree killers who are trying to rob his diner with relative ease — despite his best efforts to stay anonymous, his violent past as a mob hitman comes back to haunt him.
"Cronenberg's masterful, intelligent and gripping meta-thriller leaves us pondering about our enduringly perverse desire for alternative realities, in which surrogate violent alter egos run righteously and preposterously amok," wrote Richard Falcon for Sight & Sound.
7 (tie). "Superman II" (1980)
With all the shuffling that went on behind the scenes (director Richard Donner was fired 80% of the way through and replaced with Richard Lester), it's a miracle that this movie is watchable, let alone great.
It's carried to greatness largely on the back of Terence Stamp's performance as General Zod, an evil Kryptonian hellbent on taking over Earth and destroying Superman.
"The special effects are spare but spectacular, and the delightfully showy tricks are spaced out by comic ventures into romance, tourism and human drama," wrote Meaghan Morris for The Sydney Morning Herald.
6. "The Lego Batman Movie" (2017)
After Lego Batman was such a huge hit in "The Lego Movie," greenlighting a spinoff about his adventures in Gotham City was a no-brainer.
Will Arnett voices this petulant and somewhat callous version of Batman amazingly well. He's joined by an equally stellar voice cast of Michael Cera as Robin, Ralph Fiennes as Bruce's butler Alfred, Zach Galifianakis as the Joker, and Rosario Dawson as Batgirl.
This version of the Batman story gets at the idea, perhaps more than any other Batman story, that Batman and the Joker need each other to survive. It's a toxic relationship, but a relationship nonetheless.
"Everything is still awesome in the irreverent 'Lego Movie' universe!!! All right, maybe not everything. But enough things," wrote Us Weekly's Mara Reinstein.
4 (tie). "The Suicide Squad" (2021)
In between his second and third "Guardians of the Galaxy" movies, James Gunn briefly jumped ship from Marvel to DC (and soon, permanently joined Team DC) to write and direct "The Suicide Squad," a loose sequel to 2016's "Suicide Squad." Confusing titles, we know.
This version of the team is all heart and the epitome of the found family trope that Gunn loves so much. After a fakeout in which almost an entire team is killed, we're introduced to our main characters: Harley Quinn (Margot Robbie), Bloodsport (Idris Elba), Peacemaker (John Cena), Rick Flag Jr. (Joel Kinnaman), King Shark (Sylvester Stallone), Polka-Dot Man (David Dastmalchian), and Ratcatcher 2 (Daniela Melchior).
"'The Suicide Squad' is relentlessly unapologetic, wacky and weird, violent and bloody, and darkly humorous. It also has so much heart that you may find yourself fighting back tears by its end," wrote Kirsten Acuna for Business Insider.
4 (tie). "Shazam!" (2019)
"Shazam!" was a surprise. It's a somewhat high concept: A young foster kid named Billy Batson is chosen by an ancient wizard to be bestowed with the power of the gods. Now, any time he says "Shazam" he goes from young Asher Angel to the adult Zachary Levi.
However, the strength of this movie is the bond between Billy and his foster siblings, mainly Freddy (Jack Dylan Grazer), as they come together and become a true family.
"Once Billy says that magic word and his supersized alter ego appears, the movie goes to its happy place and comfortably embraces its own identity as a light, jocular, modest entertainment," wrote Manohla Dargis for The New York Times.
3. "Teen Titans Go! To the Movies" (2018)
The best-reviewed animated movie on this list is "Teen Titans Go! To the Movies," the cinematic continuation of the Cartoon Network series that began airing in 2013.
The Teen Titans are exactly what it sounds like: a group of teenage superheroes. This version of the team contains Robin (Scott Menville), Starfire (Hynden Walch), Beast Boy (Greg Cipes), Cyborg (Khary Payton), and Raven (Tara Strong).
In this film, the Teen Titans are upset that no one takes them seriously because they've never had a movie made about them, so they go on a hunt to find an arch-nemesis worthy of the big screen.
Tara Brady of The Irish Times called it "appropriately super."
2. "Wonder Woman" (2017)
Wonder Woman is one of the most famous and beloved heroes in the DC universe, but it took 76 years to get Diana, the Amazonian princess of Themiscyra, on the big screen.
Thankfully, she was worth the wait. This movie, put simply, rocks. Chris Pine is dynamite as WWI fighter pilot Steve Trevor, Gal Gadot plays Diana's naivety about the modern world so well, and the rest of the supporting cast is on their A-game, too.
"It's not difficult to see where this route is going, but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable to watch. The simple power of love is the cornerstone upon which Wonder Woman is built. If it seems earnest, it's because it is," wrote Karen Han for Slash Film.
1. "The Dark Knight" (2008)
There's an argument to be made that "The Dark Knight," the second of the Christopher Nolan/Christian Bale trio, is the best superhero movie ever made.
It blends action with thought-provoking ideas about the nature of good and evil — yes, we know it's cliché at this point, but in 2008, it was hitting different! — and a genuinely star-making performance by Heath Ledger, who would go on to posthumously win an Oscar for his work as the Joker.
"The haunting and visionary 'Dark Knight' soars on the wings of untamed imagination," wrote Rolling Stone's Peter Travers.
Editor's Note: This story was originally published in July 2025 and was most recently updated in November 2026.

The story so far: The Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report of 2021, released by the Office of the Registrar General of India recently, showed that India has maintained its Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.0 — the same as reported in 2020. While the national average for TFR has remained the same, there is a wide regional variation in TFR data for States and Union Territories (UTs) reported independently.
The highest TFR was recorded in Bihar at 3.0 and the lowest was reported for West Bengal and Delhi at 1.4. The data went on to reveal that in the decade between 2009-11 and 2019-21, TFR has been on an overall decline, in States, and nationally, albeit at different rates.

Ruling National Conference (NC) president Dr. Farooq Abdullah on Friday (November 6, 2026) ruled out any split in the party and assured a step-by-step approach to address the “genuine issues” raised by the 17 disgruntled legislators during a two-hour meeting with the top leadership in Srinagar.
“The baseless news of the National Conference (NC) splitting into groups is totally wrong. The party stands together. Those who think the party could be split: it was never, and it will never be split. We spoke to them [disgruntled legislators], and their issues were genuine. We heard all of them and assured them that some steps will be taken immediately and some slowly,” National Conference president Dr. Farooq Abdullah, after meeting disgruntled 17 party legislators in Srinagar.
Mr. Abdullah, who was accompanied by NC vice presidentOmar Abdullah and disgruntled leaders Mubarak Gul and Nazir Gurezi, said, “Our struggle for Statehood, Article 370 and 35A will continue.”
The meeting of the party in the wake of growing criticism from 17 legislators who held a separate meeting in Srinagar on October 27 and forwarded a joint resolution over a slew of issues, including removing CM Omar Abdullah’s adviser Nasir Aslam Wani and reassigning the portfolio of Roads and Buildings (R&B) currently with Deputy Chief Minister Surinder Choudhary.
The political upheaval was sparked hours after CM Abdullah expanded and reshuffled the Cabinet on October 27. Three senior leaders, Mr. Gul, Mr. Gurezi and Abdul Majeed Bhat Larmi showed heartburn publicly over not being inducted into the Cabinet.
“We have been raising issues with the party. We sat at a place recently, and the media blew it out of proportion and claimed a split [in the party]. There is no separate party. We placed the issues, both political and others, before the leadership, and there are assurances they will be addressed in step-by-step approach,” said Mr. Gurezi.
Earlier, a 10-point memorandum was submitted to the party leadership, which included a time-bound implementation of the election manifesto and an intensification of the struggle for the restoration of Statehood and special status. It also called for cabinet restructuring and ministerial accountability, and for the replacement of the Advisor. The memorandum also advocated a consultative advisory group of legislators and the constitution of a high-powered disciplinary committee.

A voter going to the polls Tuesday night was more likely than not to use information from their favorite influencer than traditional news when casting their vote. According to a recent YouGov survey, nearly 65 percent of 2,000 adults surveyed say they receive their political information from digital creators.
Given that that statistic jumps to 77 percent when you isolate Gen Z, it’s unlikely to change anytime soon. On the heels of a historic Democratic wave capturing the House and Senate Tuesday, Kat Abughazaleh, who ran for an Illinois House seat earlier this year as a Democrat, and Republican strategist CJ Pearson talked about the future of influencers and algorithms at the WIRED World Fair in Miami on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has been particularly aggressive in welcoming right-wing creators into the White House. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt opened formal press briefings to digital creators last year and hosted influencer-specific briefings during her tenure. (Leavitt’s move garnered hefty criticism for favoring softball questions, especially as the administration cracked down on the presence of more traditional media in press briefings.)
Pearson, who previously served on the RNC’s Youth Advisory Council, has been directly involved in these efforts, and points out that multiple federal agencies are now copying the White House’s playbook. He said that it’s simply the cost of getting people’s attention in the digital age.
“It’s a very chronically online administration,” he said. “With how short people’s attention spans are, you have to make [things] interesting.” Not all of the White House’s efforts have been received smoothly on the right: Pearson believes the administration’s decision to distribute portions of the Epstein files to 15 right-wing creators last year was “a misstep.”
For Abughazaleh, a former Media Matters reporter, the administration’s embrace of the internet signals something far more nefarious. Abughazaleh brought up the Department of Education’s recent use of the “Malfoid” meme—a gender-bent Harry Potter fascist figurehead—which, she said, was being promoted for a too-online audience of “incels.” And the White House’s embrace of “AI slop and brutality,” seen in ads about ICE actions, was turning “cruelty into content” rather than informing people, she says.
“They’re trying to ruin your attention span,” she said.
Abughazaleh and Pearson are pretty far apart on the political spectrum. The WIRED forum included some testy exchanges, including whether or not ICE facilities can be called “concentration camps”—a term Abughazaleh, who was arrested for protesting outside an ICE facility last year, used consistently. (The charges were dropped after allegations of misconduct by prosecutors before a grand jury.) They also skirmished over Pearson’s claim that Elon Musk had turned X into a “bastion of free speech.”
But both agreed that reliance on algorithms is increasingly creating echo chambers with young Americans of both parties.
“Algorithms show us what you want to see,” Pearson said, mentioning that his friends on the left will sometimes send him articles on political topics he simply hasn’t seen before. “The deeper question is, is that good for society or for democracy?”
On this, Abughazaleh agrees. “We have no shared reality,” she added.

Jane Fonda was giddy Thursday night at the Women in Film Honors gala in Beverly Hills.
“I’m so excited,” she told me while practically skipping down the red carpet.
The longtime political activist is riding the Election Day blue wave that helped the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
“I felt pretty optimistic, but I didn’t dare imagine that it would be this broad,” Fonda said. “I’m just so proud of American people, that they were paying attention and it wasn’t just about affordability. [James] Talarico’s acceptance speech was a masterpiece and in it he said, ‘We voted to love our neighbor.’”
She added, “I’m so excited with how many incredible women have been elected to high important offices.”
As for the Democrats’ next move, Fonda said, “We have to be very smart. We can’t return to the old neoliberalism. We have to take off our corporate hat, take off our donor hat, and start doing things that are going to help working people in this country, and we have to rule with love. We don’t rule yet, but we have to block what’s bad and fight for what’s good.”
She continued, “It’s not just about accountability and investigations because there’s so much corruption and criminality, but it also has to be about really putting power in the hands of working people and making life better for them.”
Fonda said she knows a lot of the candidates who won their elections. “I have a PAC and I’ve been traveling the country meeting them. These are different kinds of people,” she said. “People are just pissed. They don’t want crime. They don’t want chaos. They don’t want corruption.”
Fonda was on hand the gala to help honor Salma Hayek, who received the Jane Fonda Humanitarian Award.

Listed private market intelligence platform Tracxn Technologies reported a 25.8% decline in its net loss to ₹4.1 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 (Q2 FY27) from ₹5.6 Cr, helped by a lower tax charge. Sequentially, its loss widened 37.1% from ₹3 Cr. Operating revenue remained largely flat, rising 0.3% to ₹21.3 Cr from ₹21.2 Cr. The top line increased 1.1% from ₹21.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. The narrower YoY net loss reflects a change in tax expenses. Tracxn incurred a ₹6.2 Cr tax charge in Q2 FY26, compared with a ₹52 Lakh tax credit in the quarter under review. Before tax, the company swung to a loss of ₹4.6 Cr from a profit of ₹62.4 Lakh a year earlier. Its pre-tax loss stood at ₹2.8 Cr in Q1 FY27. The Bengaluru-based company provides private-company data and software to venture capital firms, private equity firms, investment banks, and corporate teams. Total income, including other income and gains, stood at ₹22.7 Cr, compared with ₹22.5 Cr in Q2 FY26 and ₹22.6 Cr in the preceding quarter. Tracxn’s total expenses rose 25% YoY to ₹27.3 Cr from ₹21.9 Cr. Sequentially, expenses increased 7.7% from ₹25.4 Cr. For the first half of FY27, operating revenue declined marginally to ₹42.4 Cr from ₹42.5 Cr in the corresponding period last fiscal. Total expenses increased 21.7% YoY to ₹52.7 Cr from ₹43.3 Cr, while net loss widened 60.6% to ₹7.1 Cr from ₹4.4 Cr. Tracxn reported a net cash outflow of ₹6 Cr from operating activities in H1 FY27, against an inflow of ₹1 Cr a year earlier. India Growth Offsets Overseas Decline India accounted for 53% of Tracxn’s Q2 FY27 revenue, with domestic revenue growing 6.9% sequentially to ₹11.3 Cr. The company said this represented an annualised growth run rate of nearly 30%. International revenue declined 4.8% sequentially to ₹10 Cr, accounting for the remaining 47%. Tracxn said investments in data and sales capabilities in India over the past two to three years were driving domestic growth. It is now making similar investments across its international business units, which it expects to support growth over the coming quarters. Its strategy involves creating specialised teams for customer segments, expanding relevant datasets and product capabilities, and then scaling sales teams. For instance, monthly new customer wins in its India investment banking business increased from nine to 13 during FY26 and reached 20 in Q1 FY27. It is targeting 30 monthly wins. Tracxn plans to expand the sales team responsible for closing deals from 34 members in December 2025 to around 60 by December 2026. Of these planned positions, 56 had been filled by September. Sales and marketing teams accounted for 30% of its total headcount in Q2 FY27, up from 25% a year earlier. AI And Data Expansion Tracxn has introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) connectors that allow paid users to access its proprietary company intelligence through AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor. It has also introduced an AI assistant that lets users query its database in plain English, alongside ready-to-use investor agents for tasks including due diligence, competitive benchmarking, sector research, and startup scouting. More workflows are planned. On data coverage, Tracxn said its database contained detailed financials for more than 7.5 Mn companies across over 20 countries, while its global legal entity database covered 66 Mn entities. The company is also using Tracxn Lite, which offers limited platform access, to attract potential paying customers. It reported 3.49 Lakh cumulative sign-ups and 17.1 Mn organic visits during Q2 FY27. Customer accounts increased 13% YoY to 2,419, while users grew 16% to 6,854. Tracxn said it expects annual cost growth to moderate to low single digits after its current investment phase, supported by AI-led reductions in data production costs. It expects this to help it return to profitability.

It was a bad night for data centers. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has aired ads for months calling his opponent “the face of data centers in Ohio,” cruised to victory to flip a Senate seat. Democrat Chris Pappas, who when seated will be the nation’s first openly gay male senator, mentioned his opposition to data centers in his victory speech and drew massive boos from his crowd in New Hampshire—even though the state has no large-scale data centers under construction.
Elsewhere, two separate Republicans named Derek and Derrick, whose Democratic opponents labeled them “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick,” suffered losses in House races in Ohio and Wisconsin.
As part of last night’s shocking blue tsunami, voters selected candidates with tough policies on data centers at all levels of government, in a clear rebuke to the industry’s buildout in states across the country. Almost a quarter of all voters told NBC News that data centers were “crucial” to their vote, while nearly two-thirds said it was either a major or minor factor.
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Greg Casar, the Texas Democratic congressman, said in a statement.
“Data centers and AI as a technology are fundamentally linked in many voters' minds,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI. “So you can address all of the different concerns with data centers with regards to their energy or their noise, or their pollution, and there would still be significant concerns about what these projects are enabling and the effect is having on opportunities, prices, jobs, society.”
Perhaps some of the biggest shocks for the industry came in the governor’s mansions. In stunning upsets, voters elected Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while putting Cindy Holscher on the cusp of a potential win in Kansas. All of these candidates campaigned not just for increased regulations on the industry, but for data center moratoriums. A pause on data centers in Texas and Georgia especially, two of the biggest hubs for development in the country, could have serious implications for the hundreds of projects planned for each of those states.
“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” says McCoy. “I think we'll likely see the appointment of regulators in various administrative bureaucratic bodies that pose more scrutiny on these projects and an increase in the enforcement of environmental protection regulations.”
Simply being anti-data center wasn’t enough to boost some candidates—especially Republicans. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany, who hit Democrat David Crowley early on in his campaign with ads dubbing him “Data Center David Crowley,” lost his race. (Crowley got more aggressive on the industry as the campaign went on, indicating he would support a pause two weeks before election day.) So did incumbent Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th congressional district, who aired ads slamming his opponent’s past statements that New York “needs” data centers, conceded his race even though the Associated Press has yet to call it.
Throughout the campaign, data centers proved to be a bipartisan topic of concern, and caused fractures within the parties themselves. Earlier this year, WIRED reported how many of Donald Trump’s MAGA loyalists disagreed with the president’s support for AI companies and data centers.
But it’s undeniable that anger about data centers helped elect Democrats. In the weeks leading up to the elections, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee ran ads that highlighted Republicans’ support for data centers or the backing they had received from AI companies.
“Voters aren’t stupid. The data center story is a corruption story. It's an affordability story. It's a Big Tech CEOs influence story,” says Sacha Haworth executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. “That's what voters understood when they cast their ballots and that's why Democrats routed Republicans so, so hard last night, because Republicans could not tell the same story.”
Many of the candidates who won on stricter data center regulations did so despite massive injections of cash from the AI and data center industries to their opponents. In South Carolina, Building the Future, a new industry super PAC, spent $1.5 million to support Darline Graham; she lost last night to Democrat Annie Andrews, who favors a moratorium. (Andrews registered the URL DataCenterDarline.com in late September to hit Graham on her industry connections.) Building the Future also injected more than $1.5 million into the Kansas gubernatorial race to support Republican Ty Masterson against Holscher. And Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence, who made regulations on AI and data centers a cornerstone of his campaign, has declared victory (though without an AP announcement) over Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive races in the country. Barrett had gotten $340,000 from Elon Musk’s America PAC over the course of the race.
“Despite poll after poll making it clear that the conservative rural working-class base was concerned about data centers and the impact of AI, too many politicians in Washington chose big AI’s money over their own base,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, an advocacy group pushing for democratic oversight of AI, said in a statement.
In data center ballot measures across nine states, voters rejected future construction plans, approved moratoriums, and called for greater consultation with and accountability to local communities. Ten states put forth more than 40 questions about data centers on local ballots, according to Ballotpedia, including 21 in Ohio alone. Questions ranged from outright moratoriums to rezoning questions to restrictions on development. Just one county appears to have allowed for more data center development on their ballot, according to Americans for Responsible Innovation president Brad Carson, who was tracking ballot developments throughout the night.
Tech companies appear to be smelling blood in the water. On the day of the midterms, The Hill reported that environmental groups and Big Tech companies were working together as part of a “Responsible Data Center Development Collaborative” to create a framework for data center development. McCoy calls this kind of collaboration the “right next step.”
Meanwhile, as the results rolled in, Musk posted on X, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

International sales on cult martial arts splatter comedy “African Kung-Fu Nazis,” its sequel and a behind-the-scenes documentary have gone to Hong Kong-based Cappu Films.
The deal, struck with filmmaker and producer Sebastian Stein of Humanmade Films, was unveiled on the sidelines of Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. It covers “African Kung-Fu Nazis I,” “African Kung-Fu Nazis II” and the feature documentary “African Kung-Fu Nazis – The Doc.” It applies only to rights and territories that are still open, and leaves deals already in place untouched.
Japanese distributor Transformer gave both features a theatrical run in Japan, opening the original in June 2021 and the sequel four years later in July 2025. Busch Media Group handled the first film’s German release on DVD, Blu-ray and VOD. The sequel played Sitges’ Brigadoon sidebar in 2025. In 2026 it went on to the Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival (BIFFF), Grossmann and Macabro, where it picked up an honorable mention.
Mixing kung fu action, gore, horror and dark comedy, the series takes its cues from vintage Hong Kong martial arts films and from Ghana’s independent filmmaking scene. In the first film, Ghanaian kung fu fighters square off against send-ups of wartime figures from Germany and Japan, among them Adolf Hitler, Hideki Tojo and “Horseman” Goering.
The sequel teams one-armed fighter Addo with Sek Tin to take on cyborg “Adolf Robotler,” who wants to become president of Ghana. Stein said the film, a Ghana-Japan-Germany production shot mostly in Ghana, was paid for largely through crowdfunding, with Japanese fans of the first film providing much of the backing.
“African Kung-Fu Nazis – The Doc” goes behind the camera on the original, following the independent shoot that started the franchise.
“With their love for Chinese kung fu, our Ghanaian heroes smash the threat of fascism,” said Stein, CEO of Humanmade Films. “Total freedom, beautiful madness. Because you won’t drink champagne if you don’t take a risk!”
Cappu and the filmmakers also plan a line of art-led merchandise, to be produced via sister company Winners Gallery and built on the franchise’s characters and look, as part of the international marketing push. Concepts and release plans have yet to be finalized.
“We love fiercely independent horror and cult films, and we want to support filmmakers who are doing something that is entirely their own,” said Janice Woo of Cappu Films. “There’s a real love of kung fu cinema in these films. We come from production ourselves, so we understand how much it takes to get a film like this made. We’re excited to work with Sebastian and help bring all three films to more audiences.”
Cappu also operates out of Beijing and handles select releases in its home market and mainland China. Its slate ranges from Tony Leung Chiu-wai crime thriller “Fox Hunt” to Shan Jiang’s “Ephemera,” a 2026 Tribeca Festival U.S. Narrative Competition premiere. The lineup also includes Carter Ward’s romance “Step Back, Doors Closing” and Francesco Lucente’s fantasy adventure “Sinbad,” which DNEG is co-financing and producing.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Donald Trump would like to change the subject
Who needs control of Congress when you have a ballroom?
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s midterms response is a shrug.
What happened? By now, you certainly know: Democrats won overwhelmingly in Tuesday’s midterm elections, and they won everywhere. The party will head into 2027 with commanding majorities in the House and the Senate, breaking two years of unified Republican control in Washington, DC.
The results are a sweeping repudiation of Trump, the Republican Party, and the first two years of his second administration. But you wouldn’t know it from the president’s only public appearance on Wednesday, which focused on his beloved East Wing ballroom.
How is Trump responding? To a surprising extent, he’s not. He blamed the loss on Republican candidates and his absence from the ballot in social media posts Tuesday night, but his public comments have been subdued, with none of the claims of election fraud that have become his hallmark.
One Trump adviser, according to CNN, said that Trump likely would not attempt to challenge the results (Alaska notwithstanding, potentially) because the scale of the Democratic victories was “too big to rig.”
On Wednesday, Trump gave remarks from inside the partially completed ballroom — dwelling on its size, the kitchen setup, and his choice of marble for the flooring — and signed his name on a steel beam. His only comments on the midterms came in response to questions from the press, including about the Iran war, which Vice President JD Vance has blamed for the GOP loss.
“I think it’s largely true,” Trump said, “but at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”
What’s the big picture? It’s pretty likely that we’ll see a few different versions of Trump’s response in the coming days, not to mention when Democrats actually take power in January — my colleague Astead Herndon described it on Wednesday as Trump’s “stages of grief.”
Whatever the next two years look like, though, his tepid response to a historic defeat makes one thing clear: Donald Trump’s time at the center of American politics is slipping away.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
Another result of Tuesday’s elections: More than a million low-income Texans could soon have access to healthcare, after Democratic victories in the state opened up the possibility of Medicaid expansion. You can read all about it from my colleague Dylan Scott here with a gift link.

For the last two years, the UK government has been telling the British public that the country could receive an economic boost of £400 billion, thanks to AI, a figure intended to calm fears that the technology would lead to sweeping job losses and even an economic crash.
But the UK AI minister admitted last week that figure was significantly higher than the government’s actual projections after it was revealed that assessment came solely from a report commissioned by Google, and that its own estimation of AI’s economic benefit was less than a third of that £400 billion figure.n
AI minister Kanishka Narayan, answering a parliamentary question on the issue, said that AI adoption and data investment could add £55 billion to £140 billion to the UK economy by 2030, bringing the central estimate to £120 billion. But even this “more recent assessment,” he said, was a “hugely uncertain” estimate.
Narayan said the £400b figure “was drawn from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First,” a British consultancy firm now referred to as PF Global.
Responding to WIRED’s questions about the difference between the figures, PF Global’s head of economics, Jonathan Dupont, said the disparity was partially because of what they saw as the government’s slow adoption of AI. “AI is a very fast moving technology, and, as we learn more, we inevitably have to update the assumptions lying behind our models. Compared to our older model, the numbers the government uses assume a much slower rate of adoption than looked possible back in our model that was created in 2023.”
Government departments and agencies used Google’s £400 billion figure for almost two years, under two governments. Ministers have had the lower estimate since at least November 2025, almost a year before this week’s admission, yet Skills England, a government agency responsible for apprenticeships, was still publishing the old figure four months later.
Nayaran’s parliamentary answer is the first recorded evidence WIRED could find of the government setting the two numbers side by side, or saying that the report was commissioned by Google. The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong.
Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, told WIRED: “The government is right to promote the potential for technology like AI to improve public services. However, these reports highlight one of the central barriers to delivering the digital transformation of public services my committee has identified: hype.
“Economic projects inevitably rely on assumptions, but overstating the benefits of technology risks undermining the case for change. The government needs to be realistic about what technology like AI can deliver and be transparent with the public about potential savings.”
PF Global highlighted more top-down adoption of AI and integration into civil service workflows as examples of how take-up could improve. “While we haven’t changed our view on the overall potential of technology, given the slower rate of adoption we’ve seen in practice, our central estimate for the amount of potential likely to be achieved by 2030 is much closer to the Government’s number—with growth ramping up in the next few years after that.”
Lord Holmes of Richmond, the Conservative peer who asked ministers in January 2025 about the origins of the £400 billion claim but did not receive a response, told WIRED: “It is unfortunate that the figure used repeatedly by the government, and then, unsurprisingly, by multiple other organizations has now been significantly and rightly adjusted. It would have been better for the government to clarify this much sooner and more directly.”
He added: “Robust data is critical, not least as billions of pounds of our money and how the government chooses to deploy it depend on it.”
The spat over these two numbers—£120 billion and £400 billion—is part of a wider debate over the line between government support and boosterism. Former technology minister Peter Kyle also used the £400 billion while promoting the benefits of AI, while many parliamentarians outside of government raised questions about potential issues around the technology.
“The government’s revised estimates for how much AI could add to the economy are welcome—but it’s concerning that they come after almost two years of ministers citing a figure from research that was paid for by Google,” Sumedha Deshmukh of the Ada Lovelace Institute told WIRED. “This reflects a wider pattern. Figures about AI that look precise often have assumptions and incentives built into them, and industry often funds or shapes the research behind them.
“The government should test the numbers it is given before it builds policy on them, fund independent research, and measure whether promised gains are delivered. It should always start by asking simple questions before it uses any number around economic or productivity gains from AI—where did it come from, what does it assume, and who actually benefits from a given figure?”
The Cabinet Office, the department responsible for AI in government and Google, were approached for comment.
PF Global said their work for Google continued but all research was independent and all judgments and assumptions were their own.

Block employees in the US who were hit in the company's latest round of cuts will receive at least 60 days of pay, plus severance.
Those workers are eligible for at least seven weeks of base pay, according to an internal FAQ document viewed by Business Insider, with an additional week of pay for every year an employee worked at Block.
The fintech company distributed the document as part of Block's second round of layoffs this year. It told some workers on Wednesday that it was eliminating their roles, according to an email seen by Business Insider. The exact scale of the cuts wasn't immediately clear.
A Block spokesperson declined to comment.
Affected US workers who sign a severance agreement will get another 30 days of pay without working, for a total of 90 days, the FAQ said. In terms of healthcare benefits, they will receive three months of COBRA premium coverage for themselves and enrolled dependents.
These workers will also receive a one-time $5,000 payment, which the company said was for transition assistance.
Employees outside the US would receive different severance packages depending on location, the document said.
The terms outlined in the 20-page FAQ document appear to be structured differently than those offered in February, when the company slashed more than 40% of its workforce. At the time, CEO Jack Dorsey said laid-off workers would receive 20 weeks of salary plus an additional week for each year at the company.
Adding the 90 days' pay without working and the minimum of seven weeks of severance is roughly equivalent to the 20 weeks of salary Block offered in February, before the additional payment based on tenure.
There are some differences in the other benefits. The February package included six months of healthcare coverage, whereas the company's latest FAQ says it will offer three months of COBRA premium coverage for US workers and their enrolled dependents.
Both rounds of cuts included a $5,000 payment, which Block referred to as transition assistance.
Eligible workers will also receive a prorated payment in place of an April 2027 retention bonus, according to the document.
The company said the benefits are contingent on workers signing — and adhering to — the separation agreement.
Block isn't the only tech firm making reductions. Canva this week said it would let go of 22% of its workforce as part of a reorganization. Affected employees are due to get at least six months' pay.
And at the website-building company Squarespace, which said it's cutting 19% of staff, workers will get at least 16 weeks of base pay plus added time based on tenure as well as benefits through May next year.
Unlike the prior reductions, which Dorsey said were due in part to advances in how much work AI could take on, the newest cuts didn't mention AI. Instead, in the email to staff, Block referred to "using better tools to handle routine tasks" and "refocusing our teams' time on complex cases and decisions."
The layoffs come after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter profits amid growth at Square, its seller-services business, and Cash App, its consumer financial services app.

The West Bengal Police on November 5 posted a message on X, calling for citizens to celebrate Diwali responsibly. The AI-generated poster showed a stray dog and two cats taking shelter from firecrackers. It said, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”
The post, which was made at 8:29 am, was however taken down within 3 hours. (Archive)
In recent years, campaigns highlighting the environmental impact of firecrackers and calling for restrictions during Diwali have increasingly been framed by a section of the Right wing as an affront to Hindu religious sentiments. The issue of air pollution, consequently, has often been recast as a communal debate, with calls for curbs on firecrackers portrayed as selective targeting of Hindu festivals.
In the same vein, several social media users took offence to Bengal police’s awareness post, claiming that it was a case of selective bias against Hindus. Users began commenting under the post, some of whom went as far as to tag chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, questioning why similar awareness campaigns were allegedly absent during Eid and Christmas.
Some of the comments are displayed in the gallery below. (A few of them contain abusive words. Reader discretion is advised).
Following the backlash, the post was deleted. West Bengal police offered no explanation or clarification as to why the post was removed. Many had anticipated that the West Bengal Police would backtrack on its awareness campaign as this incident forms part of a pattern of state authorities taking down posts on firecracker awareness ahead of Diwali following backlash.
Pattern of Deletion
Alt News had earlier reported that on October 25, Delhi Police had deleted an X post, which raised awareness about a cracker-free Diwali, within hours of posting it. On that occasion, too, social media users had predicted that the post would be removed soon.
Again, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a similar video featuring actress Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media handles. Both decisions came in the wake of social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters that these posts hurt the religious sentiments of Hindus. Justice G S Kulkarni of the Bombay high court then directed BMC to re-upload Mirza’s video, remarking “She (Dia Mirza) rendered a really really good message in terms of air pollution… These (opposing Mirza) are stray thoughts of very few people and we should avoid them…”
A video uploaded by AISA president Neha Bora calling for an environment-friendly Diwali was likewise condemned by the Hindutva brigade.
On November 4, actress Soni Razdan’s social media advocacy for a pollution-free Diwali was also derided by several users. “People can’t understand a simple message because they think every statement is about religion,” she retorted to an X post that had targeted her.
Then you are simply unable to see the woods for the trees. It’s not bursting crackers that is anti-national. What is anti national is the fact that you are contributing to the terrible air pollution. My goodness. No wonder we all can’t breathe. People can’t understand a simple message because they think every statement is about religion. It’s not. It’s about AIR. And children are struggling. So to make it simple for you – it is the irresponsible actions of people that seem to be anti national. To me. And should also be to you. Because it’s your children, everyone’s children irrespective of which religion they belong to., that are suffering. And so are the citizens of this country. I’m assuming that also includes you.
— Soni Razdan (@Soni_Razdan) November 5, 2026
Alt News also found that the official X handle of West Bengal Police had made similar awareness campaigns around Diwali, in both 2024 and 2025. These posts still exist.
