Russia and Ukraine trade airstrikes as reconstruction and security talks resume
Russia and Ukraine have traded damaging airstrikes as talks resume in Brussels to discuss Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia and Ukraine exchanged airstrikes overnight as talks were set to resume in Brussels on Thursday on Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and security guarantees once the fighting ends.
The latest Russian aerial barrage underscored the scale of the rebuilding task, as did the ongoing search for people missing beneath rubble after a deadly airstrike in southern Ukraine on Monday.
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at Russian targets. The Russian Defense Ministry said that its forces shot down nearly 500 drones overnight.
A Ukrainian attack killed five people and wounded 13 others on Thursday in Ukraine’s Russia-occupied Luhansk region, Kremlin-installed officials said.
The strike hit a bus traveling between the regional capital, Luhansk, and a nearby town, said Leonid Pasechnik, the region’s Moscow-backed leader. Further details weren't immediately available.
Meanwhile, rescue teams continued to search for more than 30 people believed trapped in the wreckage of a former school and a nearby shelter hit by Russian guided bombs on Monday.
The attack in Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, struck as residents waited for humanitarian aid. It was one of the deadliest strikes in the region since the full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 43 people have been confirmed killed. Efforts to identify some of the victims using DNA samples from relatives were continuing. Zelenskyy said in a message on X that one person who had been reported missing was found alive.
Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said that talks were continuing for a second day at NATO headquarters in Brussels focused on postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government's Western allies.
Umerov said that the discussions with officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the European Union and NATO were also being attended by the World Bank and the U.S. investment group BlackRock.
“We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote in an online post.
The Brussels meetings are taking place days before negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at trying to end the war. Late Wednesday, Zelenskyy said that he had held a 90-minute conversation with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
“The negotiations must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. “Ukraine is ready to take the necessary steps. Our proposals are clear, and we have given them to the American side.”
Kushner posted on X that talks are focused not only on “ending this terrible war, but on the broader security architecture needed to ensure that when the fighting stops, it never starts again.”
He paid tribute to Zelenskyy and his team's “constructive engagement and commitment to finding a path forward.”
In excerpts from an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, to be aired in full on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed hope that the Democratic Party's win in the U.S. midterm elections could usher in a new era of support for Ukraine.
“We have support from two parties — support from both parties. I am also grateful to the Republicans,” Zelenskyy said. He added that the Democrats “speak of renewing the ties between the U.S. and Europe, which have been somewhat lost in recent years. And that is very important to us.”
The European Commission on Thursday sent Ukraine 4.36 billion euros ($4.9 billion) as part of a 90 billion-euro ($101 billion) loan agreed in April by EU leaders to support the embattled nation.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the money will help Ukraine fund essential spending on defense and public services.
“As Russia continues its relentless attacks, Ukraine is about to start its fifth wartime winter,” she said. “And as efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine continue, so too does the EU’s unwavering support.”
Zelenskyy took to X to thank Europe, saying the money will help fund pressing needs “such as strengthening Ukraine’s energy resilience and procuring drones, electronic warfare, and air defense assets.”
Ukraine’s air defenses shot down or suppressed 105 of 128 Russian attack drones overnight and into early Thursday, while Russian strikes wounded four people in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv regions, Ukrainian officials said.
Russian drones struck six areas in the Dnipropetrovsk region, wounding three people in the city of Dnipro, regional administrator Oleksandr Hanzha said. A Russian attack on logistics infrastructure west of the capital, Kyiv, caused a fire and wounded a man, the State Emergency Service said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that its forces shot down 496 Ukrainian drones over 13 Russian regions overnight, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which was annexed by Russia, and the Black and Azov Seas.
More than 200 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, wounding one person, local governor Pavel Malkov said.
Malkov said that falling debris from the attack damaged power lines and sparked a fire at an industrial site. Russian media outlets later reported a blaze at Ryazan oil refinery, sharing pictures of plumes of smoke and the night sky glowing red.

Embraer pitches India-made C-390s to meet Asian demand for 500 military aircraft
Embraer sees India as a production and export hub for its C-390 Millennium, citing potential Asian demand for 500 military transport aircraft over 20 years.
Brazilian aerospace major Embraer sees the Indian Air Force’s push to modernise its transport fleet as an opportunity to establish C-390 Millennium production in India, with locally made aircraft potentially serving a wider Asian market that could require 500 planes of this class over the next 20 years, Embraer Defense & Security CEO Bosco da Costa Junior said on Friday.
Embraer and Mahindra Group are jointly bidding for the IAF’s medium transport aircraft (MTA) programme, targeting a potential ₹1 lakh crore contract for 60 aircraft.
“We believe we have the right platform, and see India as a strategic partner. We are not here just to sell 60 aircraft and return to Brazil. Embraer is looking at India as a production and export hub for the C-390 as 40-45% of the addressable market for this class of aircraft is here in Asia. That translates into a demand for roughly 500 aircraft over the next 20 years,” Costa Junior said in an interview with HT.
The remarks come three months after the government initiated the procurement of 60 transport aircraft for the IAF, inviting bids from five Indian companies: Mahindra Group, Tata Advanced Systems Limited, Adani Defence & Aerospace, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited and Reliance Defence.
The Indian firms are bidding for the programme in partnership with global OEMs (original equipment manufacturers).
The deadline for submitting bids is January 13, people aware of the matter said. The MTA contest aligns with the government’s Make in India initiative to boost self-reliance in the defence manufacturing sector. The winner must set up a production line for the aircraft in India.
The first 12 aircraft will be delivered in flyaway condition, with the rest manufactured in India. Under the MTA framework, planes built in India must have 40% indigenous content, and the contract must be executed within 11 years, the people said.
Embraer and Mahindra are considering setting up the first C-390 final assembly line outside Brazil in Nagpur if they secure the IAF contract.
“We are looking to build a complete C-390 ecosystem in Nagpur, including a state-of-the-art hangar, a highly automated aircraft assembly line, MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul) facilities, local manufacturing of aircraft structures, avionics, components and spares, system integration and supply chain development,” Costa Junior said.
The C-390 Millennium is a multi-mission military transport aircraft designed to perform a range of missions, including troop and cargo transport, airdrop operations, medical evacuation, search and rescue, firefighting and humanitarian missions. It has a payload capacity of up to 26 tonnes and is designed to operate from temporary or unpaved runways.
The IAF is looking for a new transport aircraft with an 18-to-30-tonne cargo-carrying capacity to meet its growing airlift needs. Brazil renewed its push for the C-390 under the MTA programme on the sidelines of the 18th Brics Summit in Delhi in September.
Tata Advanced Systems has teamed up with US firm Lockheed Martin, which has offered its C-130J Super Hercules aircraft for the MTA contest. The other three firms have not yet announced their partnerships for the project.
The IAF currently operates a fleet of 12 C-130J medium-sized airlifters, which have been extensively used for various missions, including supporting the military’s forward deployments in the Ladakh sector during the 2020-24 India-China military stand-off along the contested Line of Actual Control in eastern Ladakh.
The MTA is set to become only the second military aircraft to be manufactured in India by a private consortium, following the landmark C295 programme. Airbus and Tata Advanced Systems are jointly executing a ₹21,935-crore contract to equip the IAF with 56 C-295 aircraft.

How infant deaths in Keralam’s Attappady expose a deep-rooted health, social crisis
12 infants, including 10 tribals, have died in Attappady this year, sparking a political row as the State government orders an expert probe. Tribal activists say the crisis demands action beyond healthcare, addressing malnutrition, anaemia and deep-rooted social issues
Published - October 31, 2026 01:25 pm IST - PALAKKAD
In Attappady, maternal health remains a major concern. Anaemia among pregnant women continues to be widespread, while underweight mothers and low birth weight among newborns add to the risks (file image)
| Photo Credit: The Hindu
The deaths of 12 infants, 10 of them from tribal communities, in Attappady in Keralam in recent months have once again cast a spotlight on a child health crisis that has defied solutions for over a decade. While the State government has set an expert assessment in motion, tribal organisations maintain that the roots of the crisis run deeper than healthcare, demanding sustained action on nutrition, maternal health, landlessness and the wider socio-economic conditions of the community.
Figures cited by tribal activists show that 124 infants have died in the region since 2011. Since 2012, Attappady has also recorded around 300 abortions, 90 intrauterine deaths and two dozen stillbirths. The region came under particular scrutiny in 2013, when 47 tribal infants died. Tribal observers estimate that around 10 children have died annually over the years.

What new Kane deal means for England and the Premier League record
- Published
Harry Kane's decision to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich carries heavy significance for the Bundesliga giants, who have been celebrating his status as a Ballon d'Or winner, but also for England and the Premier League's record books.
Bayern have acted swiftly to secure the 33-year-old on a deal taking him through to 2029 after he was crowned the world's best player, ensuring England's captain and record goalscorer will spend the final peak years of a magnificent career at Allianz Arena.
Kane has written himself into Bayern legend since joining from Spurs for £86m in August 2023, scoring 102 goals in 102 Bundesliga matches, winning two league titles and three successive Golden Boot awards.
It is why Bayern could not contemplate his departure as other clubs eyed his next move - and why the announcement Kane is staying casts ripples far beyond Munich.
Does it mean Kane will never grace the Premier League again? And does it mean - far more enticingly - he has his sights set on two more major tournaments and two more chances to grasp the prize that has eluded him at international level?
Former England striker Chris Sutton told BBC Sport: "I certainly think, although you always have to factor fitness issues into all of this, that Harry is more than capable of carrying on for a few years yet, easily.
"People might say his game lacks a little bit of pace, but he's so strong in other areas. He is a world-class all-round player. His finishing isn't going to be affected in any way by his age. He can still link up play and his football brain is first class.
"I don't see his age being such a big deal. You think of pacy players over the years who rely on that part of the game then lose it as they get older. Harry is not one of those. He seems fit and at the peak of his powers with Bayern and England."
Kane's new contract expires shortly before his 36th birthday, certainly raising the prospect the player who left Spurs as the highest scorer in their history with 280 goals in 435 appearances may never grace the Premier League again.
His consummate professionalism, and apparent ability to develop into the complete player with age, means this can never be discounted.
The notion of an emotional return to Spurs at some point has often provided background noise, but now looks increasingly unlikely.
What it surely means is that Alan Shearer will remain the Premier League's highest scorer - who knows what will happen with Erling Haaland as Manchester City await punishment after being found guilty of breaching financial regulations they deny? - and out of Kane's reach.
Shearer scored 260 goals in 441 Premier League matches for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle United. Kane scored 213 times in 320 league games for Spurs.
With Kane still 47 short of Shearer's record, it would need a spectacular late-career flourish for him to eclipse the Geordie icon's tally to write another entry into the history books, which also have him as England's highest scorer with 91 goals from a record-equalling 125 caps.
What will be of huge interest to Thomas Tuchel - the coach who took him to Bayern and now leads England - is that Kane has delivered a clear indication that Euro 2028, to be played in the UK and Ireland, is firmly in his sights.
And, when this new deal expires, Kane is also only a year away from the 2030 World Cup, to be played in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with special centenary opening matches held in Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay.
This, of course, is a stretch given the inevitable rigours of age, but few who know Kane, who have watched him move to a new level at Bayern, would ever say never to such a driven personality, hiding fierce mental strength and a competitive instinct behind his humble 'anti-superstar' persona.
Sutton said: "Euro 2028 certainly shouldn't be a problem and who knows beyond that? If Harry has got players around him with pace and dynamism, as well as runners in and around him, then his football brain isn't going to change and he can still play a huge part.
"He's such a sharp, quick, thinker. He reads the game superbly, knows where his next pass is going and has shown an ability to drop deep and impact the game.
"Harry just seems to be getting better and more rounded with age. And as for age, just look at someone like Teddy Sheringham. He was playing and scoring goals for West Ham United in the Premier League in his 40s.
"Sheringham was an incredibly talented player with supreme intelligence. Harry Kane falls right into the same category.
"Ronaldo has just retired from international football with Portugal at 41, but he is a totally different player than Harry Kane. Harry is one who can drop a little bit deeper to use his incredible ability and range of passing.
"As well as that ability, it is about how Harry's football brain works as much as anything and that won't change with age."
And it is an argument, and a hope, that is even more pertinent as England still do not possess any other striker or forward who could be considered anywhere near Kane's class or potency.
"When you talk about 2028 or 2030, who are the English strikers coming through to challenge him to take him out of the team?" said Sutton. "There's no-one in his class or effectiveness, or anywhere near it."
What also plays into the argument that Kane cannot be ruled out of such long-term involvement is the manner in which he responded so superbly to what was a disappointing Euro 2024, not only as England lost in the final to Spain but because he looked a jaded shadow of his old self.
Kane looked so out of sorts there was a clamour for him to be replaced by Ollie Watkins, then at Aston Villa. He was substituted in all of England's knockout matches, including after only 61 minutes of that final loss to Spain in Berlin.
And yet, Kane still finished as the tournament's joint top scorer with three goals from seven games.
The notion of him being replaced with the stakes so high now is unthinkable, such is his peerless form and stature.
While Bayern are convinced their new investment in Kane's brilliance will be rewarded with further honours, Tuchel will hope it is motivation and inspiration to finally end the country's long wait for international glory.

Ravi Uppal, co-promoter of the Mahadev online betting app, has reportedly been arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Officials told news agency PTI that authorities in Dubai arrested the 46-year-old on the basis of an Interpol Red Notice issued against him at the request of Indian investigating agencies. According to the report, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Enforcement Directorate are now working to extradite Uppal back to India. This comes days after the extradition of fellow Mahadev app co-promoter Saurabh Chandrakar from Oman to India. A CBI team brought Chandrakar back after a court there permitted his extradition to India in connection with a money laundering case being investigated by the ED. Subsequently, a special court in Raipur, earlier this week, granted eight custody of Chandrakar to the CBI. Uppal’s arrest in the UAE marks a development in the ongoing ED probe into the betting platform. He was previously also detained in the UAE in 2023, but local investigating agencies reportedly subsequently found that he was in Australia. Agencies have reportedly also claimed that Uppal obtained a passport from Vanuatu, an island nation in the South Pacific, just like Chandrakar. The Mahadev Betting App Saga This comes nearly years after the Enforcement Directorate filed a chargesheet against Uppal in October 2023 in connection with the alleged Mahadev app betting scam. As per investigators, the platform operated from outside India through a network of franchised panels and branches, which enrolled users and facilitated illegal betting on cricket, football and other events. A probe by CBI revealed that the betting proceeds were allegedly routed through mule bank accounts and transferred overseas through hawala channels. Part of the money was allegedly paid to public servants to allow the syndicate to operate without hindrance. ED estimates the proceeds of crime in the Mahadev betting app case at around ₹6,000 Cr. Its investigation has also examined alleged links to senior politicians and bureaucrats in Chhattisgarh. In March, the directorate provisionally attached 20 properties with an estimated market value of nearly ₹1,700 Cr under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). These included 20 properties in Dubai and New Delhi, including villas and apartments. The ED alleges that these properties were acquired using illegal betting proceeds and held through entities controlled by Chandrakar and his associates. Overall, as of March, the ED has searched more than 175 locations, arrested 13 people, and attached or frozen assets worth around ₹4,336 Cr. The wider investigation has also examined alleged links involving EaseMyTrip cofounder Nishant Pitti and former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel. Both have denied wrongdoing.

Democrats have taken control of the House and the Senate in a blow to Donald Trump

Democrats inflicted a string of historic defeats against the Republicans to take control of both chambers of Congress.
The fate of Donald Trump’s final years in the White House will be majorly influenced by the midterm results, as his political opponents gain essential power over policymaking.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election, along with 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.
With the majority of preliminary results declared, Democrats have met high expectations, winning the Senate after a series of victories in former Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, Maine and Iowa.
The party has also regained control of the House of Representatives, which they last held in 2023, having flipped numerous seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey, Indiana and North Carolina.
Historic results have been seen in Texas, where James Talarico won, alongside Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Sherrod Brown in Ohio. It has been several decades since the Democrats held the Senate for any of these seats.
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff held his seat in Georgia, dashing Republican hopes of a victory in the state.
The 2026 midterm elections have been seen as a referendum on Trump’s second presidency, with Democratic candidates blaming the administration for the growing cost of living crisis and economic fallout from the Iran war, among other issues that are driving voters to the polls in record numbers.
Defensive Republicans, meanwhile, have sought to cast their opponents as too extreme.
Delivering his victory speech in Georgia, Senator Ossoff said: “Together, we’ve affirmed that our task is not just to contain one president’s wickedness, but to heal the brokenness beneath”.
“The American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck president Donald J. Trump,” he added.
Calling in to Fox News as results came in, Trump said that he thought the Democrats “did a good job”.
“They fought hard. They were, you know, they've been fighting for a long time. They've been fighting me for a long time,” he said.
The president signalled a willingness to work with Democrats for the last two years of his term but ruled out compromise on immigration and transgender rights.
He added: “The power of veto is one of the stronger powers that a president has, and they'll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them.”
Full results are not expected in the immediate hours after polls close; polls won’t close in Alaska until 1 a.m. Eastern, and election officials will continue processing ballots received through Election Day.
Potential Republican-led challenges and legal intervention from the Trump administration could drag results into the coming days and weeks ahead.
Preliminary results from the Associated Press will inform The Independent’s charts and maps of election results and the nation’s shifting political landscape.

Israel has shared intelligence with the United States claiming that Iran is considering the use of chemical weapons against its adversaries, triggering alarm among some American officials while drawing deep scepticism from others, The New York Times reported.
According to the NYT, Israeli intelligence agencies have told their American counterparts that Iran is moving rapidly to develop the technology needed to deploy chemical weapons through missiles or smuggle them into Israel and other countries for use in attacks.
The intelligence has also been shared with officials in Gulf countries. However, several regional officials questioned the credibility of the claims, suspecting that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government was attempting to persuade the United States and its partners to resume large-scale military operations against Iran.
The differing assessments have exposed divisions among American officials over the seriousness of the alleged threat, particularly as Washington and Tehran explore the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough while preparing for a potential resumption of hostilities.
Israeli officials have portrayed Iran's alleged chemical weapons threat as more urgent than its ambitions to develop nuclear weapons during recent conversations with US intelligence agencies and other officials over the past two weeks, the NYT reported, citing American officials.
According to the report, Israeli intelligence believes Tehran is accelerating efforts to develop the technology required to deploy chemical agents through ballistic missiles or covert operations.
Using drones to deliver chemical weapons is also considered a possibility.
Some American officials have viewed the intelligence-sharing exercise as part of a pressure campaign by Netanyahu's government to convince US President Donald Trump's administration to return to major combat operations against Iran.
Others, however, believe the warnings deserve serious consideration, particularly given recent concerns about Iran's preparations to attack American interests.
Iran has publicly denied possessing chemical weapons and previously dismissed such allegations as psychological warfare orchestrated by Israel and Netanyahu.
Israel has also briefed Gulf countries about its assessment that Iran is working to make chemical weapons operational. However, the regional governments reportedly expressed doubts about the claims.
A regional official told the NYT that Israeli officials presented their assessments without sharing supporting evidence. Gulf governments found the claims unconvincing and questioned whether Iran was actually developing plans to deploy chemical weapons.
Even among officials briefed on the latest intelligence, there are differing assessments about how quickly Iran could deploy chemical weapons and how effectively such weapons could be used.
According to the NYT, weapons experts and US officials believe that mounting a chemical weapon on a ballistic missile may not be particularly difficult. However, ensuring that the weapon effectively disperses a chemical agent presents a much bigger technical challenge.
Smuggling a chemical bomb across an international border would also involve significant operational difficulties.
The report noted that US intelligence agencies have monitored Iran's chemical weapons activities for years. Chemical weapons are prohibited under international law.
The intelligence disclosures come as the United States and Iran remain in a prolonged standoff after eight months of war, with both sides exploring diplomatic possibilities while preparing for renewed military confrontation.
Netanyahu is also facing domestic political uncertainty after failing to secure a clear path to forming a government in elections last week.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.
While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.
Point spreads
Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.
There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged.
The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable.

Keeper Owono 'would never intentionally hurt anyone'
- Published
Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and has been "deeply affected" by the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, his team-mate said on Wednesday.
Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second-division match on Monday.
The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all European games this week.
Writing on social media, Andorra centre-back Lautaro Spatz said Owono was devastated.
He paid tribute to De Miguel but added: "I also want to say a few words about my team-mate, goalkeeper and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened.
"Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
- Football world mourns Tenerife striker De Miguel 
  - Published14 hours ago
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.
The Equatoguinean Football Federation said in a statement on Tuesday the 25-year-old was going through a "situation of profound sorrow and grief".
Period of mourning
On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.
Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.
The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.
Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".
"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the statement.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and fintech startups against the growing trend of cyberattackers using AI agents for financial frauds. In an advisory issued on November 3, the National Cybercrime Threat Analysis Unit (NCTAU), under the I4C, flagged that attackers were exploiting unpatched software and misconfigured internet-facing servers to gain access to financial infrastructure. The cybersecurity agency also said that it has unearthed multiple “individual” cases, where malicious agentic AI systems were exploiting compromised financial systems to undertake unauthorised transactions running into crores of Rupees. Describing the modus operandi of these AI-led cyberattacks, the agency noted that perpetrators exploit unpatched software to compromise banking systems. Customer-facing complaint interfaces can also serve as potential entry points, added I4C. Once inside, NCTAU noted that attackers potentially target automated fund disbursement systems and APIs used for payments and transfers. The agency added that these cyberattackers then route funds through mule accounts across different banks and quickly move to withdraw the proceeds of the crime via IMPS and NEFT. The perpetrators then delete records and hide their tracks so that investigation becomes difficult, added the NCTAU. As such, the agency has advised financial institutions to take the following measures: Implement CERT-In’s critical advisories “urgently” on payment and disbursement APIs as well as AI agents Report cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours, and to RBI as well in the cases of banks or NBFCs Test payment APIs and strengthen customer-facing infrastructure Set transaction limits, verify beneficiary details and monitor sudden changes in transaction speeds, volumes and patterns Ensure KYC and approval checks are completed before funds are transferred Improve coordination between security, transaction monitoring and IT teams Conduct authorised red-team exercises to test how quickly security and payment controls respond to machine-speed attacks The warning highlights how AI is accelerating the threat of cyber fraud for financial services firms. At the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in September, both Prime Minister Narendra Modi and RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra had urged fintechs to bolster cybersecurity and strengthen consumer trust. At the same event, National Payments Council of India (NPCI) MD and CEO Dilip Asbe had also called on banks and payments companies to invest in AI to combat cyber threats. In line with this, CERT-In had also issued a critical advisory last month, raising concerns over cyberattackers using publicly-available agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions into Indian entities. The advisory follows disclosures by global AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic about their agents taking unauthorised actions during internal cybersecurity evaluations.

The Delhi High Court has given the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the Delhi government’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) two weeks to submit a joint inquiry report on the medical qualifications of two doctors accused of mishandling a child during treatment.
Justice Neena Bansal Krishna passed the order on October 30 while hearing a contempt petition filed by the child’s mother, Sapna Jain, on behalf of her minor son.
According to the petition, the child suffered severe brain damage “after being mishandled by two unqualified doctors (misrepresenting as super-specialists) in the Neonatal ICU of Fortis Hospital, Shalimar Bagh”.
The petition claims that the child is now in a permanent vegetative state and suffers from West Syndrome, epilepsy and cerebral palsy. It also states that he continues to experience severe pain and suffering.
In March 2025, the High Court had called for affidavits clarifying whether the qualifications claimed by the two doctors “are qualifications entitling these Respondents (doctors) to undertake specialisation practice in this country.”
In May 2026, the court further directed the NMC Secretary and the DGHS to conduct a joint inquiry into the doctors’ qualifications and submit a report within eight weeks.
However, the fresh contempt petition alleged that the deadline of July 24, 2026, passed without the authorities submitting the report or seeking an extension from the court.
“The matter concerns the qualifications of doctors treating critically ill newborns. The NMC, being the statutory regulator, is duty-bound to ensure transparency and accountability, and its continued failure to place a clear and conclusive report before this Court raises serious questions regarding its fairness and credibility and that of its officers. The DGHS has likewise failed to discharge the joint duty cast upon it by this Court,” the plea said.
The court has posted the case for hearing on December 16.

It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.
Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.
Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.
"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.
"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.
Blue wins, red losses
In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)
In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.
A big recruiting effort
Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.
The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.
"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.
Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.
Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.
"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."
A key vote, a damaging investigation
Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.
During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."
Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.
In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.
All the way back to 1776
Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.
"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."
In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."
The new count
To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.
In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.
In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.
Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."
He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says
A health policy shake up?
Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.
Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.
"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."
Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.
"I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."
Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

Earlier this year, Patrick Woodard had to have a talk with one of the hundreds of clinicians that work at Monument Health, where he is chief information officer. The South Dakota and Wyoming-based health system had decided to block access to OpenEvidence, the popular free artificial intelligence tool, and Woodard had gotten a few objections.
One of them, Woodard recounted, was from a super user. This doctor was storing more than a hundred patient records inside OpenEvidence, and feeding them to the artificial intelligence tool for help making medical decisions. That would have to end, Woodard told him.
In the last year, free chatbots built to answer clinician questions — including OpenEvidence, Doximity Ask, and ChatGPT for Clinicians — have grown in popularity. Hundreds of thousands of doctors use the tools, in part, because they claim to be compliant with the federal health data privacy law HIPAA, allowing users to share a patient’s protected health information directly with the AI after signing an agreement. That assurance is meant to address one potential risk of the technology, while making it more valuable day-to-day.

A 47-year-old woman in California has admitted to defrauding her employer of almost $18 million ( approximately ₹170 crore) over a period of 10 years, using the stolen money to finance an extravagant lifestyle involving luxury shopping, private jet journeys, and expensive home renovations. Lizbeth Sherman, a resident of El Dorado Hills, pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud charges on Monday, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California. The woman spent the money on designer handbags, Rolex watches, luxury holidays and other high-value purchases. Sherman's alleged fraud began in 2015 when she took up a position as an executive assistant to a retired venture capitalist from the San Francisco Bay Area. As part of her responsibilities, she was given access to her employer's bank account to manage credit card payments. However, she gradually misused this access to divert large sums of money towards her personal expenses. Between September 2015 and May 2025, she repeatedly transferred funds to cover her own credit card bills, prosecutors said. “Between September 2015 and May 2025, Sherman abused this access and stole nearly $18 million from her employer in order to pay off her own extravagant credit card expenses,” federal prosecutors said. The stolen money enabled Sherman to make expensive purchases and maintain a lavish lifestyle for years. Her spending reportedly included designer handbags from Louis Vuitton, luxury watches, expensive holidays and private jet journeys. She also spent a substantial amount on vehicles and renovations to her $2 million home in El Dorado Hills. “In this manner, Sherman spent tens of thousands of dollars on luxury handbags, Rolex watches, resort-level vacations, private jet travel, vehicles, and improvements to a $2 million residence in El Dorado Hills.” Over time, Sherman also began selling some of the luxury products she had purchased using her employer's money through online marketplaces. This allowed her to convert the expensive purchases into cash. “Sherman began reselling designer products that she bought with the employer’s money on online platforms, thus converting her credit card purchases into cash,” the release explained. According to prosecutors, she earned approximately $450,000 through one such resale platform last year. The investigation took another turn in December 2025, when law enforcement officials searched Sherman's residence and recovered more than 1,500 luxury products. Many of these items were reportedly in excellent condition, with their original packaging and tags still intact. “more than 1,500 luxury items, most in mint condition with original packaging and tags intact, stored and displayed throughout the residence.” During the search, officers discovered several Louis Vuitton handbags in one wardrobe, while another contained a “display case full of handbags made of exotic furs”. Additional designer bags were found in different parts of the property. Investigators also recovered expensive wine bottles, Christian Louboutin boots and several Rolex watches. Following her guilty plea to federal wire fraud charges, Sherman faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison and a fine of up to $250,000. Perplexity has launched Teammates, a set of always-on AI agents meant to own ongoing work, putting it in the same race as OpenAI's Dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet.
What Perplexity Teammates does
Each Teammate can be given a role, a standing brief and rules for when to bring the user in, according to Perplexity's product page. They carry over projects, skills and memory from Perplexity Computer, the company's system that deploys agents on a user's device. They also run on automations to keep work moving.
Every Teammate gets one persistent thread in the app's sidebar, and Teammates can work with each other. They can also follow up with colleagues in Slack, Perplexity said. Each one has its own desktop and browser, using the same plugins and permissions the user has installed.
Perplexity gives sample jobs including running ad campaigns, acting as an on-call engineer who investigates alerts and opens fix requests, and doing legal research. CEO Aravind Srinivas said on X that Perplexity expects organisations to eventually have hundreds of Teammates working for each person.
Perplexity Teammates: Availability and pricing
Teammates is available now on the web for subscribers of the $200-a-month Max plan. Perplexity says Max subscribers get free Teammate usage for a promotional period. After that, Teammates draw on the credits already included in the plan. Mobile and desktop versions are coming soon.
How it compares with OpenAI's Dots
OpenAI launched Dots on September 29 at its DevDay conference, powered by its GPT-6 Astra model. Each dot has its own cloud computer and browser and reaches more than 4,000 apps through OpenAI's plugins. OpenAI calls them 'remarkably capable, always-on agents built to handle everything'. Dots are available to Pro and Business Premium users in eligible markets.
How it compares with Claude Duet
Anthropic opened a research preview of Duet on October 21, according to Implicator, though some outlets date it October 22. It is a standalone app for professionals and small-business owners, with a daily briefing and tasks ranging from scheduling to building forecasts and web apps. The Standard and KSL both carried those details.
Access is limited to US Claude Pro and Max subscribers through a waitlist. Anthropic has said Duet checks connected accounts every few hours rather than continuously. The company has also said it can misjudge urgency and is less suited to personal errands such as booking tickets.

Ireland captain Stirling out of Namibia series
- Published
Ireland captain Paul Stirling will miss the final two games of his side's one-day international series in Namibia after fracturing his finger.
The 36-year-old sustained the injury while fielding during his side's loss in the third ODI on Tuesday, a result that leaves his side trailing their hosts 2-1 in the five-match series.

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.
