'A smack in the teeth' - warned coach to work at international youth event
- Published
A gymnastics coach who received a formal warning from British Gymnastics following an investigation into allegations including fear-based coaching and controlling practices is coaching at an international youth competition this weekend, BBC Sport has learned.
Clare Hague, head coach at Dronfield Gymnastics Academy near Sheffield, has travelled with English Gymnastics to coach at the Horizon Cup in Greece.
Complainants from two separate investigations into Hague and her club have told the BBC the decision is a "smack in the teeth" and "adds salt in the wound" for those who have had the courage to speak up about their concerns.
Documents seen by the BBC list fear-based coaching and emotional harm, controlling and restrictive practices, punitive attendance policies and psychological impact on children as some of the concerns considered in a recently concluded investigation.
The outcome letter, also seen by BBC Sport, states that British Gymnastics upheld a number of the concerns raised, issuing Hague and Dronfield Gymnastics Academy with a formal warning lasting two years - alongside monitoring and development measures.
The governing body did not share with the complainants which specific concerns had been upheld.
While Hague did not respond directly to a request for comment, Dronfield Gymnastics Academy shared a statement with the BBC stating the club co-operated "openly, fully and with complete transparency" with the investigation.
"We are pleased the investigation found no serious issue for Dronfield to address and that British Gymnastics received positive reports from members about their experience at the club. Following the concerns raised, the club has worked proactively and positively alongside British Gymnastics to see where improvements can be made so that a positive experience is the case for everyone," it said.
Hague, who is also squad co-ordinator for Yorkshire Women's Artistic Gymnastics, was announced by English Gymnastics as a coach for the Horizon Cup while she was still under investigation.
The Horizon Cup is an international artistic gymnastics competition for junior and pre-junior gymnasts aged 11-16.
English Gymnastics is an affiliated home country association under British Gymnastics and manages some regional and national programmes, including selection for Team England at the Commonwealth Games.
One complainant, speaking anonymously for fear of the repercussions for her daughter in the local gymnastics community, alleged to the BBC that they had raised concerns some gymnasts at Dronfield Gymnastics Academy regularly felt afraid to ask to go to the toilet - resulting in some wetting themselves and others choosing not to drink during sessions.
Allowing gymnasts opportunities to drink water throughout training and to go to the toilet at the earliest available opportunity was one of a number of safeguarding rules introduced by British Gymnastics in 2023 to stop practices it said were "on the fringes of abuse".
"We tell our kids to tell a trusted adult when something's wrong," the complainant told the BBC.
"My daughter had the courage to say something to try and protect the next child. I don't want the lesson she walks away with from this to be that there's no point in speaking up because nothing happens."
A complainant in another investigation into Hague, in 2022, alleged to the BBC their daughter endured years of emotional and physical abuse at Dronfield Gymnastics Academy. The outcome letter of that investigation, also seen by the BBC, said the coaches would be offered further training.
"I didn't have faith in the system in 2022 because it was notorious that the system was not working… I did have hope that things had changed but it's disappointing to know that the outcome effectively is the same," the complainant said.
That investigation concluded just months after an independent report - the Whyte Review - described systemic physical and emotional abuse within gymnastics in Britain and found wellbeing and welfare had "not been at the centre of British Gymnastics' culture".
The review made 17 recommendations focused on safeguarding and welfare, complaints handling, standards and educations, and governance and oversight, prompting the governing body to double its spending on welfare and safe sport to about £1m a year.
In a statement, British Gymnastics told BBC Sport they cannot comment on the specifics of individual cases but said every concern is treated "in a way appropriate to the nature of the case".
"We have a duty to all those involved to ensure that outcomes are based on a fair, balanced and thorough assessment of all information from any relevant people, with a full context and understanding of the situation and consideration of all perspectives," it said in a statement.
"We can be categoric that if we considered a member to be a risk they would be removed from our sport.
"With regards to Dronfield, it's important to highlight we have heard positive reports from members about their experience there. From any concerns raised, the club is proactively and positively working with us to see where improvements can be made so that positive experience is the case for everyone."
But campaigners argue cases such as this raise "alarming" questions about how concerns are identified, monitored and addressed, and challenge the efficacy of offering retraining for coaches who have had complaints against them upheld on more than one occasion.
"Where there are multiple complaints over multiple years, we cannot understand how it's possible that coaches are repeatedly being given retraining instead of adequate sanctions to get them out of the sport, because they're proving consistently they are inappropriate coaches to be working with children," Claire Heafford, chief executive of campaign group Gymnasts for Change, told BBC Sport.
British Gymnastics began publishing the names of banned and expelled coaches in 2023 as part of its 'Reform 25' programme, but Heafford claims this is "meaningless" as it does not extend to those who have had sanctions against them.
"If you're the parent of an athlete at the moment, you have no way of knowing whether the coach coaching your child has had previous complaints or sanctions against them," she said.
"That is an awful situation for parents and athletes to be in and in this case, it proves that the current system is continuing to put children in harm's way."

Supreme Court ends distinction between detention and arrest, says 24-hour clock starts when liberty is curtailed
SC made clear that the 24-hour deadline is sacrosanct and even a person detained for search and seizure must be produced before a magistrate within that period.
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that law enforcement agencies cannot circumvent the constitutional protection against prolonged custody by keeping a person in detention without formally showing an arrest, holding that the mandatory 24-hour period for producing an individual before a magistrate begins from the moment his liberty is curtailed, irrespective of when the arrest is officially recorded.
Rejecting attempts by some high courts to draw a distinction between detention and arrest, the court held that there could be no artificial “buffer period” during which a person’s liberty could be curtailed without triggering the safeguards under Article 22(2) of the Constitution.
The apex court made clear that the 24-hour deadline is sacrosanct and that even a person detained for search and seizure must be produced before a magistrate within that period.
The endeavour of several high courts, including Orissa, Kerala and Madras, to create a distinction between detention and arrest is highly problematic and wholly unwarranted, noted a bench of justices Ujjal Bhuyan and AS Chandurkar.
“There is nothing like a temporary disruption in liberty and any such interpretation is absolutely unconstitutional. There cannot be an artificial distinction between arrest and detention for creating a buffer period,” said Justice Bhuyan while reading out the operative portion of its judgment.
The case
The judgment arose from appeals filed by four persons arrested in a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, involving the seizure of 11.03 kg of yaba tablets in Tripura. The four were detained on September 29, 2025, at 2 pm during search and seizure operations but were formally shown as arrested only at 11 am the following day.
The bench held that they ought to have been produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of their detention at 2 pm on September 29. Their continued detention without judicial oversight for about 18 hours violated Article 22(2)and warrants their immediate release.
The Tripura high court had rejected their bail pleas, holding that the stringent twin conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act had to be satisfied before granting bail in a case involving a commercial quantity of contraband. It had also rejected their challenge to the alleged breach of arrest procedure under Section 36 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
What the ruling settles
The ruling settles an important question concerning the reach of Article 22(2), which mandates that a person arrested and detained in custody must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court. By holding that the constitutional clock starts ticking from the moment a person’s liberty is effectively curtailed, the court has taken away the discretion of investigating agencies to decide when the period of judicial oversight should begin merely by choosing when to formally record an arrest.
“The words 'arrest' and 'detained' under Article 22(2) are conjunctive and must be read together. The period of 24 hours shall start from the very moment a person is detained, and the person must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours,” Justice Bhuyan said.
The court also rejected the proposition that a brief period of detention before formal arrest could be treated as a temporary or permissible interruption of liberty, holding that such an interpretation would dilute the fundamental protection guaranteed by the Constitution.
“A statute, special or otherwise, cannot be a guide to the Constitution. It has to be the other way round. The interpretation has to be in a manner that upholds the fundamental right,” said the bench, adding that detention of a person for search and seizure beyond 24 hours runs contrary to Article 21, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.
The bench specifically disapproved of the judgments of the Orissa high court in Aryaman Pattanaik (2025), the Kerala high court in Arun K Thomas (2026), and the Madras high court in Kannan (2025), which had allowed the period preceding formal arrest to be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline.
The court underscored that the constitutional safeguard was particularly important in the context of custodial violence, which often takes place when individuals are kept in police custody without being formally shown as arrested.
“The endeavour of this court is to eliminate custodial violence, which often takes place when a person is detained and not shown as formally under arrest. Custodial violence is unfortunately a recognised truth acknowledged by this court in several past judgments and incidents, including the Bhagalpur blinding case,” it said.
The bench further directed that the 24-hour period would commence from the date and time at which a person's liberty is curtailed, including when the person is intercepted by law enforcement authorities. No period spent in custody before the formal recording of arrest can be excluded, except the time genuinely necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the magistrate.
The bench also said that any detention without warrant must be for a reasonable period and that the magistrate receiving the detained person must specifically record the exact date and time from which the person’s liberty was curtailed and examine whether the 24-hour constitutional deadline had been observed. In the event of a breach, the person would have to be released.

Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'
- Published
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

A 22-second-long clip shared by X user Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) showing a massive crowd in a large open area went viral on November 1.
Thottathil posted the video with the caption, “Early in the morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed #ChaloDilli,” thus claiming that the crowd had gathered for the INDIA’s bloc’s rally on November 1 to protest against electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Early morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed ✊🏼 🔥
#ChaloDilli https://t.co/oM5kSpCNoH
— Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) November 1, 2026
The post by Thottathil, who was till recently a social media manager of Kerala Congress, amassed over 243,000 views and was reshared over 1,400 times. (Archive)
Congress leader Harish Rawat, too, shared the video on Instagram, claiming that the visuals were from the November 1 protest rally.
View this post on Instagram
Various other X handles posted the same 22-second clip, claiming that they are visuals from the ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally held on November 1. A few of them are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
In the comments of the video posted by Vijay, X users were quick to point out that the video was not from the November 1 ‘Chalo Dilli’ protest, and instead was from another rally held at an earlier date.
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on December 14, 2025.
This video, captioned “‘वोट चोरी’ के खिलाफ जनसैलाब 🔥🔥” (A public outpouring against “vote theft”), was uploaded during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests of December 2025.
View this post on Instagram
The comparison of certain keyframes of both videos reveals stark similarities, including the backdrop, the size of the crowd, a flag being waved in the front, and even a blue tent visible in the clip. See below:
A deeper dive revealed that Congress leader Harish Rawat had himself shared the video during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests on December 14, 2025. He has now shared the same clip again as scenes from the INDIA bloc rally of November 1, 2026.
To sum up, the viral clip with the massive crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan shared by Thottathil is an old clip from the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhoro” protests that was organised by Congress in December last year. Several users have falsely presented it as visuals from the recent ‘Chalo Dilli’ march on November 1.

The leader of a German conservative party is found dead at a Berlin hotel
Hubert Aiwanger, leader of a conservative party influential in Bavarian politics, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel
BERLIN -- Hubert Aiwanger, the leader of a conservative party that has become a mainstay of Bavarian politics and sought to expand its influence across Germany, has been found dead at a Berlin hotel.
Berlin police and prosecutors said the body of Aiwanger, who was Bavaria's deputy governor and the southern state's economy minister, was found in his hotel room in the center of the capital on Wednesday evening. An investigation into the cause of death was opened.
German news agency dpa reported, without naming sources, that the 55-year-old Aiwanger had planned to make a speech Wednesday afternoon at the opening of a Berlin office of his party, the Free Voters, but pulled out of the event for health reasons.
Aiwanger had been the party's leader in Bavaria since 2006 and its national leader since 2010.
The combative politician with a strong regional accent and a populist touch made his party a serious rival to Bavaria's long-dominant Christian Social Union, which is part of the center-right bloc that currently leads Germany. On his watch, it entered the state legislature in Munich in 2008. Ten years later, when the CSU lost its majority in the state legislature, it entered Bavaria's government as the junior coalition partner.
Shortly before Bavaria's 2023 election, Aiwanger faced a furor that started with allegations — denied by the politician — that he was responsible for an antisemitic flyer when he was a high school student 35 years earlier. The Free Voters emerged unscathed from the election, gaining support and remained part of the state government.
Aiwanger's party has made only limited inroads outside Bavaria and he wasn't able to lead it into the national parliament.
Bavarian governor Markus Söder wrote on X that “the sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy.”
Aiwanger is survived by his partner, Free Voters politician Tanja Schweiger, and two children.

Amid the India-China standoff in Arunachal Pradesh (here, here), a video purportedly showing Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here). He claims that the India-China border tensions are not a major concern and that the government is fully supporting the Indian Army by providing adequate funds. The concerns raised by some soldiers over the government’s support are dismissed, and the clashes between the two neighbouring countries are described as minor, with trade relations continuing between them. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army amid the India-China standoff in Arunachal Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video has been manipulated using AI. The original video, published by ANI on 26 October 2026, shows Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father. He made no remarks criticising the Indian Army. PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the viral video was AI-manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We did not find any credible reports confirming that Union Minister Rajnath Singh made such statements as claimed in the viral video.
After conducting a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video, we found that the news agency ANI published the original video on 26 October 2026. However, in the original video, Rajnath Singh is heard expressing shock and disappointment over Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father in Patna. He criticises the Congress for defending Kharge’s remarks instead of acknowledging the mistake and expressing regret. The original audio has been replaced with a fabricated audio track. We also reviewed the full original video and found that Rajnath Singh made no remarks criticising the Indian Army.
We also noticed certain inconsistencies in the viral video. An unnatural rhythm in the speech and variations in tone are prominently seen. On verifying the video’s audio using Hive AI and Resemble AI, we found it to be a deepfake.
Further, the Press Information Bureau (PIB) Fact Check issued a clarification on 31 October 2026, debunking the viral video and confirming that it had been manipulated using AI.
To sum up, this viral video of Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army is AI-Manipulated.

Since Tuesday night, the obituaries for the MAHA movement have been piling up fast: “RFK Jr and MAHA Suffer Brutal Election Night Wipeout,” wrote the Daily Beast. Midterms could be the “‘death knell’ of the MAHA-Trump alliance,” according to USA Today. Even STAT reported “MAHA mowed down.”
No doubt it was a brutal night for MAHA-allied-candidates. STAT counts at least 11 who lost, including Ken Paxton in Texas, backed by a MAHA super PAC; Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who signed MAHA-backed legislation into law; and Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, a founding member of Congress’s MAHA Caucus (and a physician). Nowhere was the defeat more pronounced than in Iowa, where MAHA-aligned PACs poured in more than $1.5 million to support Republican Zach Lahn for governor, only to see him lose by double digits.
But while the MAHA political movement suffered an electoral wipeout, the grassroot movement’s goals of preventing chronic disease, reducing pesticides, and fighting for healthier food and water were strikingly similar to the health agendas championed by winning Democratic candidates, including Democrats Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s next senator, and Rob Sand, the next governor of Iowa.
And many voters appear to identify with the movement. Liz Hamel, KFF’s senior vice president and director of public opinion and survey research, tells us that her organization’s analysis of a midterm voter poll found that 30% of voters told surveyors they support the MAHA movement, including 22% who said they strongly support MAHA.
But as pollsters piece together what was behind the results, one verdict is clear: Only 21% of voters said the Trump administration is making the nation healthier.
In our conversations with grassroots MAHA supporters, many have told us the alliance with Trump never made sense to them, that it was an opportunistic grab for votes from the jump. Discontent has been building for months. We hear it on our podcast and in conversations with supporters all the time. The frustration was recently crystallized in a scorecard produced by a group of MAHA faithful that concluded that the administration partially kept just five of its promises to MAHA — and broke 37. Tiffany Cianci, one of the report’s authors, told us on the podcast this week, “I actually think the outcome on Tuesday was the inevitability of a bunch of self-inflicted wounds.”
Since Tuesday night, MAHA supporters have told us they aren’t done — far from it. But yes, many are looking for new allies. Which means Democrats, as they take over Congress, may have an opportunity to bring a new group into their tent.
There are some signs they will. In September, a House Democratic working group co-led by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sketched out a health agenda with a section titled “Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families.” Along with calls to “protect vaccine recommendations from political interference and restore unlawfully withheld NIH funding,” the proposal calls for blocking liability shields for glyphosate makers, setting stronger infant formula safety rules, and closing a loophole that lets companies declare their own food additives safe. Ocasio-Cortez has been meeting with MAHA grassroots leaders for months.
Similarly, Democratic Sen. Cory Booker gave an impassioned speech in April at the People vs. Poison Rally on the steps of the Supreme Court, as the justices heard a case over glyphosate and health liability. Booker stood alongside key MAHA grassroots leaders and supporters, decrying pesticide immunity shields.
It seems logical that MAHA and the Democrats would find each other. MAHA and MAGA were always the stranger alliance. Holding industry accountable on behalf of individual and environmental health is a bread-and-butter Democratic issue. 
Yet recently on health, Democrats have more often been seen as the defender of Obamacare or institutional medicine. To be clear, access to affordable care is the cornerstone of health and is perpetually under threat. But in the meantime, fighting for people’s health against industrial pollution of America’s air and water or pumping out unhealthy food has not been the defining rallying cry for the party in recent years. As Booker put it this year, “A movement called MAHA caught fire in the vacuum we left behind.”
Despite big differences over health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and vaccine policy, Booker, along with Democrats Chellie Pingree and Jim McGovern, have been working with MAHA on legislation on regenerative farming and healthy food. They’ve created real bonds with MAHA grassroots leaders and staunch Kennedy allies such as Zen Honeycutt and Kelly Ryerson. The latter told us, “My Democratic heroes on the pesticide and farming issues are Pingree, McGovern, and Booker. But they have been pretty lonely when bringing forth policy change.” In describing her conversations with reporters and organizers about MAHA, Cianci told us: “I talk more about Cory Booker, and Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie than I do about any of the Republicans that claimed MAHA in this election.”
As for the profoundly divisive issue of vaccines, Rep. Chellie Pingree has recounted telling Honeycutt she’d work with her on pesticides, PFAS (better known as “forever chemicals”), and school lunches, but not on vaccines or 5G. In other words, Pingree found a way to work with someone on issues they agree on, while setting aside ones they don’t.
These areas of potential Democratic and MAHA alignment would appear to be popular with the broader public. KFF found in April that 75% of Americans say there isn’t enough regulation of chemical additives in food, and 64% say the same of pesticides. A 2025 poll by the progressive firm Navigator Research found more than 80% of Democrats, Republicans, and independents want corporate polluters held accountable.
Of course, the change in power in Washington will usher in a season of accountability. Democratic Senate newcomer Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who just pulled off a stunning victory in South Carolina, has said that impeaching and removing Kennedy is one of her top goals, calling Kennedy her “professional archnemesis.” Abdul El-Sayed, an M.D. who worked in public health, told us he sees Kennedy as a “grifter” who needs to be held accountable.
Democrats can and should exercise oversight of the federal health agencies and the White House, including potential hearings with Kennedy. They have serious questions about disruptions to vaccine policy, the response to measles outbreaks, and the upending of scientific research infrastructure.
But when it comes to health, if hearings are all that come out of this blue wave, it will be seen as a big missed opportunity. Voters expect the new Congress to fight for real change that will improve their lives, not just be locked in partisan investigations for the next two years.
Honeycutt told us efforts to impeach Kennedy would be a “colossal mistake.” She warned, “We cannot abide by people who are trying to get rid of the only person in this administration who has vowed to die with his boots on protecting the health and safety of our children.” Responding to a post by Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks calling for Kennedy to “resign or be fired,” Vani Hari, the healthy food activist known as “The Food Babe,” responded: “Dear Democrats — This is not how you win a coalition or work together. This is how you waste time while our children continue to get sicker than any developed nation.”
None of this will be easy. Among many MAHA supporters, loyalty to Kennedy runs deep. Kelly Ryerson told us she would still work with Democrats who wanted to oust Kennedy, but she thinks they are mistaken about him. She says she wishes there was equal Democratic fervor for impeaching EPA Secretary Lee Zeldin, whom she believes deserves to be hauled before Congress.
Many MAHA supporters describe to us their deep anger toward Democrats over the party’s treatment of Kennedy back in the 2024 election primary and alignment with what they saw as public health and government overreach during the pandemic. Many continue to perceive the left as elitist, condescending, and too connected to the corporations they see as corrupting the very systems of regulation Democrats have long supported.
And even if Democrats and MAHA align and pass legislation in the House, Senate Republicans could filibuster, and President Trump has already talked about his ultimate veto pen. Democrats also have their own stated priorities, such as trying to undo Medicaid cuts now kicking in and investigating members of the Trump administration for corruption.
As election night fades, the possibility of a new alliance is coming into view: Democrats, a party with a long history regulating industry and MAHA (maybe they’ll take a new name?), a grassroots movement with energy and organization.
When it comes to food, air, and water, both seek to use the levers of government to protect Americans’ health. Will they seize the opportunity?
Brinda Adhikari and Tom W. Johnson are the co-hosts and co-creators of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

Beau Lamarre-Condon “stands by” his decision to shoot Jesse Baird but did not intend to kill him, the New South Wales supreme court has heard.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon continued giving evidence in the double murder trial on Friday, telling the court about the moment he allegedly shot Baird.
“That first shot into Jesse’s right shoulder was the right move. I stand by it,” he said.
He claimed Baird had lunged at him with a knife and told the court he deliberately aimed his gun at the right shoulder, believing it would not kill Baird.
“As police officers we are trained to shoot people at the centre of body mass … I had a split-second moment where I said, ‘Drop the knife’ … It was just police mode now,” he said from the witness box.
“If I didn’t do that I was 110% going to have that knife driven into my throat.”
However, Lamarre-Condon repeatedly told the court he “did not want to kill Jesse”.
“Jesse did not deserve anything like that to happen to him,” he told the court.
“He did nothing to me to deserve to be killed.”
During his second day in the witness box, Lamarre-Condon told the jury he entered Baird’s home on 19 February 2024 because he wanted to retrieve his belongings from the house without being recognised.
He claimed he did not want to come into contact with Baird due to a risk the other man could take out an apprehended violence order against him as Baird had previously asked him to “please refrain from contacting me”.
Lamarre-Condon told the court he had seen what he assumed to be someone’s delivery motorcycle: “As soon as I saw that I had an idea … I saw a hi-vis hooded jacket, waterproof long pants and gloves.
“This moment here … I wish that I didn’t do this … But I had the thought process that if I was to put on this helmet and outfit I could knock on Jesse’s door I would look like an UberEats driver without any verbal interaction with Jesse.”
The accused thought Baird’s room was empty when he entered the home, he told the court.
He looked through some storage boxes in Baird’s home in search of his belongings, including a Cartier ring and a $2,000 shirt, but could not find them, he said.
When he looked up, he saw Baird with a knife and tape, sealing boxes, and said the other man began yelling, “We’re getting robbed,” the jury heard.
Lamarre-Condon said he was still wearing the motorcycle helmet and had his firearm in a holster under his shirt when Baird saw him.
“He started yelling, ‘We’re getting robbed, we’re getting robbed,’ … He couldn’t see it was me because the visor was down,” Lamarre-Condon said.
He told the court Baird pinned him against a wall with his left forearm while “swinging around the knife” in his other hand as the officer yelled: “It’s Beau, calm the fuck down.”
He said he then had a “very, very clear thought”.
“[I thought] shoot him in the shoulder so you don’t kill him, so he drops the knife,” he told the court.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he then fired the gun, but the two continued to struggle and the officer’s finger remained on the trigger, the jury heard.
They tripped over a storage box on the ground, which is when Lamarre-Condon “accidentally” discharged the gun.
He told the court: “It was my fault … I am guilty of manslaughter … But it wasn’t intentional.”
Under cross-examination from crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC, Lamarre-Condon repeated that he “stands by” the decision to take the first shot.
“If I didn’t, Mr Crown, you would be sitting here today interrogating Mr Baird,” he said.
Asked by Hatfield if he shot Baird in the back, Lamarre-Condon said: “That’s not accurate, that’s not true.”
While Lamarre-Condon said Baird’s shooting was his fault, he maintained Davies shot himself.
After the first two shots, the jury heard that Lamarre-Condon dialled the emergency hotline to try to get help for Baird.
But when he looked up, he saw Davies, who he didn’t recognise at the time.
The accused claimed the other man had picked up his gun.
“It was pointed towards me at my chest and he said: ‘I’m going to fucking shoot you,’” he told the court.
“I started lowering my body towards the ground. I said, ‘Please don’t shoot me, I’m not here to shoot you. I’m not a threat I’m not here to hurt you.’
“That’s when he raised the gun towards my head and said, ‘Fuck off.’”
The former officer said police are trained to redirect gun muzzles when firearms are pointed at them.
“I saw the gun, he was holding it with both hands, I thought, ‘fuck he’s going to fire the gun’ and that’s where my police training kicked in,” he told the court.
“My left hand would have grabbed Luke’s left wrist and turned it away … my other hand pushed against the forearm and then I pushed the pivot point of the left wrist away from me.”
Asked by the defence lawyer whether the gun went off, Lamarre-Condon said: “Yes, during this motion. And it got Luke.”
Baird’s mother, Helen, left the courtroom partway through Lamarre-Condon’s evidence.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

As the air quality of the national capital deteriorated to the 'very poor' category for the first time this winter season, the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and adjoining areas (CAQM) on Monday (November 2, 2026) announced Stage 2 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
The air quality is likely to be in the 'very poor' category for the next three days, as per the Central government’s Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi. The last time Delhi’s air quality was in the 'very poor' category was on February 11 this year.
Stage 2 of the GRAP mandates NCR State governments to enhance vehicle parking fees to discourage use of private vehicles. The GNCTD (Delhi government) and NCR State governments also have to “stagger timings for public offices and municipal bodies in the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar”.
Considering the restrictions on vehicles, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has decided to run additional trips on weekdays. While the DMRC was running 20 trips since October 28, when the GRAP-1 was enforced, 20 more trips will be run now. “This is to encourage people to use public transport rather than their private vehicles and help mitigate pollution,” said a senior Metro official.
Other directions to State governments include implementing existing measures to control air pollution, such as mechanical sweeping of roads or sprinkling water on roads, among others
The GRAP is a set of short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages. The CAQM announces the different stages depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 324 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on November 2, 2026, up from 261 (poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI. A higher AQI indicates worsening air quality.
‘Very poor' levels of air pollution could lead to “respiratory illness on prolonged exposure”, as per the CPCB. On February 11, 2026, the AQI was 305 (very poor).
Every winter, air pollution spikes in the Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season also add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

It's ACA open enrollment time. Here are the changes for health insurance shoppers
Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.
Shoppers need to plan accordingly.
Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts started earlier, and some states have been allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.
A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.
But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.
Have your ID ready
One of the biggest changes for people shopping for their 2027 coverage will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents. The requirements are aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.
The new rules, outlined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.
For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.
Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed "high-risk" must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as "high-risk" first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.
Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because "someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer."
The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.
The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned "that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing" and may just give up and not get insured.
Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian's help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver's license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.
"Some people may have trouble not because they're not real, but because they don't have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names," said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
She said the changes might "be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles."
There may be fewer brokers
CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.
CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of "significant compliance concerns" in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out "hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers" this year.
Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients' coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.
"Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense," he said. However, in the short term, "I don't know if they care about the chaos it will cause."
That's because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he's unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.
He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.
"They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long," Fine said.
Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit on Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.
"Just because you're a new agent doesn't mean you are fraudulent," said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. "All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won't be able to work."
It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown's Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. "If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early."
Costs will continue to be an issue
This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.
Still, most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.
The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.
This helps offset premium increases.
"For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same," said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst forHealthInsurance.org. "That's not to say it's great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that."
But there are other factors at work, too.
Last year'saverage premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers' fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs and general inflation, and labor shortages.
For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.
Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.
"The biggest issue we will face is affordability," said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. "There definitely will come a breaking point for people."
Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.
"If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity," Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.
That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.
Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.

Actors Dia Mirza, Shriya Saran, Nikki Galrani Pinisetty, and Aadhi Pinisetty attended the launch of Ray, an experiential jewellery community and centre in Bengaluru. Speaking about the initiative, Dia Mirza highlighted how the space amalgamates fine jewellery, art, and culinary experiences while reflecting on how jewellery represents financial independence, heritage, and emotional legacy. Shriya Saran described jewellery as an emotional purchase that connects generations, noting the value of exploring bespoke pieces in an immersive setting. Founder Shikha Dada and co-founder Saad Salman detailed the vision behind Ray, describing it as India's first jewellery community where patrons can spend leisure time exploring gemstone collections, rose-cut diamond jewellery, and art. Marketing head Ritesh explained the mansion-style layout, featuring an art gallery alongside luxury collections, while Nikki Galrani Pinisetty emphasised the venue's exclusive, appointment-only model.
The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption is conducting raids across thirty locations in Tamil Nadu, including Dindigul and Tiruchirappalli, targeting prominent businessmen over alleged involvement in an illegal sand mining scam. The action follows a complaint by anti-corruption organisation Arappor Iyakkam and prior intervention by the Enforcement Directorate into the multi-crore sand mining mafia.
The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) has mounted a sharp offensive against the actor-turned-politician Vijay-led administration in Tamil Nadu, labelling it a 'reel government' focused on optics rather than governance. Highlighting widespread public dissatisfaction, DMK MP Kanimozhi Karunanidhi shared video interactions with local women who raised deep concerns regarding deteriorating law and order, safety issues, rising crimes against women and children, and surging living costs. The confrontation also comes amid political friction, with investigations into allegations of horse-trading involving state politicians ahead of an assembly no-confidence motion. The DMK criticised the administration for failing to protect the women voters who supported it, contrasting government claims with grassroots realities in the state.
A political crisis has surfaced within the ruling National Conference in Jammu and Kashmir, with 17 MLAs mounting a rebellion and demanding the removal of cabinet ministers. The dissident legislators, consisting of 16 National Conference MLAs and one independent MLA from Thanamandi, held a meeting with party patriarch Dr Farooq Abdullah and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah at their Gupkar residence in Srinagar. The disgruntled MLAs have demanded a complete restructuring of the cabinet, the removal of ministers who have completed two years in office including the Deputy Chief Minister, and the ouster of advisor to the Chief Minister, Nasir Aslam Wani. Citing governance deficits, poor ministerial performance, and repeated humiliation of senior party legislators following the recent cabinet expansion, the dissident leaders have called for transparent consultations with the legislature party. The meeting follows four separate huddles by the aggrieved MLAs, coming amid internal resentment within the National Conference following the recent resignation of Srinagar MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi.
A technical examination report submitted by BMW to investigators has revealed critical data regarding the fatal Kerala Mini Cooper crash in Kochi. Analysis from the vehicle's Advanced Crash Safety Module established that the car was speeding at 162 kilometres per hour five seconds before the collision and was travelling at 144 kilometres per hour upon impact. The data also indicated the brake pedal was pressed roughly one second prior to hitting a two-wheeler, resulting in the immediate death of three youths. The findings provide scientific backing for the police case against the 19-year-old accused driver, whose anticipatory bail plea approaches the Kerala High Court.

The Kerala High Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) granted bail to the four youths who were accused in the Nedumbassery luxury car accident that led to the death of three young two-wheeler riders.
Justice Kauser Edappagath allowed the bail applications of the four accused, considering that all accused were in their early twenties, the lack of criminal history, and the time already spent in custody. Suhail Sajeev, the first accused would be released on November 16, as the State had sought more time pertaining to the investigation. The other three would be released at the earliest.
The court held that it could not jump to the conclusion that the accused had prior knowledge of the alleged offences owing to mere alcohol consumption or speeding.
Contention of accused
The accused had contended that as students, their continued detention would negatively affect their education and that they would fulfil any bail conditions necessary to ensure their continued cooperation.
Around 1.45 a.m. on October 11, the car driven by Sajeev crashed into a two-wheeler on Airport Road near Athani, claiming the lives of Gopika, Devika and Iyas. The other accused – Ninav, Joyal S. Anto and Ameen Shah – were in the car with Sajeev during the incident. All four were charged under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for rash and negligent driving, culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and abetment with a common intention.

Netanyahu rival Eisenkot tipped to seek Israeli government with backing of Arab lists
Former Israeli military chief secures 67 recommendations, but faces uphill battle to build majority
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition’s Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog held a second day of consultations with political parties on Thursday after the October 27 election, in which neither Netanyahu - a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war - nor Eisenkot - a former military chief promising to restore national unity - secured enough votes for a majority.

Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise — especially girls
The World Health Organization recommends adolescents spend at least one hour a day exercising enough to basically break a sweat — a brisk walk or a more intense pick-up soccer game. Lot's of research suggests this level of activity is crucial for supporting growing bodies and minds.
But new global data suggests only a small minority of kids and teens get that much. In fact, one in four report not hitting 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise any day of the week, according to a new study in The Lancet Global Health. Girls, as well as adolescents from middle- and lower-income countries reported even lower levels of exercise.
"The findings are disappointing, because one of the major results is that the trend over the last 15 years is flat," says Fiona Bull, head of the physical activity unit at the World Health Organization, who co-authored the study. "These data are a call for us to relook at what we're doing. Business as usual will not change these trends."
Changing habits in those teen years could have a lifelong impact, says Solveig Cunningham, a global health researcher at Emory University. "As an adolescent, if your baseline is zero days of physical activity, that's going to be your baseline as you go into adulthood."
What 3 million teens revealed
So how do researchers know whether adolescents are — or aren't — working up a sweat? It's tricky. Researchers would love to be able to strap smartwatches to kids to get detailed data, but that would be costly. The next best strategy is to ask a basic question — how many days during the past week were you active for at least 60 minutes?
The report draws on data from surveys posting some version of this question to over 3 million adolescents from 140 countries over the past 15 years. Only about 14% of kids worldwide reported getting an hour a day of exercise. Globally, the average adolescent reported less than 3 such days a week, the study found.
Kids from low- and middle-income countries tended to be less active than their counterparts from wealthier Western countries, the study found. There's no one explanation for this pattern, but a few likely causes stand out.
"Physical activity is an issue of opportunity," says Andrea Ramirez Varela, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas Health Science Center in Houston. In many lower income countries, she says that the environment — where they live, go to school and play — often restricts opportunities to be active. The study didn't break down the urban and rural divide, but some research suggests rural adolescents in lower-income countries move more, she says, often out of necessity. In increasingly populated urban areas, activity is lower.
Many cities aren't designed to be walkable, says Varela. In Latin America, where she does most of her research, "many parents think it's unsafe to just let your kids walk alone to and from places," she says — much less go out and play independently. In some urban centers, air pollution can make being active outdoors unhealthy too.
Screens may play a role as well. After school, "kids and adolescents, when they arrive home, they start watching TV, they are in front of a screen," says Valrela. "Because this digital world is so attractive, they are going to be sedentary the rest of the day."
Cultural barriers
The report also revealed a stubborn gender gap.
Girls were less active than boys in virtually all countries. Nearly 30% don't exercise at all during the week compared to 22% of boys. Only 11% of girls were active daily compared to 17% of boys. And girls' weekly average of active days was lower (2.4 vs 3).
"It's very worrying to see this gender difference so early," says Bull, noting that the difference often persists into adulthood.
Different norms around what's appropriate for girls often drive that divergence.
"In many places, when girls reach puberty, there are taboos to engaging in physical activity," says Cunningham. Take India, for example, where Cunningham has focused much of her research. "Mothers or grandmothers will say, 'Well, you know, we don't want girls spending a lot of time outside. Their skin might get darker. That might have negative implications for whether they can get married."
Cunningham notes that girls are active in other, often less intense ways. "In South Asia, as well the United States, a substantial proportion of girls' active time is doing chores," she says "If the guys are outside playing and the girls are inside sweeping, they're both active, but it's kind of not the same thing."
What would get them moving?
Improving these trends won't be easy, experts told NPR. Redesigning cities to be more walkable, for instance, takes many years and substantial investment. Many experts point to schools as a practical place to start. "To move the needle, we need to focus on the settings where kids and adolescents spend most of their time," says Varela.
In fact, data suggests that countries with higher levels of adolescent exercise tend to have more structured time for sport during or after the school day. Building up such programs in other countries might help close the gap, says Varela, especially if done in ways that make sport accessible and affordable.
Such efforts will require sustained attention from policymakers, Varela says, who face pressures from all sorts of competing interests. But she says it's worth it.
"Not solving the problem in this stage of life will perpetuate the problem in adulthood," she says, where the costs to society, in terms of poor physical and mental health, only become greater.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed expanding the network of authorised entry points for the import of drugs, medical devices and cosmetics into India, adding 10 inland container depots (ICDs), a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and an international airport to the existing list of notified locations.
The proposed amendment to Rule 43A of the Drugs Rules, 1945, is aimed at easing import operations, reducing inland transportation distances and improving the movement of healthcare products across the country.
The additional locations proposed include ICD Sonipat, Piyala and Harsaru in Haryana; ICD Dadri in Uttar Pradesh; ICD Gandhidham/Mundra in Gujarat; ICD Sanath Nagar and Thimmapur in Hyderabad, Telangana; and ICD Whitefield in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The Ministry has also proposed including SEZ Bommasandra in Karnataka and Noida International Airport in Uttar Pradesh for the import of drugs by air.
The proposed additions will supplement the existing network of authorised import gateways, which includes ICDs at Dhannad and Tihi in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, besides airports already notified for drug imports.
Rule 43A specifies the ports, airports, railway stations, road crossings and other entry points through which drugs can be imported into India.
According to the Ministry, expanding the network is expected to allow importers to clear consignments closer to their manufacturing facilities, warehouses and distribution centres. This could reduce inland transportation requirements, optimise logistics costs and minimise delays in the movement of imported consignments.
The move is also intended to improve operational convenience for importers and strengthen the supporting infrastructure for the supply of medicines, medical devices and cosmetics.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders on the draft amendment. Responses can be submitted to the Under Secretary (Drugs Regulation), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
The amendment will be taken forward after consideration of the objections and suggestions received, noted a release issued by the Ministry.

MADISON, Wis. — An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state’s first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.
The Wisconsin Department of Health Services did not specify where the death happened or provide any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.
The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said.
“My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease.”
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
As of Thursday, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
- Published
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.
In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.
When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.
Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.
Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.
"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.
While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.
His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.
"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.
Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.
He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.
Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.
But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.
In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.
And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.
The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.
He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.
In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.
Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.
"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.
Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.
International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.
"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.
