Taiwanese audiences are consuming entertainment across film, television, music, publishing and gaming, creating opportunities for cross-platform IP development, according to research presented by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei on Friday.
At the “Exclusive Insights Report: Taiwan Cross-Platform Audience Data × AI Application Evaluation” session, TAICCA research analyst Joy Lin presented findings from the agency’s annual cultural consumption survey and a 2026 cross-platform genre study incorporating Nielsen television ratings data and online questionnaires.
The annual survey, which collects approximately 2,000 valid responses each year, found that 96% of respondents watched audiovisual content in 2025, while 75% read published works and 75% played video games. Audiovisual content and music showed particularly strong audience overlap, with 90% of respondents engaging with both.
The separate cross-platform study surveyed 2,018 people aged 15 to 69. Among the 1,242 respondents who had watched Taiwanese audiovisual productions in the previous year, 40% had also watched Taiwanese screen adaptations.
Genre preferences revealed differences between local and imported content. Taiwanese productions were more closely associated with everyday life, family relationships and romance, while foreign productions showed greater strength in action, fantasy and suspense.
Romance emerged as a promising genre for cross-platform development, with the research identifying connections between romance, school-life stories, comics, popular music and mobile games. Among viewers of Taiwanese romantic dramas, 84% also watched foreign series, 63% watched foreign films and 58% watched foreign animation.
In the second presentation, TAICCA research analyst Chhoa Hiok-chong examined AI adoption in audiovisual production, highlighting potential cost savings alongside legal uncertainty and technical limitations.
Broader industry estimates cited in the presentation, rather than Taiwan-specific figures, placed AI adoption in post-production and visual effects at 70% to 85%, compared with 60% to 75% in pre-production and 15% to 25% in on-set production.
International examples included Netflix’s Argentine science-fiction series “The Eternaut” and South Korean entertainment company CJ ENM’s AI-assisted productions, illustrating potential savings in production costs and visual-effects workflows.
However, technical obstacles remain, including visual consistency across shots, camera control, narrative continuity and integration into established production pipelines.
Citing the Database of AI Litigation, the presentation identified 489 AI-related legal cases through August 2026, including 153 involving cultural and creative industries. The presentation also examined AI-related protections negotiated by Hollywood unions, including SAG-AFTRA, the Writers Guild of America (WGA), the Directors Guild of America (DGA) and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE), covering digital replicas, consent, compensation and creative control.
Consumer resistance presents another challenge. According to a November 2025 survey by entertainment research firm Luminate, 51% of U.S. respondents rejected fully synthetic virtual performers. A Japanese consumer survey published by English Hub and GRAS Group in September 2026 found that 44.7% would be less willing to purchase content once they knew it was AI-generated.
In South Korea, a survey published by Embrain Trend Monitor in January 2026 found that 81.6% supported advance disclosure of AI-generated content, while 80.3% favored mandatory AI labeling.
During the Q&A session, attendees questioned whether reported AI production savings adequately accounted for the upfront costs of adopting new workflows, including experimentation, revisions and trial-and-error processes. Others asked about the lack of Taiwan-specific production examples illustrating copyright disputes and legal responsibilities, given the presentation’s reliance on international cases.
Responding to questions about Taiwan’s regulatory framework, Chhoa pointed to the Ministry of Culture’s existing guidelines on generative AI in arts and culture.

Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.
When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.
The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.
When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.
What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.
When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."
The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.
If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.
It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.
We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.
The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

New Delhi, Nov 06: A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the 'severe' category, with the overall Air Quality Index (AQI) settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded severe air quality at 9 am, while the remaining stations were in the very poor category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472.
According to the Air Quality Early Warning System, Delhi is likely to record its first severe air quality day of the season on Friday, with the situation expected to persist until November 8, the day of Diwali.
The forecast comes amid the ongoing peak stubble-burning period in the National Capital Region, while firecracker emissions due to Diwali could further add to the pollution load.
The AQI was in the 'very poor' category Friday morning and rose from 389 at 8 am to 391 at 9 am, indicating a further deterioration in air quality.
As per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), an AQI between zero and 50 is classified as 'good', 51 and 100 as 'satisfactory', 101 and 200 as 'moderate', 201 and 300 as 'poor', 301 and 400 as 'very poor', and 401 and 500 as 'severe'.
Weather experts said several pollution hotspots in the city could record AQI levels above 450, particularly in view of Diwali festivities and stubble-burning.
The minimum temperature at the Safdarjung weather station, Delhi's base observatory, settled at 17.2 degrees Celsius, 1.9 notches above the season's normal.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast a maximum temperature of around 30 degrees Celsius for the day, with shallow fog likely during the morning hours. Shallow fog is expected to persist in the capital until November 9.

Public records and an email first obtained by KARE 11, a Minnesota news station, indicate ICE purchased the vacant facility for $495.6 million roughly a year after private prison operator CoreCivic offered it to the Minnesota Department of Corrections for $75 million. The Department of Homeland Security and CoreCivic said the price was set through the standard federal appraisal process, which involves independent estimates of the property's value.
In late October, a claim emerged that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement paid roughly $495 million for a private prison previously offered for sale to the state of Minnesota for $75 million.
Snopes readers sent us images of Instagram (archived) and Facebook posts featuring the story, which spread amid the White House's highly-publicized attempts to portray Minnesota as an example of poor governance and a hotbed of fraud.
On X, Democratic lawmakers like U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California also shared the story.
This claim originated from a credible Oct. 29 report by KARE 11 (archived), a Minneapolis-based television station and NBC affiliate. 
In August, the Department of Homeland Security paid a private prison operator, CoreCivic, $495.6 million for a vacant facility in Appleton, a rural town in southwestern Minnesota. KARE 11's investigative report found that roughly a year before the sale to DHS, the Minnesota Department of Corrections had declined a $75 million sale offer for the same prison — Prairie Correctional Facility — from the same company. 
Snopes independently verified the facts behind the report via publicly available documentation, as well as emails shared by KARE 11's lead reporter on the story — A.J. Lagoe — and the Minnesota DOC. CoreCivic stated in its news release announcing the sale that it was under contract with ICE, which DHS oversees, to manage Prairie Correctional Facility. As such, we have rated this claim true.
It is unclear why ICE paid so much more than the previous asking price for the facility. The purchase occurred shortly before the Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan "congressional watchdog" of the U.S. government, published a report on Sept. 24 saying ICE has "wasted" taxpayer funds "on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments" (Paragraph 2, Page 13). 
During an Oct. 30 press event, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent denied knowing anything about the overpayment for the Minnesota facility and said a question about it was a "waste of our time."
DHS emailed Snopes the same statement KARE 11 published on Nov. 2 (as an update to its Oct. 29 article), saying the department followed "the standard federal appraisal process." The statement reads, in full:
DHS acquired the Prairie Correctional Facility to strengthen America's ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people's mandate for mass deportations.
The 1,600-bed site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction.
The purchase price was set through the standard federal appraisal process. Independent appraisers applied a replacement-cost method, current cost of equivalent secure space, adjusted for depreciation, land, and condition, including the security and fire upgrades required for ICE operations.
The $75 million figure was a preliminary, non-binding indication offered during earlier discussions with the Minnesota Department of Corrections. Those talks never advanced to formal appraisal or agreed scope. The number was not based on replacement-cost analysis and did not reflect the intervening rise in construction costs or federal operational standards. Minnesota's own estimate to replace Stillwater was roughly $1.3 billion.
(In the statement above, "Stillwater" appears to reference a Minnesota prison scheduled for closure in 2029. In May 2025, the Minnesota DOC said maintenance needs for that facility were estimated at $180 million, with full modernization or replacement of the prison estimated at $1.3 billion. It is a similar size to the vacant Prairie Correctional Facility.)
In an emailed statement to Snopes, CoreCivic echoed DHS' statement, saying the price was set by "an independent, state-certified appraisal firm engaged by the government."
Proof of sale and previous offer
In an Aug. 5 news release, CoreCivic announced that DHS purchased Prairie Correctional Facility in Minnesota for $495.6 million (emphasis ours): 
CoreCivic, Inc. (NYSE: CXW) (CoreCivic or the Company) announced today that it has completed the sales of its 1,600-bed Prairie Correctional Facility in Appleton, Minnesota and its 1,033-bed Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, Kansas to the United States of America and its assigns, by and through the Department of Homeland Security for an aggregate gross sales price of $734.0 million, including $495.6 million for the Prairie Correctional Facility and $238.4 million for the Midwest Regional Reception Center.
In an email to Snopes, KARE 11 reporter Lagoe shared a link to the Aug. 4 purchase agreement between the U.S. government and CoreCivic on the official U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission website, which also confirms the sale price. Here is the relevant part of the agreement (emphasis theirs):
Dated as of August 4, 2026
PURCHASE AND SALE AGREEMENT
THIS PURCHASE AND SALE AGREEMENT (this "Agreement") is made as of the 4th day of August, 2026 (the "Effective Date") pursuant to 6 U.S.C. §§ 202, 251, and 551, and 8 U.S.C. §§ 1226 and 1231 by and between CoreCivic, Inc. a Maryland corporation (successor by name change to Corrections Corporation of America, a Maryland corporation) having an address of 5501 Virginia Way, Suite 110, Brentwood, Tennessee 37027 ("Seller"), and United States of America, by and through the Department of Homeland Security ("Buyer") (each of Buyer and Seller being a "Party" and collectively being the "Parties"), and is joined in for the limited purposes set forth herein by Chicago Title Insurance Company, as escrow agent (the "Escrow Agent").
[ ... ]
Purchase Price. The purchase price for the Property shall be $495,639,588.00 (the "Purchase Price") and shall be paid at the Closing (as defined in Section 12.1 below) by wire transfer or immediately available funds, subject to any prorations, adjustments, and credits made pursuant to the terms of this Agreement including without limitation Section 4 below.
Lagoe also shared a May 7, 2025, email between CoreCivic and the Minnesota DOC deputy commissioner, Safia Khan, which Lagoe said KARE 11 obtained through a public records request.
In that email, CoreCivic executive Kelly Durham said the company would sell Prairie Correctional Facility for "$75M inclusive of the upgrades CoreCivic has identified would be needed to re-activate the facility."
Minnesota DOC spokesperson, Shannon Loehrke, provided an attachment of the same email to Snopes, further confirming its legitimacy.
Loehrke also shared an Aug. 4 email from CoreCivic notifying the Minnesota DOC that the company had entered into "a 5-year contract last night with the federal government to reopen our Appleton facility." Federal spending records show the U.S. government awarded CoreCivic $18.6 million to run the prison for a year.
Response from Minnesota officials, reports of taxpayer waste, unproven fraud allegations
The New York Times reported that, according to Khan, "company officials seemed eager to get rid of the prison, at one point offering to sell it for a fraction of that price." 
Both KARE 11 and the Times said state officials declined to purchase the prison, citing a lack of funds, its remote location and staffing challenges. The two news outlets also reported that Minnesota officials said the facility's final sale price stunned them.
In reference to Prairie Correctional Facility, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in an Oct. 30 X post that he was calling on Congress to investigate ICE's "corrupt misuse of [the public's] tax dollars."
Even before KARE 11's story ran, U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum, a Minnesota Democrat, said in an Oct. 5 X post that DHS overpaid for the facility and questioned whether it was because "its owners are mega donors to Trump and Republicans."
According to nonprofit campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets, which aggregates Federal Election Commission data, individuals tied to CoreCivic donated $223,223 to the Republican National Committee in 2024.
CoreCivic's emailed statement to Snopes denied allegations of fraud:
To be clear, any allegation or implication of fraud, corruption or bribery related to this transaction is categorically false. The transaction followed the federal government's long-established appraisal process, conducted by independent appraisers the government engaged. These claims are not only unsupported — they are defamatory, and we take them seriously.
As of this writing, there is no evidence disputing CoreCivic's statement.

- Pilot Benjamin G. McDaniel III has created a GTA 6 sky tribute using his 1978 Cessna's flight path.
- The pilot spent over eight hours creating the sky art, flying from November 5 to November 6, 2026.
- The GTA 6 sky art features the game's logo, the iconic palm trees, a bikini-clad woman, and more Leonida imagery.
Sky’s the limit for the anticipation behind GTA 6’s release, and one Arkansas pilot has taken that quite literally. Benjamin G. McDaniel III, better known as “The Pilot Picasso,” created an incredible GTA 6 sky tribute across Arkansas skies using his Cessna’s flight path between November 5 and 6, 2026, tracing the game’s logo and other imagery.
McDaniel took off from Bentonville Municipal Airport in his 1978 Cessna 182 Skylane RG on November 5 and started the journey, which reportedly took him over eight hours to complete, as showcased live on FlightRadar24’s official website, along with flight history documenting the entire journey.
McDaniel painted the “Grand Theft Auto 6” logo in the style of the official GTA 6 cover art, featuring a woman holding a pistol in a bikini, a sports car, an alligator, the iconic palm trees, and a helicopter at the top of the creation.
“The Pilot Picasso” has previously taken to the skies to recreate iconic imagery from Spider-Man, The Odyssey, and even Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa. Now, he added GTA 6 to his growing collection, flying his 1978 Cessna across Arkansas to recreate imagery from Rockstar’s upcoming game.
Of course, we don’t know if Rockstar has anything to do with this GTA 6 sky tribute, so for now, McDaniel created it independently as a fan to celebrate the game’s massive launch in less than two weeks. With the GTA 6 countdown to November 19 underway, Rockstar and fans are ramping up their celebrations ahead of the release of the open-world title.
Previous GTA games never saw this level of hype-driven promotion, official or otherwise, so the GTA 6 hype has officially skyrocketed, quite literally. That said, what do you think about the GTA 6 sky tribute from pilot Benjamin McDaniel? Tell us in the comments section below.

CBI seeks Chandrakar’s custody to identify Chhattisgarh officials who received money
The CBI alleged that Chandrakar and associates secured the protection of police and administrative officials
Custodial interrogation of Saurabh Chandrakar, the alleged mastermind of the ₹6,000-crore Mahadev online betting syndicate, is crucial to identify police and administrative officials in Chhattisgarh who allegedly received huge amounts as money to allow the illegal operations to continue, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) told a special court.
The CBI alleged that Chandrakar, other promoters and associates of Mahadev Book secured the protection of police and administrative officials and influential politicians by regularly paying them.
The special court in Raipur on Wednesday granted the CBI eight days of custody of Chandrakar, who was extradited from Oman on November 1. It permitted the agency to take him to Delhi for interrogation.
Deep Dive
The CBI said custodial questioning was necessary to identify other masterminds and beneficiaries of the alleged fraud, trace the channels through which the proceeds were collected, layered and transferred outside India, and identify assets created from the illegal earnings.
It sought Chandrakar’s interrogation to identify public servants in Chhattisgarh, who allegedly received or were receiving illegal financial benefits in return for allowing the betting syndicate to operate.
The CBI said hawala operators were used to arrange and distribute the alleged protection money. Police officers and employees were also allegedly engaged to channel these payments to police and administrative officials.
Investigations have indicated that Chandrakar, Ravi Uppal and their associates promoted the Mahadev Book app and ran online betting operations through an extensive network of panel and branch operators, the agency said.
The promoters allegedly retained 70-80% of the illegal earnings, while the remaining amount was distributed among panel operators. The CBI claimed that Chandrakar and other promoters were generating around ₹450 crore every month through online betting since the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020.
The accused allegedly arranged hundreds of bank accounts using forged documents to facilitate transactions involving the proceeds of crime. These accounts were operated on a commission basis, while betting proceeds were transferred by panel operators to Chandrakar and other promoters in the UAE through multiple bank accounts, the agency alleged.
A substantial portion of the illegal earnings was also allegedly spent on advertising betting websites and organising lavish annual events attended by celebrities. The agency claimed that celebrities were paid from the proceeds generated through online betting.
The CBI alleged that police and administrative officials and influential political persons misused their positions to obtain illegal financial benefits and subsequently acquired assets from such proceeds.
Chandrakar and other promoters operated the Mahadev Book syndicate from Dubai, which they referred to as their head office. Several youths from Chhattisgarh were allegedly employed as managers, supervisors and other staff to run the betting operations, the agency said.
According to the CBI, Chandrakar left India in 2022 to evade the process of law and deliberately remained abroad without joining the investigation.
Following his extradition from Oman, he was brought to Raipur in a private aircraft on Tuesday evening for production before the trial court.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has been separately investigating the alleged money laundering in the case, which came to light during the previous Congress government led by Bhupesh Baghel in Chhattisgarh.
After the BJP government came to power, the state’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) registered an FIR in March 2024 on the basis of an ED report, invoking charges of criminal conspiracy, cheating and provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Baghel, Mahadev app promoters Ravi Uppal, Saurabh Chandrakar, Shubham Soni and Anil Kumar Agrawal, along with 14 others, were named as accused in the EOW FIR. Baghel termed the case against him politically motivated.
In August 2024, the state government transferred cases related to the alleged betting scam registered at various police stations, along with an EOW case, to the CBI.
The ED has estimated the proceeds of crime in the alleged scam at around ₹6,000 crore and attached several properties in India and abroad linked to the syndicate.
Chandrakar and Uppal are from Bhilai in Chhattisgarh’s Durg district. Uppal was arrested in the UAE, and India is pursuing his extradition, officials said.

HT exclusive: Delhi Police informed MCD of unauthorised construction at Chawri Bazar building months ago
At least two people were killed in the Chawri Bazar building collapse on Thursday morning, officials said.
The Delhi Police had informed Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) officials about unauthorised construction at the three-storey building in Chawri Bazar that collapsed on Thursday nearly five months ago, but no action was taken by the civic body, officers aware of the matter said.
At least two people were killed and one was injured in the Chawri Bazar building collapse on Thursday morning, the latest in the series of such mishaps in the Capital. The number of people trapped under the debris was not immediately known. Track LIVE updates from Chawri Bazar building collapse rescue operation here
“After receiving complaints, we had informed MCD about unauthorised construction at 4547 Gali Sheesh Mahal, Chawri Bazar on June 15 but we are not aware of any action being taken,” a senior officer aware of the investigation told HT on condition of anonymity.
HT has reached out to MCD officials for a response. This report will be updated as and when the civic body responds.
The incident was reported at 9.50 am from Gali Sitara, near the Chawri Bazar Metro station, according to PTI news agency.
MCD suspends 2 engineers
Hours after the building collapsed, the MCD suspended assistant engineer (AE), Mohd Naeem, and junior engineer (JE) Aman Dalal on the orders of chief minister Rekha Gupta. The chief minister also ordered thorough inquiry into the incident and the registration of FIR against the contractor.
The chief minister's office (CMO) also said on X that strict directions have been issued to ensure best possible medical treatment for the injured and immediate ex-gratia assistance to the affected families.
Stringent action will be taken against those found responsible, in accordance with the law, the CMO X post stated.
A witness said about eight to ten labourers were working at the site when the building collapsed.
“…Work was underway on the lanter of the third floor. It collapsed at around 9:30 am, while approximately seven to eight labourers were working at the site,” said the witness, on condition of anonymity.
Chief minister Rekha Gupta visited the mishap site and said that overlooking safety and security measures during constructions poses a fatal risk to lives. She said, while speaking to media persons, that further investigation will reveal the exact cause of the collapse.
“Two bodies have been recovered so far, and one injured person has been rescued. The structure was a ground-plus-two-story building. Further investigation will reveal the exact cause of the collapse. In the meantime, the Municipal Corporation has suspended the concerned JE and AE, and an FIR has been registered against the contractor responsible for the construction. I must emphasise that the way people often overlook safety and security measures while constructing their homes poses a fatal risk to their own lives,” CM Gupta said.
Any construction work must be carried out with strict adherence to safety and security protocols, she said, adding that any official who overlooks such negligence will not be spared.

Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads. The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to expand its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery, while supporting the validation and optimisation of promising molecules. Founded in 2026 by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, Venomics AI is working to tap the largely unexplored molecular diversity found in animal venoms to identify potential drug candidates. Animal venoms contain complex molecules that have evolved over millions of years to interact with specific biological targets. Some of these compounds have already inspired medicines. However, a large part of the molecular diversity across venomous species remains unexplored, presenting an opportunity for drug discovery. Venomics AI is building a platform that combines molecular sequencing and venom biology to map this diversity through its Venom Atlas. It then uses AI to prioritise promising molecular candidates and validates its predictions through functional laboratory screening. “Animal venoms represent one of nature’s richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and at Venomics AI, we are combining cutting-edge experimental science with artificial intelligence to unlock this extraordinary potential,” Sunagar said. India's bioeconomy is on track to reach $300 Bn by 2030, with the country's rapid emergence as a global biotechnology hub, based on IBEF data. Notably, the biotech sector in the country has been booming in recent years. The country is home to more than 11,000 biotech startups. Also, as part of the Budget 2027, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a new ‘Biopharma SHAKTI’ scheme with an outlay of ₹10,000 Cr. Meanwhile, investor interest in this space has been gradually seeing an uptick, where earlier this year, Cellogen Therapeutics secured ₹20 Cr in funding from Kotak Alternate Asset Managers (Kotak Alts), while StrainX Bioworks has raised $13 Mn in a funding round led by Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital.

Why managers can learn a lot from leaders like Napoleon - Pulis
- Published
The November international break is almost upon us, which always means one thing - the managerial merry-go-round is about to properly get into gear.
It's known as 'sacking season' for a reason - the new campaign has started to take shape and I know from experience that any manager who is not winning games will always be sleeping with just one eye closed, and the other one open.
At any club on a poor run of results, the owners and supporters will be questioning whether the manager is the right fit to continue.
This two-week break from domestic games is the ideal opportunity to blood the new incumbent and give them a period of getting to know everyone before the games start up again.
That means it is 'hiring season' too, but there are always far more out-of-work managers than vacant positions.
Since the start of last season, 60 different managers have resigned or been sacked by teams in the Premier League and Football League. Three of them left to take up offers from other clubs but, in total, 37 of them - or 62% - are not currently in management.
For most managers, it's rarely the case where you walk into a new club within a few weeks of leaving your last one, so what do out-of-work managers do between jobs to make sure they are ready to take the next opportunity that fits?
'Get your backside off the sofa'
It is more than 32 years since I received my marching orders from my first job at Bournemouth, who were in what is now known as League One. I was devastated.
I had - as I always did - given everything I could do to benefit the club, and with it being my first sacking I honestly did not know where my next step would take me.
But, on the second day of me being out of work, my home phone rang and at the end of the line was Jim Smith, who was in charge of Portsmouth, a few miles down the south coast.
I knew Jim then, but not really well. I'd been a manager for two years, but by then he had already spent 25 years in the dugout, at eight different clubs.
He asked how I was and, before I could even reply, recited these immortal words, which always stuck with me - "son, you're not a real manager until you get sacked at least three times - so get your backside off the sofa and get on with getting another job" - then he put the phone down!
I've used that sentence myself many times since to managers who have lost their job and are struggling to come to terms with it.
That can happen a lot. People outside the game maybe don't realise how difficult it can be when you are sacked, and how it affects certain individuals differently - you can easily fall off the merry-go-round and, as a manager, you never know for sure whether you will get another chance.
'When you are out of work, you can still learn a lot'
Someone else who phoned me up in the summer of 1994 was another great name in the game as a player and manager, Bruce Rioch.
At the time, Bruce was having a lot of success as manager of Bolton - he would get the Arsenal job a few months later - and he asked me if I would scout for him while I was trying to find my next manager's post.
He was very keen to get me involved and very helpful in keeping me busy watching games.
I was equally keen on helping Bruce and ended up scouting for him for that entire season. To this day, I owe him so much in respect of what he asked me to do, because of what I learned during that time.
Football is the best team sport in the world and the fundamental thing I picked up that season is that its 'product', the players, were the secret to success.
By that, I mean that I realised that at all levels there are good players, and at all levels there are managers working on budgets. I learned that knowing the level you were at, and placing the right players at that level who you could afford, would be an enormous factor in your chances of success, or failure.
Yes, there is more to it than that - you then also had to pick good characters, coach them well and motivate them with a driving force they could handle and enjoy - but you have to start by getting the right players for the level you are at.
The following summer, I was appointed manager of Gillingham, who had just finished 89th out of the 92 clubs across the top four divisions.
I was lucky enough to inherit a club who had quite a few players out of contract, so it enabled me to reset the first team with several players I had watched during my time scouting for Bruce and Bolton.
All the hours and miles I travelled that year paid off, with Gillingham finishing second in what is now League Two and gaining promotion in my first season. Those players who we recruited kick-started four years of my managerial career in Kent, and left me with some fantastic on-field memories.
'Napoleon Bonaparte kept me busy'
My time and success at Priestfield opened up an ever-revolving door of work and rest.
Whenever I was out of work in the years that followed, watching games still occupied my midweeks and weekends for the same reasons as before - I wanted to watch players who I might end up signing.
Lots of games I went to were watched from the terraces with either home or away supporters, which was always interesting and illuminating - I've always valued the views of match-going fans on different players.
Down the years, I was also invited to spend a few weeks coaching abroad, in Kuwait and the United States, by friends I had in the game.
Whatever I was doing, I always felt like I was learning, and not just by watching football around the world. I became an avid reader of sports books and also finding out about great leaders of men through history.
So, as well as visiting Bayer Leverkusen, Athletic Bilbao and RB Leipzig - who back then had only just started their rise from the bottom tier of German football - I would analyse and investigate historic battles or events.
Napoleon Bonaparte really kept me busy. His attention to detail and his command of his generals was only superseded by his troop's loyalty to him - they would literally die for him!
His 250th birthday was celebrated in Corsica in the summer of 2019, and a French newspaper invited me to go along and give a British perspective on how we see Napoleon as a leader and a person.
I was delighted to accept and was amazed by how many people from all over Europe turned up too.
Hated by many countries, but still adored by his followers, Napoleon also produced the Napoleonic Code, which is still the foundation of French civil law today.
'It's better to be in a job than out of football full-stop'
As well as great military triumphs, I studied defeats too - they are as much a part of football management as victories, after all - and you can compare the organisational brilliance of Napoleon to the disaster of the Battle of Balaclava and the Charge of the Light Brigade.
One summer, I travelled out to Crimea to witness the scene of that tragic charge by the bravest of brave men.
Lord Raglan, the British commander-in-chief, was based on the high ground and could see everything in the Russian positions and the brigades.
His order to attack was ambiguous and although Lord Cardigan, who led the charge, questioned it, he still followed it through - leading to one of the most infamous military disasters in history.
It should never have happened but, just as in football, leadership and communication from the top was key. The instructions were passed down from Raglan to Lord Lucan to Cardigan and became garbled - too many cooks, in my opinion!
The last book which really stuck with me, in terms of inspiring me as a leader, was the story of HMS Endurance - disaster strikes during a journey through the ice fields of the southern hemisphere when the ship becomes stuck.
I cannot do justice to the deeds of Sir Ernest Shackleton in this column but his leadership of his men, along with his number two Frank Worsley, was extraordinary.
Both dovetailed in a way that gave their men the energy, desire and determination to believe and follow instructions in the most appalling conditions, never once questioning their leaders' abilities to help them survive.
Over the years, I've never stopped reading about, or watching, great leaders like that - there is so much that young coaches can learn from other sports or history that will benefit then, the same way it did me.
Going to games was still the most important thing when I was between jobs, because I would always believe my own eyes when watching players.
There were times when that became more of a challenge, especially at the back end of my career, but times change and if you are not in tune with what is happening in the game then you can get dropped very quickly.
But I am sure that most of my managerial compatriots would also agree with me that experience in all walks of life can be invaluable.
I learned so much when I was out of work, about all aspects of leadership, individually and collectively.
My advice to managers out of work now is the same that I received from Jim, all those years ago - pick yourselves up and get off the sofa to get back in work as quickly as possible.
You should never be afraid of dropping down a level the way I did, too. It is better to get a job, any job, than be out of football full-stop. That hasn't changed since my day, either.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.
Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."
"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."
The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.
He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.
Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.
Brand said in the witness box that the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.
Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

After Democrats swept up the legislatures and governorships of five U.S. states in the November midterm elections, a rumor spread they were now in a position to abolish the Electoral College — the group of 538 electors who cast votes for the U.S. president on behalf of their states.
Several social media posts made the claim, including on Instagram and X. One X post said "Dems now have the power to pass the National Voter Compact to effectively abolish the Electoral College" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers reached out, seeking to confirm the veracity of the rumor.
It is true that Democrats swept the legislatures and governorships of five states (Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin). It is also true that, combined, they have enough electors to join and enact an existing agreement between 18 states and Washington, D.C. — a "compact" — to bypass the Electoral College.
However, the compact would not abolish the Electoral College altogether. In addition, as we outline below, some experts say the move would require congressional approval.
We contacted the Democratic leadership of all five states and a constitutional law expert seeking more clarity. We will update this report should we receive responses.
The Electoral College
In the United States, voters do not elect the president directly. Instead, they vote for electors in each state who, for the most part, cast their ballots for the presidential candidate who wins a majority in that state (Maine and Nebraska cast two electoral votes to the statewide winner, then they allow each congressional district to cast its vote for that district's winner). There are currently 538 electors in the Electoral College; presidents win with a simple majority of 270 electors.
This system has led to five instances where the elected president lost the national popular vote. For example in 2016, Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton won the popular vote, but her Republican opponent, Donald Trump, became president. In 2000, George W. Bush, a Republican, was elected despite earning fewer votes than Democrat Al Gore. The same thing happened in 1824, 1876 and 1888.
In practice, critics say, the Electoral College gives way to a minority rule — a system in which less-populated states have disproportionate political power. This, they argue, undermines democracy, which on principle allows the majority to decide.
There has long been a battle to restore balance by abolishing the Electoral College, which is enshrined in the 12th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. This fact sets a high bar for abolition. Per Article 5, any change in the Constitution requires an amendment proposal by two-thirds of both chambers of Congress, which must then be ratified by three-quarters of the states.
Bypassing the Electoral College
How elections are run is the prerogative of each state. Nothing in federal law compels a state to give its electors' votes to the statewide winner. This freedom has led to an effort, called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, that aims at electing the presidential winner of the nationwide popular vote while bypassing the constitutional amendment process.
An interstate compact is an agreement between two or more states. The states that joined the NPVIC agreed to give all their electors' votes to the winner of the popular vote in a presidential election. Eighteen states and Washington, D.C. have joined the compact since its 2006 launch, for a total of 222 electors.
In order for the compact to become effective, the total number of electors for all of the states that adopt it must reach or surpass 270 — the simple majority. This, its supporters say, has become more likely now that Democrats have won both state houses and the governorship in five states during the 2026 midterms: Pennsylvania (19 Electoral College votes), Michigan (15 votes), Arizona (11 votes), Wisconsin (10 votes) and Nevada (6 votes). Should they adopt the NPVIC, these states would bring the total of electors above 270.
Legal challenges to the compact
But others say that even if the five states agree to join the compact, legal challenges lie ahead. One such challenge is that the compact may need Congress' approval, University of Notre Dame Law Professor Derek Muller wrote in a 2023 blog post, citing two U.S. Supreme Court decisions. We reached out to Muller asking for more details.
It is true that the Compact Clause of the Constitution says states may not agree to anything without congressional approval (emphasis ours):
No State shall, without the Consent of Congress, lay any Duty of Tonnage, keep Troops, or Ships of War in time of Peace, enter into any Agreement or Compact with another State, or with a foreign Power, or engage in War, unless actually invaded, or in such imminent Danger as will not admit of delay.
In other words, it is possible that these states may consider joining the NPVIC. However, the path to enacting it may not be straightforward.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several claims related to the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections, including a rumor that Trump is considering a nuclear strike on Iran.

England check on Palmer - what are Tuchel's other big choices?
- Published
England have made medical checks on Cole Palmer as Thomas Tuchel considers whether to select the Chelsea forward in his next squad.
The 24-year-old missed all four games during the previous international window with a minor injury.
He completed 90 minutes for Chelsea against Brentford before those matches, and started for the Blues in the first game afterwards.
Tuchel, who names his squad to face Croatia and Spain on Friday, said at the time that Palmer was "playing with discomfort and pain" but was "missing too many opportunities" with England.
Whether he is recalled will be a key theme on Friday. While it is normal for England medical staff to check on players under consideration, it also underlines that Palmer remains on Tuchel's radar despite his stark comments in September.
In addition to deciding whether to select Palmer, head coach Tuchel has a number of other dilemmas to resolve.
Bukayo Saka's injury absence opens the door to another attacker, with his Arsenal team-mate Noni Madueke pushing for a recall following a string of impressive performances.
Manchester United forward Marcus Rashford has not played since mid-October and is not fit for selection, while Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah is a major injury doubt.
Defenders Ben White and Djed Spence are pushing for recalls after missing out on the previous squad through injury.
The likes of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice and many others are now stonewall selections - but the intrigue is around the remaining few spots still seemingly up for grabs.
Will some old faces earn a recall or will there be new faces soon pulling on the England shirt? BBC Sport runs down some of the potential candidates for selection.
Josh King
The 19-year-old Fulham midfielder has already been close to a senior England debut.
King travelled to the US as part of the preparation squad before the World Cup, along with Alex Scott, Ethan Nwaneri and Rio Ngumoha.
Scott and Ngumoha have already made their debuts for the senior side and Nwaneri is currently on loan at Borussia Dortmund.
Tuchel said in his last news conference how King is close to a senior call-up and the midfielder has impressed for England Under-21s too.
The biggest challenge for King will be finding a chance to shine in his favoured number 10 position with Bellingham being England's best midfielder and the position being one of real strength for the Three Lions.
Will Lankshear
There is a lack of number nines in the English game and the job of being Harry Kane's understudy is harder than it sounds.
The England captain has just won the Ballon d'Or, likes to play almost every minute for his country and is the captain, record goalscorer and arguably the best player in Tuchel's side.
Dominic Calvert-Lewin has been selected in the squads before and since the World Cup but, despite doing well for Leeds, it has not quite clicked for him under Tuchel and he was given just 15 minutes in two substitute appearances in the last window.
Tuchel has started to use Bellingham as the back-up to Kane, but he could opt for more of a prospect in his squad in this shorter window and turn to Lankshear.
The 21-year-old striker, who like Kane started at Tottenham, was sold to Middlesbrough this summer for £20m and has scored 15 goals in all competitions so far this campaign.
He has scored 13 goals in as many games in the Championship, helping Middlesbrough to the top of the division.
He only made his debut for the England Under-21s during the last international window and scored in that game so it would be quite a rise for a player who is not in the Premier League.
Tuchel is aware of Lankshear and with a lack of number nines across the age groups it could be an interesting option for a manager who is not afraid of making big calls.
He did miss Middlesbrough's loss to Wrexham on Wednesday with a tweaked hamstring but could return in time for Saturday.
Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall
The Everton number 10 has turned down call-ups from the Republic of Ireland as he focuses on his dream of trying to represent the Three Lions.
He has been one of the Toffees' standout performers having scored two goals and registered two assists in all competitions, helping Everton to seventh in the league.
Dewsbury-Hall, 28, is a clever technician with an eye for a pass and his ability on the ball would likely suit international football.
But team-mate James Garner, who Tuchel called a mini-Valverde, was called up before Dewsbury-Hall when there were dropouts in the last international break with that showing perhaps he has more to do to get on Tuchel's radar.
Morgan Gibbs-White
Gibbs-White was probably the unluckiest player to be left out of the initial squad last time around when Tuchel got his players together in September.
But the Nottingham Forest midfielder was called up as a late replacement after a number of high profile pull-outs and left a family holiday to join up with the Three Lions squad.
Tuchel values that kind of dedication and referenced the willingness of Gibbs-White, 26, to join up.
The Forest captain featured during every game of the last break although he did not start a game.
But with Forest struggling at the bottom end of the Premier League table - and competing against the likes of Bellingham, Phil Foden, Palmer and Eberechi Eze - the midfielder could miss out again.
- A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma 
  - Published13 hours ago
Ben White
White has been unlucky since he ended his international hiatus to return in March.
The Arsenal defender missed the World Cup with a knee injury that forced him to also miss the Champions League final.
White then missed the first England squad of this campaign with injury, with Tuchel saying the 29-year-old would have been called up if he had been fit, citing his partnership with Saka as potentially good for the Three Lions.
But White has been available for all but one of Arsenal's games this season and would add a quality defensive option at right-back if selected, especially with Reece James missing through injury.
Jordan Henderson
Henderson has not been in the England set-up since the World Cup, where he fell over an advertising hoarding following the win over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium and broke his arm.
Many would have thought the 36-year-old's international career was over but Henderson, then at Brentford, made a move to Chelsea as they looked to add experience to their young squad.
After recovering from the arm injury, Henderson has surprised some to become an important part of the Chelsea midfield, starting five games in a row and scoring twice in a win over Bournemouth, before he missed the Blues' win over Manchester United with injury.
Henderson is a popular figure, respected by staff and players and is again performing at the top level.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."
- The runner who went viral and sparked a campaign for change for women

- Mashed potato & 19 minutes' sleep - Entrekin's epic race
