Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high ground with about $112 billion in investor cash.
The chatbot industry, though, may find selling ads necessary to defray the high costs of generating AI responses. OpenAI is all in, with over 100,000 customers advertising in ChatGPT since ads debuted there in February. Last week, Google expanded ads in its search chatbot AI Mode to 10 more countries beyond the US and declared that users “find them highly relevant.” Advertisers are far from satisfied with the experience, but they expect it to improve.
Ads stand to be particularly vital for the long-term viability of niche chatbot platforms, which can’t rely on the same degree of venture capital largesse as the top AI labs or the massive revenues of tech giants. I recently spoke with Koah Labs, one of a number of new ad technology companies focused on AI experiences. The San Francisco startup markets itself as bringing ads to over 200 apps, such as DeepAI, which offers tools for creative queries, and Liner, which focuses on providing citations in AI answers. It works with brands like telehealth giant Hims and flower delivery service UrbanStems.
Koah has attracted just a tenth of the advertisers OpenAI has, but CEO Nic Baird still believes he’s getting a good sense of what’s working and what’s fuzzy as chatbots take over from traditional search engines—and what their rise will mean for your AI experiences.
Machine-Crafted
Ads composed partly by AI rather than fully by a human generate double the clicks, Baird says. It’s difficult to assess exactly why, but AI-generated marketing copy likely feels more natural next to the output of an AI model.
Because ads shown by Koah are grounded in product details and imagery supplied by the advertiser, users don’t seem to be encountering AI-hallucinated, erroneous information. But some advertisers, such as drugmakers, face government requirements on what they must—or cannot—say in ads, Baird says. These companies default to more human control over their ads, generating weaker results, according to Baird.
Since ads with dull messages or that feel like clutter could drive users away, the onus is on ad tech companies to find a middle ground that’s engaging to users without triggering risk-averse brands. That balance might be harder to strike when a human is out of the loop.
Creative Targeting
Google searches for “help with stress” are likely to bring up ads for therapists. Chatbots can get more creative, in Baird’s view. For instance, ads for spas have performed well within Koah’s network when shown after users’ prompts related to “stress,” he says.
The key difference, according to Baird, is that Koah can select and customize the ad based on “not only the prompt, or the Google search, but also the response from the AI platform, which brings context from the rest of the conversation thus far.” In addition, chatbot prompts tend to be at least double the length of Google queries, giving Koah more information to determine a relevant ad.
Baird claims users are accustomed to navigating through multiple topics within a chatbot conversation, which could make them more receptive to adjacent marketing than they are in traditional search. Koah says users are clicking on about 3 percent of ads, about on par with the performance of the more mature Google ads system.
All the Context
When called on to show an ad, Koah generally receives a user’s entire conversation up to that point to help inform what it displays. While traditional search queries generally look for specific information, people often use chatbots as not just conversation partners but confidants. It’s unclear whether users will accept the privacy trade-offs that come with personalized chatbot ads as they begin to proliferate.
Baird says Koah anonymizes the queries it receives and stores them in a de-identified way, but he declined to comment any further on the data collection and storage. While acknowledging that personalization can become intrusive, he argues that there are benefits for users and advertisers alike as the tech matures. Nonsensitive information about chatbot discussions, for instance, could inform personalized content on the page that loads after an ad click. Perhaps someone expressed interest in a specific feature, or the AI model didn’t highlight a particular downside of a competing product. The advertiser could fill in the gap.
Koah doesn’t have data on whether people actually want these customized pages, but the tech industry has long argued that people prefer when ad experiences feel relevant. Having the conversation history also could benefit advertisers when Koah enables retargeting, or repeating, an ad to the same user.
Negative Triggers
By Koah’s estimate, one out of every four chatbot queries about a retailer or brand concerns a return, exchange, or other support issue. Baird believes chatbots provide an opportunity not replicated easily elsewhere for advertisers to address what they might politely call a “customer success” matter.
He expects manufacturers and retailers will eventually target disappointed customers to remind them about warranties, engage them in an AI-intermediated support, and potentially steer them away from a more costly customer service interaction. It’s possible that the AI chatbot’s response may provide users with similar help, but buying an ad guarantees companies get their message across.
The ideal outcome is users reaching resolution they can live with more swiftly than through other means. In the worst case, it's a wasted ad buy and a more irate consumer.
Great Unknown
None of the apps Koah currently serves ads in offer users AI agents that can shop on their own. However, apps like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are starting to take over shopping chores for some users. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said Muse could become the company’s biggest source of revenue but suggested it would come from transaction fees rather than ads.
That doesn’t mean advertising will be entirely cut out from bot-dominated ecommerce, with initial studies suggesting that ads could influence AI agents.
Baird expects an opportunity to give “the user's agent the best possible recommendation, and that’s going to be a combination of a great discount, a really relevant product,” and an easy digital path to make the purchase. The chatbot must make “abundantly clear” to the agent what content is sponsored or else risk losing user trust, Baird says.
It’s also possible the chatbot ad market fizzles out before agents take hold if more AI developers adopt Anthropic’s stance. Kevin Baragona, CEO of DeepAI, says while ad revenue has been meaningful, he’s not committed to it because the experience just doesn’t feel right yet in terms of privacy, design, and more.
“I don’t think the ads are working terribly well for anyone,” he says.

A review of 578 patients who presented with breast-related concerns at the Head & Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), Mumbai, over more than three years found that 82.5% had cancerous conditions and 17.5% had non-cancerous conditions. The diagnoses were confirmed through tissue examination.
The findings reveal patients assessed at the institute and cannot be generalised to the wider population or used to estimate the likelihood that a breast lump is cancerous.
Patients diagnosed with breast cancer ranged in age from 23 to 98 years, with an average age of 52.7 years. Tumour sizes varied, with 35.2% measuring up to 2 cm, 43.3% measuring between 2 and 4.9 cm, and 19.3% measuring more than 5 cm.
The institute also reported that 52% of patients had more than four lymph nodes positive for cancer. Lymph node involvement is one of the factors doctors consider when assessing the extent of breast cancer and planning treatment.
Mastectomy, which involves removing the breast, was the most common surgery recorded.
Recognising unusual breast changes and seeking medical advice can help establish a diagnosis and guide appropriate care. Not every lump requires cancer treatment, but changes should be assessed .

How one family gave a critical boost to gene therapy research
A family's fundraising for gene therapy research pays off
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
When Eliza O'Neill was little, she was one of those kids who always needed to have an accessory, like a hat or a scarf.
"She would always go get my high heels from the closet and clop around in those — which she scared us to death," says her mom, Cara O'Neill, a pediatrician in Columbia, S.C.
But by the time Eliza turned 3, her parents noticed she was falling behind on developmental milestones. She was diagnosed with a pragmatic speech delay, meaning she had learned a lot of words, for example, but she wasn't using them in a typical way in social situations.
In 2013, one of Cara's colleagues suggested testing Eliza for a group of metabolic disorders — just to rule them out.
But the test came back positive for something called Sanfilippo syndrome.
Cara remembered learning about the rare inherited disease back in medical school.
"When they said the word, it all kind of came rushing back," she says. "And it was just this bale of dread, like, oh, my goodness, this is horrific."
Children with Sanfilippo have a faulty gene that leaves them unable to break down heparin sulfate, a molecule critical to normal cell function. As it builds up in the body, it causes severe complications.
Kids with Sanfilippo lose their ability to speak and walk. They have seizures, and they usually don't live past their teens, according to the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation, which the O'Neills started and continue to run.
For Eliza's dad, Glenn O'Neill, it took a little while after learning Eliza's test results for the diagnosis to sink in.
"It wasn't really until I got home that I realized how quickly the degeneration happened," he says. "And that was really the point where we said, 'Gosh. Whatever we need to do, we need to do it now.'"
Researching a treatment
At Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio, researcher Haiyan Fu had been working on a gene therapy in mice for Sanfilippo since the late-1990s.
The therapy used a modified virus to deliver a working copy of the broken gene to patients' cells.
Fu realized the experimental therapy was promising. "And if we treat early, it could be potentially a cure," she says. "So I can't give up."
Keeping it going – and funded – was challenging, though. She thought she would have to quit in 2009. But the families of kids with Sanfilippo stopped her.
"They said, 'You can't leave. Can we give you some of the funds for you to, you know, carry on?'" Fu recalls, explaining that these families had helped her from the beginning and didn't want to see her work stop.
In all, eight patient foundations, including Ben's Dream and a Cure for Kirby, kept Fu's work going until the research was ready for the first human trial.
Raising the money
But a clinical trial would be expensive. Glenn O'Neill had an idea for how to raise the money.
"We reached out on a whim to some strangers that we found on the internet about making a viral video," he says, referring to filmmaker Benjamin Von Wong, who made them a video over a few days in 2014.
It worked.
In the spring of 2014, the Saving Eliza video helped the O'Neills break GoFundMe's record at the time, raising a million dollars in just a few weeks. Soon, it hit $2 million.
The money raised helped fund the first human trial, which started in May 2016.
The experiments were promising enough for the biotech industry to take notice.
Ultimately, a biotech company called Ultragenyx acquired the rights to the gene therapy in 2022 and kept studying it. A few years later, the company submitted data to the Food and Drug Administration for review.
The FDA approved the gene therapy in September. The one-time infusion is called Fayuvi.
"The treatment will work best the younger the child is because the more brain is remaining," says Ultragenyx CEO Emil Kakkis. "By the time they're 2 or 3 or 4 years old diagnosed, getting figured out, they've lost a lot of ground. And we have treated a few kids that were in the 6-month age that have done really well. And our view is that when you treat them really young, you actually get better gene therapy results."
Ultragenyx set the price for the treatment at nearly $4 million, tying it for the second most expensive gene therapy ever, according to 46brooklyn, a drug price research firm.
Kakkis says Ultragenyx is committed to making sure every patient is treated, regardless of the price. "There should be no logistical location, site or state or other kind of rule that stops us from getting the patient treated. We understand what [we've] got to do."
Moments after the FDA approval was announced, Fu got a call from Cara O'Neill — and messages from other families that funded her research. Some had lost a child along the way.
Fu says Fayuvi's approval is good news, but it brings mixed emotions for her: "It shouldn't take this long."
As for Eliza, she's almost 17 now. She was the very first patient to get the gene therapy as part of a clinical trial back in 2016.
Because she was 6 years old when she was treated with the gene therapy, she had already lost her ability to speak. It never returned, but she can communicate with picture cards and devices. Eliza goes to school. And this summer, she swam and learned to float on a pool noodle.
"I just feel proud of my girl. You know?" Glenn O'Neill says. "I feel proud of her. It's been a rough road for her, but we also know she's very lucky."

This luxury festival is the first exhibition supported by a HK$100 million government fund, spearheaded by the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau to attract large-scale, distinctive international exhibitions to Hong Kong. It brought yachts, prestige cars, jewellery and art to AsiaWorld-Expo (AWE), connecting its indoor halls with the newly developed AWE Waterfront.
Organised by Informa Markets and held from November 4 to 6, the Festival of Connoisseurs (TFOC) offered more than a showcase of fine craftsmanship and luxury living. For AWE, the event also marked an investment into a new setting for exhibitions - the AWE Waterfront, which includes a dedicated pier. Airport Authority Hong Kong (AAHK) took the lead in the construction work, collaborating with AWE on assessments, design and delivery to bring the waterfront showcase to life.
Meticulous Planning for the Waterfront Exhibition Area
Behind the visitor experience was approximately a year of festival preparation. The result was a “sea-and-land dual-stage” format that gave visitors different ways to explore the festival. Along the waterfront, they could board yachts, examine their design and craftsmanship, and meet brand representatives. Luxury cars and dining experiences added to the outdoor offering.
AWE Waterfront was jointly coordinated by the engineering team of the AAHK and AWE. The teams conducted site visits to renowned international yachting events in Australia, Monaco, USA and Singapore, while advancing planning and design, procurement and component prefabrication in parallel. Once the components arrived on site, the entire construction process and safety testing were completed in just three weeks.
The airport location presented its own set of engineering and operational challenges. The team had to account for wave conditions, airport height restrictions and seabed characteristics, developing a temporary wave attenuation system comprising six large flat-top pontoons working alongside floating wave barriers. Berthing positions, anchoring arrangements and floating access walkways were also carefully planned to ensure the safe operation of the exhibition.
Given the site's proximity to major high-speed ferry routes serving the fire and rescue pier and SkyPier, early coordination with relevant government departments was essential to secure approvals and establish maritime access arrangements. Emergency response protocols and tugboat standby arrangements were also put in place, enabling the airport's waterfront to accommodate an international yacht exhibition.
AWE Waterfront offers a glimpse of SKYTOPIA, AAHK’s vision for a world-class airport-city destination integrating commercial activity, culture, tourism, entertainment and leisure. It offered visitors an early glimpse of this vision, including an early look at the future Airport Bay Marina, an essential component in the blueprint.
Inside, nine themed “worlds” brought together yachts, automobiles, jewellery, watches, art and other lifestyle interests. More than 60 expert presentations, masterclasses and performances unfolded across five stages, complemented by whisky tastings, food pairings, watchmaking workshops and private jewellery viewings.
The appeal lay as much in the connections between these experiences as in the individual displays. Visitors could move from an intimate workshop or viewing inside the halls to a yacht visit outdoors, exploring different aspects of the festival without leaving the venue.
That flexibility is central to AWE’s ambitions: an exhibition need not stop at the hall doors, and waterfront activities need not stand apart from the main programme.
“We are excited to bring a new land-and-sea exhibition concept to life at AsiaWorld-Expo, taking the exhibition experience beyond traditional boundaries.” She added, “We worked closely with the organiser to bring TFOC to Hong Kong, investing in dedicated berthing facilities and waterfront upgrades to make this concept possible. By connecting the indoor exhibition with the waterfront Marina Showcase, we are opening up new possibilities for international events in Hong Kong.”
Indoor and outdoor integration for connected experiences
This vision of connected experiences also underpins AWE’s Phase 2 expansion, which is targeted for construction completion by the end of 2028. Its centrepiece, the Super Arena, is being designed to host international productions, major live events and elite sporting competitions, with flexible staging configurations and room for more than 20,000 spectators.

‘Don’t need blessings of foreign powers': Hasina on if she wants US, India to pressure Bangladesh for her safe return
Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Sheikh Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for the deadly crackdown on youth protesters.
Former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she does not need the backing of any foreign country to return home. Her decision to return to Bangladesh from exile in India by December remains unchanged despite the possibility of arrest or death, Hasina said on Thursday.
Asked whether she expected countries such as the United States and India to put pressure on Bangladesh to ensure her safe return, the ousted leader said she was not seeking foreign protection.
“I value friendship and cooperation with all nations. That has always been our (Bangladesh's) foreign policy. But I do not need the blessing of a foreign power to return to my own country,” Hasina told news agency AP in an email interview.
ALSO READ | Exclusive: Return to Bangladesh not about power but to stand by people, says ex-PM Sheikh Hasina
Hasina fled Bangladesh in August 2024 after a student-led uprising forced her out of power. She has been living in India ever since and has repeatedly expressed her intention to go back to Bangladesh in December, despite being sentenced to death by a Bangladeshi tribunal over the crackdown on protesters.
“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she told AP. “So, I will return to Bangladesh. That decision has not changed.”
Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for crimes against humanity over the deadly crackdown on student-led protests in July-August 2024. Nearly 1,400 people were killed during the violence, according to the United Nations. Hasina has denied wrongdoing, rejected the verdict and questioned the legitimacy of the trial.
Bangladesh has repeatedly sought her extradition, but India has not handed her over.
Hasina acknowledges risk of arrest, torture on return
Earlier this year in a virtual press conference from Delhi, Hasina acknowledged the risks involved in returning, saying she could be killed, arrested or tortured as soon as she landed in Bangladesh. "Now I have decided. Yes, I know. If I go back, the moment I will land they can kill me, or they can arrest me and torture me," she said.
She also thanked the Indian government and people for providing her shelter after she fled Bangladesh, saying she had not planned to leave her country.
In a September interview with HT, Hasina said that she intended to return by December and would announce the date, time and point of entry later.
"I have said I intend to return by December because Bangladesh’s political crisis cannot be allowed to continue indefinitely. I will announce the specific date, time and point of entry in due course," she said.
She also maintained that her return was not about regaining power but about standing with the people of Bangladesh.
"My decision to return is my own, and it is a matter of political discussion within my party," she said, adding that the timing of the return of other Awami League leaders living abroad would depend on consultations within the party and an assessment of the security situation.
ALSO READ | Indian envoy on giving shelter to Sheikh Hasina: 'It was our duty...she was still Bangladesh PM'
Hasina alleges persecution of Awami League members
In the HT interview, Hasina also accused the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government of continuing the persecution of Awami League leaders and workers, alleging that party members were being killed, arrested and targeted through criminal cases.
She claimed that more than 600 cases had been filed against her and described the judicial proceedings as politically motivated. She also alleged that party workers and their families had faced attacks, harassment and displacement.
Questioning the ban on the Awami League, Hasina said the party should be allowed to contest elections and let voters decide its political future. "Why did they ban the Awami League? If the Awami League has done a lot of bad things, let the people decide," she said.
Hasina also criticised the BNP government's reported plan to acquire Chinese J-10CE fighter jets under a $2.3-billion deal, questioning the spending at a time when Bangladesh was facing power and gas shortages, rising prices and economic difficulties.
She further raised concerns over the growing influence of extremist groups, warning that developments in Bangladesh could have implications for regional security and neighbouring countries.

Elon Musk’s X account went unusually dark Tuesday evening as US election results rolled in, each new count deepening a reckoning for the world’s richest man, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns this year.
Shortly after 1 am, Musk posted twice: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote first. About a minute later, he added, “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time” with a shrug emoji.
By Wednesday morning, candidates backed by Musk’s America PAC had lost 20 races and won only one, with 21 uncalled, according to a WIRED analysis of election data. Tesla and SpaceX stocks have plunged in value.
Musk and his PAC spent more than $400 million since Trump retook office backing Republican candidates—nearly $87 million of it on ads targeting 42 midterm races. He also funneled more than $229 million into other political groups, chiefly the main Republican super PACs for the House and Senate, along with smaller ones formed to fight single races in Kentucky and Texas.
Of every traceable dollar Musk put into a race that has now been decided, more than 99 cents went to a race he lost.
America PAC ran ads in seven Senate races this cycle; six have been called, and Musk’s side lost all six. Sherrod Brown took back Ohio, Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan (where the PAC spent $9.2 million on ads), Josh Turek flipped Iowa, and in Maine, Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins, a feat Democrats had long thought impossible, ending Collins’ 30-year career in the senate. As of publication time, only Alaska remains uncalled.
America PAC did not respond to a request for comment.
Texas hosted the costliest Senate race in American history, and Musk paid for more of it than anyone. Through mid-October, Texas PAC, a group funded entirely with money he routed through the Senate Leadership Fund, had spent $148 million on the contest, nearly $79 million of it attacking Democrat James Talarico and nearly $70 million propping up Ken Paxton, the state's scandal-plagued attorney general. America PAC added another $47 million, straight from Musk.
In October, Musk posted: “There is something deeply wrong with Talarico.” Talarico replied: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”
Musk’s millions were wasted: Shortly after 11 pm, the Associated Press called the race for Talarico, sealing Paxton’s defeat and opening a night in which Democrats toppled the Republican leadership in Austin that had spent years courting Musk’s companies with grants and tax breaks.
Come January, Democrats will hold sway over much of his Texas empire, including the more than $1.6 billion in tax incentives overseen by the office of ousted governor Greg Abbott—who lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday night. (Nathan Johnson will also become the state’s first Democratic attorney general in decades.) Musk’s interests in Texas are exceedingly expensive, and they include a SpaceX chip plant the state valued at more than $16.8 billion, Tesla’s robotaxi fleet, and SpaceX’s Starbase launch site.
Musk’s defeat in Texas was long in the making. Lone Star Liberty PAC, which his personal trust gave $10 million, spent $6.7 million clearing Paxton’s path to the nomination. It put $3.6 million against John Cornyn, the state’s senior senator for more than two decades, and $3.1 million against Houston congressman Wesley Hunt. Hunt finished third in March, and Cornyn lost the runoff in May. By June, Musk had his nominee: Paxton, a top law enforcement official who had spent nearly a decade under indictment for securities fraud, been reported to the FBI by his own top deputies over bribery allegations, and survived an impeachment trial in the Texas Senate.
In Michigan, America PAC spent $5.5 million attacking El-Sayed and $3.7 million propping up Mike Rogers, a former congressman who had lost a Senate bid two years earlier. In the closing weeks, Rogers, Trump and vice president JD Vance each suggested El-Sayed or his family were tied to the Muslim Brotherhood. Haley Stevens, the congresswoman El-Sayed had beaten in the bitter Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers days before the vote.
The AP called the race for El-Sayed at 2:27 am. Addressing the outside money in his victory speech, he told supporters they had “built something bigger than a bank account.” On the same ballot, Michigan voters approved a measure barring political donations from utilities and large state contractors.
Musk put $10 million into Fight for Kentucky in January, a group formed to win the Republican nomination for the open seat of retiring Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell. It spent $9.6 million promoting Nate Morris, who quit two weeks before his primary after Trump offered him an ambassadorship to Colombia. Andy Barr, the seven-term congressman the group had spent an additional $3.8 million attacking, won the seat by 12 points on Tuesday.
Weeks earlier, after Politico reported that Democrats were weighing investigations of his companies, Musk posted: “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.” Asked by an X user Tuesday evening when the televised trials of Big Tech executives would begin, senator Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, wrote, “They are going to need to plant new forests for all the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

Multi-family office and wealth management group Daksham Capital has launched its maiden consumer-focused fund, Daksham Growth Ventures (DGV) Fund I, with a target corpus of ₹150 Cr and a ₹150 Cr greenshoe option. The fund has secured around ₹125 Cr in its first close, following its registration as a SEBI Category II AIF last month. Family offices, high-net-worth individuals (HNIs), ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNIs), and entrepreneurs participated in the first close. The fund will continue raising capital towards its target, including the greenshoe option. Led by cofounder and managing partner Shivam Diwan, DGV plans to invest in 10-15 startups, with cheques ranging from ₹5 Cr to ₹20 Cr. It will primarily back Pre-Series A and Series A startups, while considering select later-stage investments. Its investment mandate spans D2C brands, consumer enablers, B2B2C platforms, supply-chain businesses, and startups using AI in consumer services. Betting On Capital Efficiency DGV will focus on businesses with established product-market fit rather than those still testing demand, Diwan told Inc42. “We will only come where the product-market-fit risk is established,” he said. The fund will typically evaluate startups with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of ₹25-75 Cr, assessing their unit economics, addressable market, founders’ execution capabilities, and differentiation. It is targeting businesses with the potential to scale annual revenue to ₹300-500 Cr. Startups need not be profitable when DGV invests, but the fund expects them to have positive or neutral contribution margins, even if they remain loss-making at the EBITDA level. “Growth by burning an enormous amount of money is not the mantra. It should be a capital-efficient business,” Diwan said. Beyond capital, DGV plans to help portfolio startups with corporate governance, financial reporting, brand positioning, leadership development, and distribution expansion. It also intends to provide board-level guidance and access to its industry network. The fund will evaluate businesses across food and beverages, apparel, snacking, beauty and personal care, accessories, jewellery, and bags. Direct consumer businesses are expected to account for 50-70% of its investments. The remainder will go towards consumer enablers, including contract manufacturers, sourcing and supply chain companies, and B2B2C platforms. DGV is also open to businesses outside the traditional consumer sector, provided their growth is linked to consumer demand. Diwan said the fund is evaluating startups across food and beverages, accessories, and B2B2C segments, including a few D2C brands. It is yet to make an investment. DGV will also consider a small number of late-stage investments in startups that could go public within two to three years. These deals are likely to comprise largely secondary transactions, Diwan said. Bullish On Consumer AI And Enablers DGV expects AI to play a growing role in consumer businesses over the next decade, particularly in product discovery, personalisation, customer acquisition, and fulfilment. While it does not intend to invest directly in deeptech or standalone AI startups, the fund will evaluate consumer businesses using AI to improve customer engagement and operations. Diwan expects consumer AI to gain momentum over the next 12-24 months, with startups increasingly integrating the technology into how consumers discover, evaluate, and purchase products. The fund is also bullish on consumer enablers, particularly contract manufacturers and B2B businesses supplying multiple brands. Diwan said these businesses offer exposure to demand across several brands, reducing dependence on a single consumer-facing startup. Daksham’s launch adds to the pool of dedicated capital targeting Indian consumer businesses. Earlier this year, Kairon Capital announced the ₹90 Cr first close of its maiden consumer-focused fund against a ₹150 Cr target and a ₹50 Cr greenshoe option. Fireside Ventures closed its fourth fund at ₹2,265 Cr ($253 Mn) in December last year. The fund aims to invest in 30-35 early-stage consumer brands, with initial cheques of $1 Mn to $12 Mn, across categories including health and wellness, food and beverages, beauty and personal care, and lifestyle.

A video circulating on social media purportedly shows External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar recounting how a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute, questioning India’s position on China before he advised Russia on its conflict with Ukraine. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar recounting how a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute.
Fact: The viral video is manipulated. It features an actual video of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar speaking in Atlanta, US, about discussions on the Russia-Ukraine conflict at the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. The original audio has been replaced with fabricated remarks. The MEA Fact Check also flagged the viral video as fake. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements confirming the claim.
We also reviewed the official social media accounts of the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) (here, here, and here) and S Jaishankar (here, here, and here) but found no mention of the alleged exchange or the remarks attributed to him.
We noticed that the viral video carries a watermark from the news agency ANI. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 01 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Jaishankar, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, his actual remarks in the original video were entirely different. He was speaking in Atlanta, US, about the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and discussions on the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The viral clip has been manipulated, with fabricated audio added to the original footage.
Suspecting the video was doctored, we analysed it with multiple AI detection tools, including Hive AI and NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector. Hive AI gave an aggregate score of 99.4%, indicating a high likelihood of AI-generated or manipulated content. NVIDIA’s detector also classified the footage as synthetic media.
The MEA Fact Check also debunked the claim in an X post (archived) dated 3 November 2026, flagging the viral video as fake and cautioning against the circulation of such malicious posts on social media.
To sum up, this viral video of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar allegedly saying a Russian minister mocked him over the India-China border dispute is a deepfake.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Australian woman shot during Bondi Beach attack dies almost a year later
- Published
A 90-year-old woman who was shot during Australia's Bondi Beach attack last December has died in a Sydney hospital, almost a year after the mass fatal shootings.
Eva Geller was one of dozens who were seriously injured after two gunmen opened fire on a Jewish event in Bondi Beach on 14 December. Fifteen people were killed including a ten-year-old girl.
Rabbi Aron Moss from the Nefesh Synagogue said Geller, who escaped the Holocaust as a child, had remained as "positive, loving, and strong throughout her life, right until the end".
Australian leader Anthony Albanese has expressed his condolences, saying the country would never forget those who "continue to carry the pain" of last year's attacks.
The attack last December was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One of the gunmen, Sajid Akram, 50, was killed by police at the scene. His son Naveed Akram was arrested and charged with 15 counts of murder, 40 charges of attempted murder and one count of committing a terrorist act. He remains before the courts.
Police have not provided any detail on possible further charges as a result of Geller's death.
On Friday, Rabbi Moss confirmed that Geller - who celebrated her 90th birthday earlier this year - had passed away last on Thursday night.
"She escaped the Holocaust as a child, eventually coming to Australia, and built a beautiful family," he said.
Her injuries from the shootings meant regular hospital treatment.
"Ever since being shot at the Bondi attack she'd been in and out of hospital, always wanting to come home. She was told she will never walk again but miraculously and with incredible determination she did walk again," said Rabbi Moss.
Geller had "came to shul (Yiddish for synagogue) this past High Holidays with an incredible show of strength," he added.
New South Wales police said it was aware the woman had died overnight and "are now awaiting further advice and are working with the office of the Coroner".

A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.
A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.
The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.
Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.
In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”
Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.
British health authorities say the risk to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.
There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.
Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.
As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.
Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included:
- High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.
- Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.
- Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.
- LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.
North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.
One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.
He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.

"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.
The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

Srinagar, Nov 06: National Conference legislator Nazir Ahmad Gurezi on Friday rejected speculation about the emergence of a breakaway group within the ruling party, saying legislators who had recently met among themselves had only sought to raise their concerns before the party leadership.
Speaking to reporters after meeting National Conference president Farooq Abdullah and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah along with other party legislators at the Gupkar residence, Gurezi said the leadership had assured them that their grievances would be addressed, with some matters to be resolved immediately and others in a phased manner.
“We are legislators of the National Conference. Whenever we have issues, we take them to our party leadership. A few days ago, we sat together at one place, but social media portrayed it as if a separate party had emerged from the National Conference. There was no such group,” Gurezi said.
He said the legislators had placed their concerns directly before Farooq Abdullah and Omar Abdullah during the meeting.
“There were certain issues which we brought before the honourable Chief Minister and Farooq Sahib. They have assured us that whether these are political issues or other matters, some will be addressed immediately while others will be resolved gradually,” he said.
The remarks come amid speculation over differences within the National Conference following the recent cabinet expansion, which had triggered discontent among a section of party legislators.
The legislators had earlier held consultations among themselves, prompting speculation about the emergence of a separate faction within the party.
Gurezi, however, maintained that the meetings were intended to discuss concerns and seek their resolution through the party's established leadership rather than challenge its authority.
He said the latest interaction had provided an opportunity for the legislators to present their grievances directly to the leadership and receive assurances on their resolution.
The meeting assumes significance against the backdrop of recent political developments within the National Conference, with the leadership seeking to address concerns raised by its legislators.
Gurezi's statement indicated that the legislators would continue to pursue their demands within the party, while awaiting action on the assurances given by Farooq Abdullah and Omar Abdullah. (KNS)

Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
- Published
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

Gujarat: Bhavnagar court sentences man to life for murdering live-in partner at ST bus stand
A Bhavnagar court convicted Faizal Lakhani in the Kajal Baraiya murder case, citing eyewitness accounts, CCTV footage and forensic evidence.
A sessions court in Gujarat’s Bhavnagar has sentenced Faizal alias Khatki Rafikbhai Lakhani to life imprisonment for murdering his live-in partner, Kajalben Dilipbhai Baraiya, at the Bhavnagar ST Bus Stand, holding the charges proved beyond reasonable doubt on eyewitness testimonies, CCTV footage, forensic evidence and the postmortem report.
The court’s verdict came just over two months after the murder, with district and sessions judge R.V. Bukhari convicting Lakhani in the case registered by the Nilambag Police on September 4.
The prosecution, led by Special Public Prosecutor Utpal Dave, relied on eyewitness testimonies, CCTV footage, forensic evidence and the postmortem report from Sir T. Hospital.
Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi posted on X: “62 days. Life imprisonment until the last breath. In the Kajal Baraiya murder case in Bhavnagar, swift investigation by Bhavnagar Police and a strong prosecution led to a landmark verdict. Gujarat’s zero tolerance for crimes against women is clear.”
According to the complaint, Kajalben was attacked at the main gate of the Bhavnagar ST Bus Stand on September 3 between 3 pm and 4 pm. Her mother, Bhaguben, told police that the couple had lived together on the footpath near the bus stand for around eight years and often quarrelled.
An eyewitness said Faizal arrived, accused Kajalben of having a relationship with the eyewitness while he was in jail, then kicked and threw her down, slamming her onto the tiles. She died at Sir T. Hospital.
According to a statement by the Nilambag Police, a Special Investigation Team (SIT) under Range Inspector General (IG) Rajendra Asari, Superintendent of Police (SP) Nitesh Pandey and Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) R.R. Singhal filed the charge sheet on October 4, completing the investigation process within 31 days, in what police said was the first such case in the district.
Police said Lakhani, a native of Vartej living on the bus stand footpath, had been involved in five to six earlier cases, including loot, violence and assault on police. He had been released on bail with the victim’s help shortly before the murder.
The press statement also said that the accused arranged the kidnapping of a key eyewitness and kept him confined for three days to prevent him from testifying; a separate case was registered, and the witness later deposed in court.
Days after the murder, during the reconstruction of the crime scene, police flogged Lakhani at the same spot, with officials claiming that the action was taken to appease public sentiment. A video of the flogging was widely shred on social media.

Google, Meta and TikTok sue California over its child safety social media law
In separate lawsuits, the firms said the law violates the US Constitution's First Amendment free speech protections

Tech giants Google, Meta Platforms and TikTok have launched legal action against California to block the enforcement of a new state law designed to curb social media addiction in children under 16.
The legislation, titled Assembly Bill 1709, bars platforms from exposing minors to "psychologically exploitative features" that trigger compulsive usage, including algorithmic recommendations and autoplaying video functions. It further mandates the removal of young users' accounts that incorporate such tools.
In distinct lawsuits submitted on Wednesday, the companies claimed the statute unfairly compels them to follow California’s favoured method of displaying content to children, overriding parental control.
The platforms asserted that the law infringes upon First Amendment free speech guarantees within the US Constitution, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which provides broad legal protection to websites regarding user-submitted content.
Responding on Thursday, the office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the sole defendant tasked with enforcing state legislation. said it was reviewing the legal challenges.
"Our office is committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online," the office stated. Google is an Alphabet subsidiary that owns YouTube, Meta operates Facebook and Instagram, and TikTok belongs to Chinese firm ByteDance.
What the companies say
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10, saying children's safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk."
The law takes effect on January 1, 2027, unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold. "Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda said on Thursday.
"Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts, while leaving children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services. TikTok, meanwhile, said protected speech "cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable."
Other critics also accused California of overreaching. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law "a massive privacy and free speech nightmare."
Thousands of lawsuits allege addiction
Many US states regulate children's access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and limit teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all US states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws. Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.
The companies and Snapchat parent Snap still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

EXCLUSIVE: Halloween may be over, but the horrors never cease — election notwithstanding. With that, some big news today: Sources tell Deadline that Lionsgate and subsidiary 3 Arts Entertainment are partnering to launch Render Road, a new horror production banner.
This is the initiative Lionsgate CEO John Feltheimer alluded to on today’s Q2 earnings call, when he referred to something to come “soon” from 3 Arts in the horror space. Luke Maxwell and Will Rowbotham, two of the manager-producers leading the charge in cultivating new generations of horror filmmaking talent, will spearhead the effort for 3 Arts.
Render Road, we’re told, will develop, produce and finance projects for digital alongside traditional films and television series. This comes as those two lanes continue to converge. The company will collaborate with up-and-comers and established artists alike; they’’l shepherd some projects independently, alongside these artists, and guide others in partnership with other studios and production companies.
Watch on Deadline
The new banner allows Lionsgate to benefit more directly from 3 Arts’ talent pipeline. Serving in a sense as curators, 3 Arts’ Maxwell and Rowbotham will in turn build on Lionsgate’s legacy as home to such major horror properties as Saw, Blair Witch and House of 1000 Corpses.
To be clear, Maxwell and Rowbotham will remain managers at 3 Arts while at the helm of Render Road, which will be open to all, rather than collaborating exclusively with 3 Arts talent. Meanwhile, it’s understood that Maxwell and Rowbotham will take their clients’ lead on the destination for their own projects.
3 Arts — and the Render Road duo of Maxwell and Rowbotham, in particular — have made major waves in horror in recent years, demonstrating a savvy in identifying the star filmmakers of tomorrow and bringing them through their breakout projects.
Most notably, client Kane Parsons smashed records this summer with over $400M for horror phenomenon Backrooms, the highest grossing film in A24 history. Alongside Curry Barker’s Obsession ($523Mww), the film was one of the biggest of the year in the horror space and has brought creator-driven horror to the town’s attention as the next big thing in theatrical. This, as Gen Z and millennials lead the way in theatrical attendance growth, per a recent Fandango study. Outgrossing The Mandalorian and Grogu, it set A24 opening records in 41 countries; Parsons was just 19 years old when we exclusively reported that he’d been signed to direct the film, based on his same-name web series and the creepypasta that inspired it.
Beyond Parsons, 3 Arts reps such buzzy talents as Ian Tuason, of A24’s Undertone, who is directing the next installment of the Paranormal Activity franchise, and Nic Curcio, who made Play House for little more than 100K after winning a Fantastic Fest pitch competition and a year later wound up with distribution through Focus Features. Then, there’s Dylan Clark, who is directing Lionsgate and Blumhouse Atomic’s new Blair Witch as well as Lionsgate’s Portrait of God, starring Chase Infiniti. The latter time is bringing horror icons Sam Raimi and Jordan Peele together as producers for the first time.
As previously alluded to, Parsons and Curry led the industry toward a fundamental shift in recent months that has broadened or reshaped their thinking on the kinds of projects to greenlight and who to make them with. Their success followed that of Markiplier, who with the self-financed and self-distributed video game adaptation Iron Lung ($50M), took the first shot across the bow to demonstrate that creators will play a substantial role in the future of Hollywood, and entertainment, more broadly.
The summer of Obsession and Backrooms has led studios down the path of investing further in young digital native filmmakers, and quickly. Focus Features set up Barker’s follow-up Anything but Ghosts while inking the deal to release Obsession. Meanwhile, studios have also gotten behind young talent on horror titles such as The Mandela Catalogue (Amazon/UA/Amblin), Siren Head (Warner Bros.), Cartoon Cat (TriStar) and Portrait of God (Lionsgate) — some based on preexisting IP, some not.
Most recently kicking off production on a new chapter of Blair Witch and greenlighting Portrait of God, Lionsgate is presently at work developing the next installment of Saw, directed by Mike P. Nelson, as well as Sam Raimi’s remake of the ventriloquist dummy horror flick Magic.

Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates, resident tells BBC
A resident of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region, says that the atmosphere is calm but people are very stressed after fighting broke out between government troops and the party that controls the region on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to full-scale civil war.
He says that many banks have been running low on cash for months, leaving people to rely on mobile banking, with fears that could now be blocked.
An adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister accused the Tigray People's Liberation Front of launching an all-out offensive, including in the two neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. The Tigrayans say they are engaged in defensive combat.

Katon Moyong, popularly known as ‘Abor Man’ and a prominent voice opposing the proposed 11,200-MW hydropower project in the Siang valley of Arunachal Pradesh, has rejected the State government’s offer of talks, saying the time for negotiations has passed.
The engineer-turned-activist, whom the Delhi Police detained recently for protesting the project in the national capital, dismissed the government’s national security argument for building the dam on the Siang river as an attempt to overcome public resistance.
The Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), one of the biggest hydropower projects planned in the north-eastern State, envisages the construction of a large dam across the Siang. It will be executed by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation.
The project has been facing stiff resistance from the Adi community, particularly in the Siang region, over concerns about the displacement of people, the submergence of ancestral lands and forests, and the impact on their cultural and ecological heritage.
The Arunachal Pradesh government has said the project is primarily aimed at storing and managing water in the Siang basin, particularly in view of concerns over China’s proposed mega dam on the river upstream.
Mr. Moyong said the Adi community’s position against the dam remained unchanged, alleging that the government’s push for the project was politically motivated, with an eye on the 2029 Assembly elections. He appealed to the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh to remain united against the project, and cautioned them against “attempts to divide” different tribes over the issue.
“The time for discussion on the SUMP has passed,” he told a press conference at the Arunachal Press Club in Itanagar on Thursday (November 5, 2026). “Let there be dams on smaller rivers, but not on the Siang. Either the entire Adi community will have to be exterminated to build the Siang dam, or there will be no Siang dam.”
Mr. Moyong claimed the first proposal for a dam on the Siang was introduced in 1979 under the banner of Brahmaputra flood control, but was rejected by the Adi community. He blamed the government of the late Chief Minister Dorjee Khandu for signing 145 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with power developers and private companies, which he alleged had pushed the State into a huge debt burden.
Successive governments changed the justification for the project over the years, describing it as a flood mitigation initiative, a project of national interest and a national project, before the present government began promoting it as a national security imperative, he claimed.
Protesters have been demanding an immediate stop to the continuing Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) activities and survey work for the project. They have also sought the withdrawal of security forces deployed in areas likely to be affected.
The government, however, has maintained that the 11,000-MW project would drive economic and social growth, generate employment and self-employment opportunities for youth, and strengthen water and energy security for the State and the nation.

The US Food and Drug Administration has approved an India-made generic version of the world's only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV -- a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organisations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy's Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
The drug is expected to cost USD 40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they're needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don't always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Perez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organisation Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS -- and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV programme for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organisation.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can't be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is USD 28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that's similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casa said she's optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”

Voters approved Question 1, which places protections for first- and second-trimester abortions in the state constitution. However, it also gives the state Legislature the power to pass some restrictions on abortions in the third trimester.
As the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections rolled in, posts on social media suggested that Virginia voters had approved an amendment to the state's constitution that would allow, as one X post put it, "the abortion of babies who are minutes from being born."
Snopes readers also contacted us looking for more information about the supposed vote.
The claim is false.
The posts used common anti-abortion framing to create a misleading description of a real proposal on the ballot, Question 1. The measure, which voters overwhelmingly approved, does enshrine in Virginia's constitution an individual's right to receive an abortion.
However, the measure explicitly contains an exception allowing the state Legislature to pass laws that restrict access to some abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy. Because this exception exists, Virginia voters did not approve "abortions up to birth."
It's also worth reviewing basic facts about abortions — doing so reveals that the anti-abortion posts are using dramatic language to attack a strawman argument they created.
The strawman argument
The misleading posts do not mention how far into their pregnancies women generally receive abortions. That's because the language of the claim relies on the idea that late-term abortions are a common practice, while the medical data shows they are quite uncommon.
According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the premier professional association for OB/GYNs in the U.S., less than 1% of abortions in the country are performed in the third trimester, and about 1% of abortions are performed after the woman has reached 21 weeks of pregnancy. The nonprofit Guttmacher Institute, a highly reputable source of information on abortion data, estimated that doctors performed 1.13 million abortion procedures throughout the country in 2025. Therefore, only about 11,300 abortions total were performed after the 21-week mark, still seven weeks shy of the third trimester.
In sum, late-term abortions are incredibly rare. The ACOG lists the following reasons why they are performed:
- As a result of a fetal diagnosis received later in pregnancy that may have a profound impact on the pregnancy's prognosis
- As a result of a diagnosis related to risks to their own health during pregnancy that did not present until later in pregnancy
- Not recognizing that they were pregnant until later in the pregnancy, which may delay them in presenting to start care
- Barriers to obtaining care earlier in pregnancy, including limited financial means, inability to travel, or work or childcare obligations
- A combination of any of the above
To put it another way, doctors, who take an oath to do no harm, perform late-term abortions because the baby is "life-limiting," the mother may not survive the pregnancy or the mother couldn't have the procedure earlier, even if she wanted to.
Question 1, explained
Question 1 enshrines the right to an abortion without any limitations through the first and second trimesters of pregnancy, amongst other reproductive care. This language reinforces the access currently available under Virginia law, according to reproductive healthcare nonprofit Planned Parenthood.
The amendment specifically permits the state Legislature to enact laws restricting abortions in the third trimester of pregnancy, with caveats. Those laws may not restrict abortions "unless the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive," according to the wording on the ballot.
The following paragraph is the actual language of that caveat that will be added to the state constitution, according to Ballotpedia:
Notwithstanding the above, the Commonwealth may regulate the provision of abortion care in the third trimester, provided that in no circumstance shall the Commonwealth prohibit an abortion (i) that in the professional judgment of a physician is medically indicated to protect the life or physical or mental health of the pregnant individual or (ii) when in the professional judgment of a physician the fetus is not viable.
In addition, Question 1 also protects both patients and medical providers from punishment for providing or receiving abortion care.

Jacksonville Jaguars 33-10 Baltimore Ravens: Joe Fagnano throws two interceptions as Ravens suffer heavy loss
Baltimore Ravens' third quarterback of the season, rookie Joe Fagnano, throws for just 60 yards and two interceptions in his first NFL start as the Baltimore Ravens (4-5) suffer a fourth straight loss at home to the Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) on Thursday night
Friday 6 November 2026 06:58, UK
Joe Fagnano had a forgettable first NFL start as the Baltimore Ravens quarterback - their third of the season - threw for just 60 yards and had two interceptions as the Jacksonville Jaguars earned a convincing 33-10 road win on Thursday night.
Fagnano came in due to Lamar Jackson and backup Tyler Huntley both being injured, with the 25-year-old rookie finding things a big struggle as Baltimore (4-5) lost a fourth straight on the season.
With their top two quarterbacks on injured reserve, the Ravens now await Jacoby Brissett's arrival in a trade from the Arizona Cardinals as they try to prevent their season from falling apart.
Jacksonville (6-2) did not need to do anything extraordinary to beat a badly weakened Baltimore team. Trevor Lawrence threw for 242 yards and a touchdown as the Jags won their fifth in their last six to take further command of the AFC South.
