Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.
Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet, Perplexity’s Teammates can perform an array of tasks while running 24/7.
Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.
Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools. Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing.
The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times, which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.

What if improving the health of a village meant doing more than building a hospital, treating patients and performing surgeries? In Aragonda, a village in Andhra Pradesh’s Chittoor district, an initiative that began with a 50-bed rural hospital has evolved into a community development model that links healthcare with education, nutrition, sanitation and preventive health.
Through its Total Health programme, Apollo Foundation is attempting to address the wider social determinants of health, with interventions spanning different stages of people’s lives, from maternal and child healthcare to youth development, women’s economic independence and elderly care.
The programme’s interventions include 1,200 antenatal and postnatal check-ups for new mothers, training in hygiene practices across 2,600 schools and industry-related and sports skills for more than 545 young people. It has also conducted over two lakh yoga sessions, alongside free screening and care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while more than 10.8 lakh meals have been served to elderly people through its geriatric nutrition centres.
Prathap C. Reddy, founder chairman of Apollo Hospitals Group, said the initiative reflected his belief that quality and affordable healthcare should reach every Indian, irrespective of where they lived. While the hospital initially brought modern medicine to his village, the larger vision was to create conditions in which people could lead healthier lives, he said. “Medicine can save lives, but to change the health of a generation, we must also change the conditions in which life is lived,” he added.
Specialised orthopaedic care in a rural setting
Alongside preventive and community healthcare, Apollo Hospitals Aragonda has also expanded its specialised surgical services, completing 1,000 total knee replacement (TKR) procedures. Established as a 50-bed hospital in 2000, it has served more than 1.67 lakh patients and performed over 12,000 surgeries in 26 years.
The knee replacement programme has grown from 100 procedures in 2019 to 500 in 2022 and 1,000 in 2026. “The 1,000 procedures have been completed without a single reported infection,” said Sangita Reddy, joint managing director of Apollo Hospitals.
From a rural hospital to a community health model
Telemedicine was another early intervention. With a network of three telephone lines, Apollo connected specialists in cities with patients in rural areas, allowing doctors to examine CT scans and ultrasound images remotely. The initiative enabled specialists to guide local doctors in treating patients who otherwise would have had to travel to distant hospitals. She recalled that former President of US, Bill Clinton, witnessed a telemedicine demonstration from Aragonda during his visit to Hyderabad.
A healthcare model looking beyond the hospital
Preetha Reddy, executive vice-chairperson of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited said the organisation remained committed to narrowing the divide between rural and urban healthcare. “The ability to perform specialised procedures such as knee replacements in a village demonstrates the potential for such models to be replicated in other parts of the world,” she added.

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.
What else we’re reading about
Student protests | Bikaner House, one of Delhi’s premier arts venues, asked visual artist Raihan Vadra to remove from his show more than 70 photographs that featured recent student protests. Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.
Fashion | Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted a Diwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled a high-jewellery collection inspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.
Air pollution | Emergency measures, including a ban on coal-fired tandoors in restaurants and restrictions on diesel generators, have come into effect in Delhi, as air quality dropped to the poor category at the onset of the annual pollution season.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:
“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
7,633
That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
- Published
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.
One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.
Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.
Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).
The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.
The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.
But the critical response so far has been mixed.
Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".
Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.
"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.
Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".
There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.
Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.
Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.
"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.
Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".
Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.
The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".
In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.
When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.
Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.
Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.
Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.
The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.
Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.
Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.
It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.
The 2023 film Adipurush, another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts.
Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.
For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt.
"I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."
He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.
Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.
How the film is being received will become clearer soon, as audiences head to cinemas.
But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

A Christian family was allegedly attacked at their home in West Arjunda village, Panskura, East Midnapore district of West Bengal, on the evening of October 26, Monday. An FIR was registered in connection with the case on October 28, Wednesday at Panskura police station.
Parvati Hembram Soren (27) alleged that a mob of around 30 people, including members of their extended family, neighbours and others who associated themselves with the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), assaulted her, desecrated Bibles present in their home and threatened them to renounce Christianity and accept Hinduism.
Some of the accused named in the FIR include extended family members of Parvati and her husband, Santu Soren, namely Gorachand Soren, Balaram Soren, Sombari Soren, Mamani Soren, Arati Soren, Arjun Soren, Logen Hansda, Geeta Soren, Kanka Soren and Nera Bou.
Parvati, Santu, and his uncle and aunt had embraced Christianity over a year ago and is associated with Christ the King Mission Church under the Balichak Catholic Parish. Parvati’s sister-in-law had also embraced the faith, but since she is a minor, her conversion certificate has not yet been published.
The alleged assault comes within days of a family in Patlapur village, Paschim Midnapur district, being allegedly subjected to three days of physical assault, sexual harassment, and continuous intimidation by a group of men who identified themselves as belonging to the Hindutva outfit Bajrang Dal.
ALSO READ: Christian families in Bengal attacked, allege ‘rape and death’ threats by ‘Bajrang Dal’ members
‘Dragged, Slapped, Kicked, Clothes Torn’
Speaking to Alt News, Parvati recounted that on Monday evening, she was praying with her husband and their two children while playing Christian religious songs and carols on a speaker. At around 7:30 pm, a group of approximately 30 people allegedly barged into their home. “Initially, they verbally abused us, snatched our Bible and threw it away. Then, they locked my family members in a room and beat me. They slapped, kicked and punched me,” she alleged.
Hearing her screams, Parvati’s other family members tried to intervene but were unable to protect her because of the sheer number of people attacking her, she added.
Further, the attackers allegedly attempted to tear up the Bible and set it on fire. When Parvati tried to stop them, they allegedly grabbed her by the hair, dragged her out of her house and assaulted her again. “Sombari, Mamani, Arati, and Geeta grabbed me by my hair and dragged me out of the house. They also tore of my clothes,” Parvati alleged.
“I have endured several injuries due to this physical assault and have immense pain in my body. Even my sister-in-law was beaten,” she alleged, adding that her husband was spared the physical assault because he was holding one of their children, she said, although he was verbally abused. The assault continued for approximately an hour, after which Parvati became unconscious.
Parvati underwent medical tests at 10:36 pm on Monday. The following morning, October 27, she went to Panskura police station to lodge an FIR. “The police took my written complaint and said that they would do a preliminary investigation and then lodge an FIR,” she said.
Parvati further alleged that her sister-in-law was recording the incident, but the attackers quickly snatched the latter’s phone, deleted the videos and photographs, before throwing the phone to the ground and damaging it. “Later they took all four Bibles from my house, destroyed them and threw them into a nearby pond. The mob also tried to break open my aged uncle-in-law’s home, located next to our house,” she added.
‘Death Threats, Social & Economic Boycott’
Moreover, Parvati told Alt News that the attackers repeatedly demanded that the family renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism. They allegedly threatened to wreak havoc in their home, harm or kill family members, and impose a social and economic boycott if they refused to comply.
While Santu works as a toto driver, Parvati works on the farmlands. Their neighbours, who were also part of the assault, have allegedly forced them to plant Tulsi and Manasa plants in their courtyard and perform Hindu rituals. “To continue harassing us, they have tied two cows in our courtyard, and the cows keep littering near our water tap,” she claimed. Additionally, the neighbours are allegedly constructing barriers along the local pond’s bank to prevent Parvati’s family from using the pond water.
During the incident, the family managed to contact a local volunteer of Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in Monirampur, who alerted the organisation’s legal team. Subsequently, advocate Aditya Tewary contacted Parvati.
However, the lawyer told Alt News that a man answered the phone after the attackers allegedly snatched it away from Parvati. “I called Parvati, but a man answered the phone, who said he was from Vishva Hindu Parishad. He told me, ‘We are here to set things right. We have received information about Christian conversion here’. As soon as I told him I’m an advocate, he disconnected the call,” Tewary said.
Not An Isolated Incident
This is not the first time that the Soren family was allegedly harassed and intimidated for practising Christianity. On October 11 around 6 pm, members identifying themselves as belonging to Bajrang Dal, along with their extended family members, arrived at their home and demanded that they renounce their faith in Christianity and return to Hinduism, Parvati told us, adding that she had then filed a complaint via email on October 12.
Even then, she named members of her extended family in the complaint as she did not know the names of the Bajrang Dal men. However, no action was initiated by the police.
Police Inaction
“When we were trying to call the police [on Monday], they told us that they [the assailants] would call the police themselves,” Parvati said.
However, she alleged that the police did not reprimand the assailants and instead schooled her and her family. “Instead, shockingly, the police told us to perform and practice our religious rituals inside our house and asked us not to use a speaker, claiming it to be an attempt to convert others,” she said. “Our Hindu neighbours keep playing religious songs on loudspeakers. We have never complained. How can playing songs on a small bluetooth speaker convert others?”
Upon being contacted, Panskura police told Alt News that they do not have the authority to brief us on any case and asked us to contact the headquarters. We then contacted East Midnapore Superintent of Police (SP) and Additional SP, but the phone went unanswered.
The FIR has been lodged under Sections 115(2), 3(5), 303(2), 324(4), 329(4), 351(2) and 76 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, pertaining to voluntarily causing hurt, common intention, theft, mischief, house-trespass, criminal intimidation, and assault or use of criminal force against a woman with intent to disrobe her, respectively. Despite the two complaints, no arrests have been made yet.
‘Don’t Give Them Loan’
Meanwhile, Parvati told Alt News that the harassment continued on Wednesday when a representative from a loan agency visited her home to process an application submitted by her and her husband. According to Parvati, her extended family surrounded the representative and allegedly pressured him not to process the loan because the couple had converted to Christianity.
“We bought a toto, but now we do not have enough money to pay the remaining instalments. That is why we had applied for a loan. Today, a person from the loan office visited my house. When he was leaving, my attackers surrounded him and asked him not to give us a loan, because we are not Hindus. If the police do not lodge an FIR and protect my family and me from this daily harassment, then we have to commit suicide,” she said, adding that even though she demanded police protection, her demand went unheeded.

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.
Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.
Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.
The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.
In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.
The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.
In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.
South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
- Published
Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured.
"We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC.
On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded.
Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing.
He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.
Earlier this week, Lissu went on a hunger strike as he was not being allowed access to his lawyers - an allegation the prison authorities denied.
His lawyer Dickson Matata told the BBC on Wednesday he had now been granted a meeting and would be eating again.
In its statement, Amnesty said it had documented how over the past year security agencies had committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organisations and dissenting members of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party.
"Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters," said Tigere Chagutah, the group's regional director for East and southern Africa
"In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear."
The authorities in the East African nation have repeatedly denied accusations of widespread abuses and say the government is committed to respecting human rights.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her.
Last year, the BBC verified multiple videos of police shooting towards protesters. Footage posted online showed demonstrators being confronted by heavily armed units blocking their progress and firing tear gas to disperse crowds.
The BBC has since spoken to families of some of the victims of the electoral violence, who are still seeking answers.
Many, like Mwajuma Hamisi, have been left destitute. Her husband George Kisivani was shot in the northern city of Arusha on 29 October 2025, the day of the vote, and died two days later.
"I lost my husband, upon whom we, a family with five children, depended. We now have no other source of support. I am left to fight for the family on my own. We have no other assistance," the 32-year-old told the BBC.
She now sells vegetables at a nearby market to support the family - and would like help from the government.
Sane, who shot in the leg in Arusha, has been suffering physically and financially.
The father of three says he has undergone more than five major operations to deal with the gunshot wound. He still needs further surgery but says he can no longer afford treatment.
"We have done everything within our means, but we have reached our limit," the 33-year-old told the BBC.
"The government should look into the situation of those of us who have suffered these tragedies, so that we can receive medical treatment, as some of us are still very sick."
He explained how in the wake of the violence hospitals initially refused to treat injured people.
In the intervening months, his relatives have sought help from local officials and the district commissioner, but he says they were told the government had not allocated a budget for victims of the violence.
The BBC has not independently verified his account of those conversations.
A commission of inquiry's report into the violence was handed to President Samia in April, officially recording 518 deaths.
But Amnesty has criticised the fact that the full report has not yet been made public, saying it "entrenches a culture of secrecy".
The president has since set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
"It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown," Chagutah said.
The rights group says that between 3 and 17 September 2026, it interviewed 17 people who gave details of a continuing crackdown by the authorities.
Some of them were targeted after demonstrations were called for 7 July to demand democratic reforms and justice for those killed last year.
These marches were banned by the authorities. A 26-year-old man who had expressed support told Amnesty how he was arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam and held without charge for 47 days.
He said he was blindfolded by his interrogators who wanted to know who was funding the protests and threatened to kill him.
"On the first day, they didn't give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said, 'That is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise'," he said.
"On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand."
The right groups also cites other "acts that may amount to torture... arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions".
The authorities did not respond to the BBC's or Amnesty's request for comment.
Many of those who lost relatives a year ago want the government to acknowledge their suffering and address their questions about justice, like 40-year-old Neema Munuo.
She says her grief over the death of her 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami, who had gone out to buy phone credit in Arusha when she was shot, has often left her too distraught to leave the house.
"It is a date I will never forget for the rest of my life, because whenever I recall it, I feel as though I am burning inside," Munuo told the BBC.
This feeling resonates with farmer Juma Nasibu, who lives near the city of Mwanza on the shores of Lake Victoria.
He has not seen his 25-year-old nephew Juma Shabani since the unrest.
The young man had been at a cinema hall in the evening when his uncle later heard unconfirmed reports that he was amongst people rounded up and shot. His family have fruitlessly searched for him at hospitals, police stations and prisons.
"To date, what still pains me is that we were never able to recover the body," Nasibu told the BBC.

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country.
Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

Three social media content creators from West Bengal — Akash Sarkar, Surajit Shee and Srimoyee Chakraborty — were recently arrested after making posts which questioned the ruling BJP government and its policies.
While Sarkar was granted bail on October 29 after spending three days in police custody, Chatterjee was released from detention on a personal bond on October 26. Shee was first sent to judicial custody and held at Medinipur Central Jail. At present, he is in police custody till November 6.
An FIR was lodged against Shee under Sections 152, 197 and 353 of the BNS, pertaining to acts endangering integrity of India, assertions threatening national integration, and statements amounting to public mischief, respectively.
In the FIR registered against Sarkar, the police invoked Sections 356(1), 353(1)(2) and 299(1) of the BNS, pertaining to criminal defamation, spreading false information/hate speech, and intentionally outraging religious feelings, respectively.
Surajit Shee: Posts on Durga Puja Stampede
Surajit Shee, hailing from Dantan village of West Midnapore district, runs a Facebook page called ‘Core Bangla-Janakantha’, which has over 2,52,000 followers. Shee shares posts on a range of social, political and scientific issues. The two last posts on his page were made on October 19. In one, he is seen appreciating the BJP government for banning DJs and loudspeakers during processions in the state, and in the other post, he talks about allegations that followed the Chorbagan stampede which killed 19 people in Kolkata at a Durga Puja.
Another post by Shee from October 18 caried a video that has been restricted in India. The caption reads, translated from Bengali, “What is the actual truth behind the Chorebagan incident? Which version is correct? The official government figures or the claims made by the public? The government itself is abusing the law. Those in power are misusing their authority to silence the voices of ordinary citizens.”
Shee is a member of ‘Bharatiya Biggyan o Juktibadi Samity’ — an organization which aims to promote scientific temperament in the society.
Alt News spoke with Dipak Roy, a key member of the outfit. Roy mentioned that beside discussing political issues, Shee was vocal about various scientific and social issues.
“Surajit had been telling us that for almost a year that a section of local BJP-RSS workers had been harassing him over his social media content. The intensity of the harassment increased after May 4 (as BJP came to power in the state). On either October 17 or 18, Shee told me that his house had been attacked by the same group, who claimed that he was posting anti-national content. I suggested that he take shelter elsewhere. He then went to a friend’s house in Contai. The police arrested him from there on October 24,” alleged Roy.
Although Shee was detained by police on October 24, he was shown as arrested on October 25, Sunday, from his residence in Dantan, instead of Contai.
According to Roy, the group that attacked Shee’s house claimed that a complaint had been lodged against him at Dantan police station over his alleged ‘anti-national’ activities. Roy told Alt News that when Shee’s father and father-in-law went to the police station to enquire about the alleged complaints, the police could not produce any complaint lodged against him. Police allegedly told them that the chief minister had ordered Shee’s arrest and that it “would be better if he surrendered” or else they would “make an example out of him”.
During the arrest, Roy alleged that only three to four police personnel were present while nearly 20 RSS-BJP workers rounded him up. “Around 15-20 RSS-BJP workers surrounded the house of his friend in Contai. These people assaulted him before handing him over to the police, who then took him away in a car,” alleged Roy. “We thought Contai police had arrested him and arranged for a lawyer to represent him at the Contai sub-divisional court. However, later we realised that Shee had been arrested by Dantan police and was produced before the Dantan court.”
Roy further alleged that Shee’s family could access the legal documents related to the case two days after his arrest. Police have also allegedly seized Shee’s mobile phone, but no seizure list has been provided to his family.
Alt News’ attempts to contact both Dantan and Contain police were unsuccessful till publication time.
Alt News spoke to Tapan Jana, Shee’s maternal uncle, who said, “Surajit was produced in Dantan court on November 2, and police sought seven days of custody. However, the judge allowed only four days.”
“After he was remanded to police custody, an officer from Dantan police station verbally abused us when we went to meet him. The officer said that Surajit had insulted Sanatan Dharma, the state and central governments, and was inciting the public through his Facebook posts. He told us to make sure that Surajit reveals during questioning who had instructed him to make those posts,” Jana said.
“The officer further said that unless Shee confessed, he would make it difficult for him to get bail,” Jana added.
Akash Sarkar: Posts on Stampede and Suvendu Adhikari
Akash Sarkar (30) was arrested from his home in Nagerbazar on October 25, produced before the Barrackpore court on October 26, which ordered three days of police custody. He was released on bail on October 29.
Sarkar told Alt News that during interrogation, police pointed to three aspects of his posts which they claimed led to his arrest — his reference to Suvendu Adhikari’s ‘bhaipo’ (nephew) in connection with the Chorbagan stampede, his comments about the government’s handling of the situation following the stampede, and his use of the term ‘teen bati’ (three bowls) to refer to Adhikari.
Sarkar said, “In one of my Facebook posts, I had mentioned that Suvendu’s nephew was the chief patron of Chorbagan Sarbojonin, the puja where 19 people were trampled, and that he should take responsibility for the tragedy. I had also flagged the manner in which the Durga idol, with its hands tied, was taken away by the police for immersion.”
“I had written in my Facebook post that, according to the BJP, previous governments in West Bengal were not Sanatani. But even those governments did not treat the goddess in the way the Sanatani government treated her. The police flagged my post as religiously inflammatory and kept me in custody for three days,” added Sarkar.
According to Sarkar, in another post, he had addressed chief minister as ‘teen bati’ — a political jab aimed at Adhikari.
“The ‘teen bati’ jab was popularised by Ali Aftab Chand, a lawyer at the Calcutta high court who identifies himself as a ‘Rashtravadi Muslim’. He was not arrested. Is it because he is close to the BJP?” asked Sarkar.
According to the FIR, a person named Soumen Das had lodged a complaint against Sarkar, alleging that Sarkar “has been using his Facebook profile to publish false, defamatory, religiously inflammatory and provocative posts concerning the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Sri Narendra Modi and Hon’ble Chief Minister of India, Sri Suvendu Adhikari.”
“While I was in the lock-up, I heard from a few police personnel that our local MLA, Tarunjyoti Tiwari, had visited the police station and taken a personal interest in my case. Police hinted that although the charges against me were flimsy, orders from higher-ups were forcing them to keep me in custody,” he alleged, adding that the police was yet to return his phone.
Srimoyee Chakroborty: Posts Critical of State Government
Chakraborty had posted an update on her Facebook profile on October 26, mentioning that she had been held at the Bidhannagar East police station. She was later released the same day on a bond of Rs 2,000.
On October 26, she announced on Facebook that she was detained, while vowing to continue her fight. Her posts on Facebook reflect a similar pattern of posts critical of the BJP-led state and central government and its policies. However, it is not clear which particular post led to the administrative action.
A scroll through her Facebook timeline shows her vocal support for the Left.
Similar to Shee and Sarkar, Chakraborty had also made a series of posts critical of the government’s management of the Chorbagan stampede and the immersion process. On October 21, she shared the chief minister’s video where he announced that only people who follow Sanatana Dharma would participate in the Durga idol immersion process. In the caption, she referred to Adhikari as ‘teen bati’.

The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention
A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too
About three-quarters of emerging human infections originate in animals. India, with 1.4 billion people, some 536 million livestock and the world’s largest milk output, sits at the centre of this arithmetic. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

Students' chances of tossing their graduation caps on time can vary widely by the US state where they attend high school.
In Alaska, the rate of students who graduate from high school in four years is 79.87%, compared to 93.60% in Kentucky, the highest in the country.
While graduation rates are one way to monitor academic achievement and are used by local and state governments to track educational progress, they are complex metrics to define and measure. Diploma requirements vary from state to state, and students in different states face different course and testing requirements to earn it.
Still, the diploma matters.
Across the nation, higher levels of education are almost always associated with higher earnings, and high school degrees are no different. On average, US adults aged 25 or over with a high school degree earn $8,216 more a year than those without one, according to Census data.
Using data from state education agencies and public data portals across all 50 states, Business Insider compiled a list of the most up-to-date high school graduation rates from each.
While most percentages reflect the 2024-2025 school year, Oklahoma's most recent data is from the 2023-2024 school year.
Most states follow the four-year adjusted cohort graduation rate formula, which measures the share of first-time ninth graders who earn a regular high school diploma within four years. The formula adjusts the student cohort by including those who transfer into the school system and removing those who transfer out, emigrate, or die.
To put graduation rates into context, we also listed each state's public school spending per pupil and median household income.

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the State's first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced on Monday (November 2, 2026).
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometres) north of Syracuse, Governor Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Ms. Hochul, a Democrat, said the child's death is “a devastating reminder of what's at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but State health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Ms. Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring States and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

The Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections saw major gains for Democrats both in the House and Senate, including key Senate victories in Michigan, South Carolina and Texas. News media outlets reported the results as a sweeping rebuke of President Donald Trump's administration, with vote tallies exhibiting sizable differences from his second-term victory in 2024.
In the hours after the election results began coming in, some people began claiming a screen-recorded video showed that tech entrepreneur Elon Musk — who reportedly contributed $474 million to support Republicans in the midterms — had deleted his post from Election Day that read, "Vote red today!"
For example, one X user's popular post featured the screen recording showing the post still loaded on the person's device but not properly displaying after refreshing Musk's feed. That clip appeared to originate from a different user, with many (archived) others (archived) reposting (archived) the content.
Others shared (archived) a screenshot with a message reading, "The post you are trying to reply to has been deleted or is not visible to you."
(@PollTracker2024 via X)
In sum, Musk, or another person who manages his X account, truly deleted the post reading, "Vote red today!"
While knowledgeable users can create fake screenshots and videos, we found definitive proof that the post once existed. Someone archived the post prior to its removal. As of that archiving, the post had nearly 12 million views.
Attempts to access the original post displayed the message, "Hmm...this page doesn't exist. Try searching for something else."
We also confirmed firsthand that DuckDuckGo search results still displayed a link to the deleted post, which we further archived.
(DuckDuckGo)
The DuckDuckGo search results displayed the time 14:35:34, appearing to correspond to GMT. That timing aligned with the post first appearing just after another one visible in the screen recording, in which Musk answered "Yes" in a quote repost of another user's post (archived) about how to properly use artificial intelligence.
Snopes emailed an apparent media relations email address for X to ask whether Musk wished to comment about this matter. In the past, journalists' correspondence sent via a similar email address did not result in receiving answers to questions. We will update this article if we receive more information.
For further reading, we previously investigated whether Musk paid Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan to endorse GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

‘Parliament is supreme forum’: Amit Shah counters Rahul Gandhi’s public debate call, accuses Congress of disrupting proceedings
Amit Shah asserted that Parliament is the supreme forum for democratic debate and criticised Rahul Gandhi for taking political confrontations to the streets.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday launched a sharp attack on leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, accusing him of disrupting parliamentary proceedings, avoiding discussions on substantive issues and turning walkouts and protests into the Congress party's political culture.
Shah asserted that Parliament is the supreme forum for democratic debate and criticised Gandhi for taking political confrontations to the streets instead of engaging in discussions inside the House.
At BJP's 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' foot march in Karnal, Amit Shah highlighted the mandate received by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the 2024 elections and accused the Congress leadership of converting legislative disruption into standard party culture.
"Today, I want to explain why we have been compelled to organise this rally. For the third consecutive time, the people of this country have elected Narendra Modi as Prime Minister with a massive mandate. Since 2024, the Congress party has faced repeated defeats under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi," he said, as quoted by ANI.
Shah asserted that the LoP, Rahul Gandhi, does not allow Parliamentary proceedings to run smoothly and instead spreads anarchy, much like an anarchist.
"In a democracy, Parliament is the supreme forum for debate; yet, Rahul Gandhi, you do not allow Parliament to function. You refuse to engage in discussions on substantive issues, having instead turned the creation of a ruckus and the staging of walkouts into the very culture of the Congress party. You prevent Parliament from operating, choosing instead to gather crowds on the streets and spread anarchy, much like an anarchist," he said.
Shah declared that the Bharatiya Janata Party is fully prepared to counter the opposition across all arenas, from legislative halls to grassroots village centres.
"Do you truly believe that an 80-year-old democracy will fall for your deceptions? Rahul ji, we are the people of the streets. The BJP will provide a fitting response to you in Parliament, in the Legislative Assemblies, in our villages, and in our fields; and should you choose to gather crowds, BJP workers will be there to give you a befitting reply. The 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' rally has served to deliver a strong and decisive response to Rahul Gandhi," he said.

A technical examination report submitted by BMW to investigators has revealed critical data regarding the fatal Kerala Mini Cooper crash in Kochi. Analysis from the vehicle's Advanced Crash Safety Module established that the car was speeding at 162 kilometres per hour five seconds before the collision and was travelling at 144 kilometres per hour upon impact. The data also indicated the brake pedal was pressed roughly one second prior to hitting a two-wheeler, resulting in the immediate death of three youths. The findings provide scientific backing for the police case against the 19-year-old accused driver, whose anticipatory bail plea approaches the Kerala High Court.

The State government on Friday (October 30) told the Karnataka High Court that it would not insist, for now, on the implementation of the circular which mandates that all hospital pharmacies disclose the landing base/purchase price and maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines, medical devices and consumables on bills.
An undertaking in this regard was given to the court on behalf of the State’s Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) during the hearing of a petition filed by Private Hospitals and Nursing Homes Association, Bengaluru, and a private hospital. The petitioners have challenged the legality of the October 1 circular.
Justice C.M. Pooncha, before whom the petition came up for hearing, has adjourned further hearing on the petition till November 12 after recording the undertaking given by an Additional Advocate General on instruction from the officials of the FSDA.
Having a re-look
The government also informed the court that “the officials concerned are in the process of having a re-look at the circular dated October 1, 2026, and will not enforce the mandate of the circular till November 12, the next date of hearing on the petition”.
The undertaking was given while requesting the court not to stay the circular to allow the government to re-examine the issues raised by the petitioners.
It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the FSDAhad no statutory power to impose such conditions for disclosure of purchase price, which is a commercial agreement between the sellers and buyers that vary depending on suppliers, purchase quantity, discounts, credit arrangements and other factors.
Sans consultation
Mandating disclosure of purchase price would result in exposing confidential commercial arrangements between the suppliers and health establishments, it has been contented in the petition, while pointing out that the circular was issued sans adequate consultations with the stakeholders, even though the circular has direct implications on their finance.

Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
