The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.
 
“Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

Traffic on Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) Road is set to be affected for 18 months from November 6, with the BDA beginning work on a four-lane elevated corridor along Ballari Road.
The movement of KSRTC and private buses, along with all goods vehicles, has been prohibited on the stretch, the Bengaluru Traffic Police announced on Thursday.
The elevated corridor is being built between UAS Staff Quarters and Mekhri Circle, under the jurisdiction of Sadashivanagar and Sanjaynagar traffic police stations.
The restrictions have been imposed to ease congestion and ensure smoother traffic movement during the construction work.
Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards KIA and Bengaluru city, including emergency vehicles, have been advised to take alternative routes.
Alternative routes for vehicles heading towards Bengaluru airport
Via Cantonment railway station: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards KIA can take the route via Old High Grounds Junction, Kalpana Junction, Old Udaya TV Junction, Cantonment Railway Station, Tannery Road and Nagawara Road before proceeding towards the airport.
Via BEL circle: Vehicles travelling from Yeshwanthpur towards KIA should take Mattikere Road, turn right at BEL Circle and continue via Ring Road towards the airport.
Alternative routes for vehicles heading towards Bengaluru city
Via Nagawara Junction: Vehicles travelling from KIA towards central Bengaluru can take a left turn at Hebbal, proceed towards Nagawara Junction, take a right turn and continue via Bamboo Bazaar and Queens Road towards the city.
Via Goraguntepalya: Alternatively, vehicles travelling from KIA towards central Bengaluru can take a right turn at Hebbal and proceed via Hebbal Ring Road and Kuvempu Circle towards Goraguntepalya Junction. They should take a left turn at the junction and continue via Dr Rajkumar Road towards the city.
Via Margosa Road: Vehicles travelling from Yeshwanthpur towards central Bengaluru should proceed via BHEL Junction, take a right turn near Maramma Circle and continue via Margosa Road towards the city.
Via CBI Junction: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards Bengaluru city should enter the service road in front of Baptist Hospital after descending the Hebbal Flyover and continue along it up to CBI Junction. They can then proceed towards the city via Ballari Main Road.
Via Anand Nagar main road: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards Anand Nagar and RT Nagar should enter the service road in front of Baptist Hospital and proceed towards Anand Nagar Cross. They should take a left turn at CBI Junction to join Anand Nagar Main Road and continue towards RT Nagar and Jayamahal Road.
The Bengaluru traffic police have requested commuters to cooperate and follow the alternative routes during the construction period.

AI agents can, in theory, book your vacation for you, but that doesn't mean it's happening much yet.
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says he's not worried about AI agents like Meta's Muse or Instinct AI taking traffic, citing a low number of agent bookings so far.
"We're not seeing a lot of traffic, and even fewer bookings, from Muse and Instinct yet," Chesky said on Airbnb's third quarter earnings call Thursday.
Of the nearly half a million Airbnb bookings each day, a "very non-material" number are coming from Muse or Instinct, the CEO said. He added that traffic from agents peaked in early October and had not increased since.
"My general philosophy on agents are, I'm generally excited about them. I don't see them as a threat," Chesky said. "I see them kind of like Google, as an opportunity for more people to discover Airbnb. I think they'll be great handoff to us."
Airbnb beat Wall Street estimates and reported a 19% year-over-year increase in revenue for the quarter. The company said it posted its fastest revenue growth in three years and was "back in growth mode."
Personal assistant AI agents had a moment this summer when Instinct's invite-only agent went viral in Silicon Valley around the same time Meta launched its own version called Muse. There have been some concerns that AI agents could be bad news for travel companies, many of which rely on direct bookings and customer loyalty.
Brian Chesky said general AI agents shouldn't do everything
Chesky said he thinks general-purpose AI agents aren't the best option for booking travel, and that people will increasingly turn to specialized agents rather than using a single agent to do everything.
That's why, he said, Airbnb plans to begin rolling out its own AI agent in the first half of next year. The agent will be built specifically for travel, and aims to provide guests a custom experience.
"Today's AI agents, like Muse and Instinct, are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different," he said. "Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience."
Chesky said 80% of travelers report enjoying the time they spend planning trips, and that they want to look at photos, compare homes, and make decisions with their travel companions.
He said that's clear in the way customers use Airbnb, adding that 90% of people message the host. He said users typically look at a dozen listings and often swipe through 25 photos per listing. Most of Airbnb's traffic also comes during work hours, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., he said.
"These people are supposed to be working, and they're not. We have evidence. People are actually secretly using Airbnb," Chesky said. "Maybe they're trying to escape their job. But the idea is that it's highly aspirational, so I don't think a lot of people want to offload all that to an agent."
Executives at Booking.com and Expedia also said on earnings calls this week that AI agents had so far resulted in very little traffic. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said last week that third-party agents had generated "several hundred orders in total."

Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries
There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday. “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”
When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.
Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.” Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.

First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.
"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.
First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.
NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.
For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."
The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."
Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.
"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.
But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.
High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth. Miller sees more clients getting help from family members who may have paid off their own home, or have equity in a second property they can sell and "are gifting some or all of that money." They're viewing it as a kind of "future inheritance," he said.
For some younger first-time buyers, relatives may only be "lending them the cash" to make a bid more attractive, said Nate Johnson, a broker associate with RedKey Realty Leaders in St. Louis. Even with much of the national housing market in a major slump, he said his local market is still intensely competitive for buyers.
"They just know that if we're looking at five or six offers on the table, let's call it 10 offers on the table, which is not uncommon…maybe three of those offers will be all cash," he said.
After closing on a property, Johnson has seen some buyers refinance into a mortgage and pay back their family member.
The rise of all-cash offers makes the market even tougher for those who struggle to save up for a down payment with today's sky-high home prices.
"For a long time I thought I wanted to buy a house," said Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33. They and their spouse have good jobs, but also debt, including a car payment and student loans. Not only does Esmeson think they may never be in a position to buy, they've also decided it does not make sense at today's prices.
"Being that debt burdened, and also having to fix things on your home, like, it sounds really terrible," they said.
Esmeson is also not convinced that home equity would outpace other investments. They like their current rental and landlord so are sticking with it for now.
Still, it's frustrating that the housing market worked better for previous generations. "We have the short end of the deal," they said, and "the gap is expanding."
There's probably only one way they might ever be able to buy. "If I received an inheritance," they said. But "I love my mom dearly and I don't want to look forward to that, or really want to strategize around that."

Keralam court rejects plea to cancel bail of judge’s minor son ran over man in Kochi
The Ernakulam Sessions Court rejected appeals by the State and the victim’s family against bail granted to the 17-year-old in the fatal Kochi crash.
A Keralam court on Thursday rejected appeals seeking cancellation of bail granted to a 17-year-old boy accused of driving a luxury car into a scooter, killing a 55-year-old street food vendor in Kochi last month.
The Ernakulam Sessions Court upheld the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB)’s decision to grant bail to the teenager, whose father is an additional district judge.
The court was hearing appeals filed by the State and the victim’s family challenging a JJB ruling granting bail to the teenager.
A Mercedes-Benz driven by the judge’s minor son hit the two-wheeler near Cheranalloor at around 2.30am on October 25. Jayabalakrishnan, a resident of Manjali who ran a street food cart in the Chittor area, was thrown into the air and died on the spot.
The teenager was immediately caught and handed over to the police. He was later produced before the JJB, which granted him bail citing the absence of any prior criminal record.
Bhadrakeerthy, daughter of Jayabalakrishnan, told reporters that she and her family were losing faith in the judiciary. “We expected a verdict in our favour. But there was so much drama and so many twists inside the court. I am losing trust in the judiciary. There have been lapses on the part of the police and the judiciary. We will speak to our lawyers and reassess,” she said.
A detailed copy of the court order is awaited.
The father of the minor, an additional district judge presiding over the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal in Keralam, was granted anticipatory bail by the high court on Thursday. The court orally told the prosecution that he is a judicial officer who has been cooperating with the investigation.
He was booked on additional charges of attempting to destroy evidence on Monday, police said. The judge was earlier booked on charges of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, along with rash and negligent driving, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.
According to Cheranalloor police, the family of the victim, Jayabalakrishnan, lodged a fresh complaint on Sunday, alleging that the minor’s father spent a lot of time at the accident site in a bid to destroy evidence in the case. The complaint also alleged that the judge visited Cheranalloor police station after the accident and forced an officer to delete a photograph of his son that had been clicked by a member of the victim’s family.
The judge had earlier been granted interim protection from arrest by the Kerala High Court. He told the court that he was asleep at the time of the incident and was not aware that his son had taken the vehicle from the house.

Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
- Published
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”

Filmmaker Ben Rekhi’s Last Man In Tower received high critical acclaim after it was released earlier this year. Based on author Aravind Adiga’s novel of the same name, the film is about one man, played by Manoj Bajpayee, standing against the redevelopment of his housing society in Mumbai. The film also had a remarkable performance by Divya Dutta in a complex and layered role as Mrs. Puri.
EXCLUSIVE: Divya Dutta on redevelopment in Mumbai amid Last Man In Tower Zee 5 premiere, “We have to take a step forward but…”; also recalls Manoj Bajpayee cooking in between shots
Last Man In Tower has started streaming on Zee 5 from today November 6 onwards. Happy that the film will now reach more audience, Dutta got talking about the film and her experience in an exclusive chat with Bollywood Hungama.
Sharing why the film is special for her, Divya Dutta said, “My role was written beautifully. There was also some magic of improvisations that happened on the sets, which was very neatly done. My role has received a lot of love. I didn’t know this kind of relatability would come with my role. Whoever has seen the film, it’s been a beautiful watch as a film for them. The confusion about whose side is right or wrong is something different from all the roles I have done.”
When asked about her preparations for playing Mrs. Puri, the actor said, “You just have to feel the agony of the woman, who is so helpless. She hasn’t dared to dream as she is too busy with what life has to offer. Then she sees a ray of hope. In that situation when you see the vulnerability of the person, it touches you very much.”
Dutta said it was sheer pleasure to work with the likes of Manoj Bajpayee and Boman Irani, who plays the ambitious real estate developer Dharmen Shah. “They are magicians with what they do yaar,” she said. “What I like the most and what I must talk about is that they are amazing human beings. They have been in the industry for so long. They are so grounded. There are no starry tantrums. There is no feeling of, ‘Oh I know my job so well and people look up to me’. There is so much security and joy on the sets that it kind of trickles on everyone being there.”
A poignant moment in Last Man In Tower is the one where Dutta’s character breaks down in front of Irani’s. “That’s my most favourite scene,” she said. “The other is with Manoj when she has an outburst at him. It’s so helpful to have these people around you. To see them perform, be with them and keep doing different things is amazing; to get into an intense scene, cut out and have a joke is fun. You look forward to being on that kind of set.”
Interestingly, during the shoot, Bajpayee displayed his immense passion to feed his co-stars while the shoot was going on simultaneously. “I remember we were shooting on the third floor without a lift because we were shooting in an actual location,” recalled Dutta. “So, he would come down, make it, then go up, stir it and then go up again, give an intense shot, come down again and stir it again. So, I was like, ‘Man, you have a passion for both – for cooking and feeding people and acting’. He would feed us with immense love.”
Right after Last Man In Tower, Dutta and Bajpayee were seen in the recently-released OTT film Gajab Raat. “It’s amazing to be in two totally different and distinctly different roles in two different stories. There is so much security (in Bajpayee). He will do his bit and he will say, ‘Oh this is yours’. So, it becomes such a comfortable and nurtured place. There is no other way but to give your best and enjoy it. When you enjoy, it comes really well.”
Last Man In Tower couldn’t have come at a better time when almost the entire city of Mumbai is going through rampant redevelopment. Divya Dutta was asked what does she personally feels about what’s going on in the city. She gave an elaborate answer to that.
“I feel we do have to take a step forward,” she said. “Of course, there has to be development and progress. Old has to give way to the new. But I do feel that you have to hold hands with what is there; be it your relations, environment, everything. You have to go hand-in-hand. You can’t take away something to make something. Even in our families, our old traditions are also followed. As we progress, the old values and things that keep us together – compassion, love, empathy and co-existence; that is something we are forgetting. I think that along with development is very important.”

Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
- Published
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
Peña has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
In his video message posted on X, Peña said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

California governor commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
- Published
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

Helene Hahn Lloyd, the former Disney executive vice president and a founding executive of DreamWorks, has died. She was 78.
According to her management team, Lloyd “died peacefully in her sleep” on Tuesday, Oct. 24 in Park City, Utah, where she moved after leaving DreamWorks in 2004 and lived with her husband of more than two decades, Charles “Chuck” Lloyd Jr., who died this July.
Born July 13, 1948 in Westbury, New York, Lloyd (née Burlakoff) graduated from Hofstra University in 1970 before moving to Los Angeles, where she worked as a temp for Paramount Pictures while attending Loyola Law School, where she graduated in ’75.
In 1977, Lloyd returned to Paramount as senior vice president, earning a reputation for her dealmaking skills.
Watch on Deadline
Lloyd then became executive vice president at Disney in 1981, reportedly the highest position achieved by a woman in Hollywood at the time. During her time at Disney, along with Jeffrey Katzenberg, she helped solidify the studio’s landmark partnership with Pixar.
In 1994, Lloyd became one of the first executives hired to build DreamWorks, eventually becoming its chief operating officer until her departure in 2004.
The family asks those who wish to make a donation in Helene and Chuck’s memory to do so with U.S. Ski & Snowboard, in honor of their shared love of skiing and their support for the next generation of athletes.

Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition that causes thick, scaly patches on the skin. However, it often remains unidentified and undiagnosed because it does not look the same on all parts of the body: it could be mistaken, for instance, for dandruff on the scalp, persistent eczema on the palms, or a fungal infection. You can’t always judge psoriasis by looking only at visible parts of the skin.
Why does this happen? Our skin isn’t the same everywhere. The thickness of the skin can vary considerably depending on the diversity of the environmental conditions that it is exposed to and the kind of treatment given to it. These factors can contribute to how psoriasis appears and feels.

Many forms of ear infections strike children and adults alike, but among the most common is acute otitis externa, also known as swimmer’s ear.
About 10% of Americans will experience swimmer’s ear during their lifetimes. Adults are affected more commonly, and children only rarely, generally ages 5 to 12.
But you don’t have to be swimming to get swimmer’s ear. Go out jogging or walking, or do yardwork on a hot day, and moisture from perspiration can drip in your ear. However, the occurrence increases fivefold in swimmers – thus the reason the condition came to be called “swimmer’s ear.” It also occurs more frequently in tropical climates because of humidity and higher temperatures.
As doctors who specialise in ear problems, we are actively involved in research and clinical treatment for children and adults struggling with ear, nose and throat problems. Practicing in the state of Florida, we’ve certainly seen our share of patients with swimmer’s ear.
Causes and symptoms of swimmer’s ear
Swimmer’s ear is an infection in the external ear canal, the tube leading from the ear opening to the eardrum. Typically, swimmer’s ear occurs only in one ear, and sometimes the eardrum itself is affected. Moisture trapped in the canal leads to a break in the skin barrier and creates an opening for certain bacteria types to enter or existing ones to overgrow.
One of these culprits is the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is present in soil and water throughout the world. These bacteria favor moist areas, such as sinks, toilets, inadequately chlorinated swimming pools and hot tubs, as well as outdated or inactivated antiseptic solutions.
If you have the infection, you’ll know it. Symptoms generally appear a few days after infection. The main symptom of swimmer’s ear is severe pain and discomfort. It’s particularly noticeable when the outer ear is tugged, or by touching the tragus – that’s the small bump at the front of your ear. Other symptoms include itchiness inside the ear, redness, swelling and drainage. A feeling of fullness, or the perception of a plugged ear, may also occur, along with disturbed balance and temporary hearing loss.
Predisposition to swimmer’s ear
Numerous factors can predispose someone to swimmer’s ear. They include a narrow ear canal, and skin diseases such as eczema or psoriasis. In addition, individuals wearing ear plugs, ear buds or hearing aids may be at an increased risk. Diabetics may also be more prone to the infection.
Swimmer’s ear can also come from something getting stuck inside the ear, excessive ear cleaning or contact with chemicals in hair dye or hairspray.
Diagnosis and treatment
Swimmer’s ear is diagnosed after a health care provider has gathered a thorough history and examined the inside of the ear. The ear canal will typically look red, swollen and moist. There is also a possibility of fluid drainage or the appearance of scaly, shedding skin. Depending on the degree of swelling, the eardrum may be hard to see. A sample of fluid may be removed from the ear and sent to a lab to look for bacteria or fungus.
Eardrops are commonly used to treat swimmer’s ear. These drops often contain antibiotics to kill the infection and steroids to stop the swelling.
One such eardrop is Ciprodex. It contains ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic, and dexamethasone, a powerful steroid. Patients will need to place about four to five drops in the infected ear canal twice a day for seven to 10 days.
Another commonly prescribed drop is Floxin, which contains an antibiotic but not a steroid. It is commonly prescribed in less swollen but still infected ears.
Other drop preparations include Cortisporin, which contains a commonly used combination of neomycin and polymyxin B, as well as hydrocortisone. However, neomycin is also damaging to the inner ear, so doctors nowadays often turn to Ciprodex or Floxin.
In some cases, the ear canal is too swollen for drops to reach the infected area, so the physician may place a wick or stent in the ear canal to keep it open. This will usually be left in place for three to five days until removed by the doctor, although occasionally the wick falls out once the swelling subsides. Usually, after 10 days the infection is resolved and the ear canal skin returns to normal.
Managing a persistent infection
Sometimes swimmer’s ear may not resolve after seven to 10 days of treatment with eardrops. Oral antibiotics are typically recommended if the infection has spread beyond the ear canal or in patients with poorly controlled diabetes. Hospitalization for swimmer’s ear is rarely necessary; however, complications that can occasionally lead to hospitalization include fever, worsening discharge, extensive narrowing of the ear canal or failure of previous treatments.
Among the precautions you can take to prevent swimmer’s ear: Keep the ear canal dry. Tip your head to one side to help the water drain. Use a soft towel or cloth, or gently use a hair dryer near it. If the self-cleansing mechanism of the ear canal is impaired, then the ear canal should be cleansed by a physician.
Since most bacteria prefer a pH-neutral environment, reducing the pH in the ear canal can prevent bacterial overgrowth. A homemade liquid tincture can be mixed from a solution of half rubbing alcohol and half distilled white vinegar. The alcohol combines with the water in the ear and then evaporates. This removes the water while the acidity of the vinegar keeps bacteria from growing.
Two to three drops are usually sufficient and can be applied as a preventive measure soon after the ear has been exposed to moisture. This liquid solution is not a replacement for medical treatment of an actual ear infection and is meant to be used only in people who are prone to such infections because of prolonged or frequent exposure to moisture.
Also, it is important to differentiate swimmer’s ear from a middle ear infection, the most frequent reason for the use of antibiotics in children under age 5. Middle ear infections are usually associated with a viral upper respiratory infection, and they are more often seen during fall and winter, when influenza and cold viruses are more prevalent.
(Thomas Schrepfer, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Otolaryngology, University of Florida; Rex Haberman Associate Clinical Professor of Otology and Neurotology, University of Florida)

After protests in Arunachal Pradesh against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent on October 23, the state has unleashed a massive crackdown on the movement. The response has included the use of force by armed forces and law enforcement agencies, internet shutdowns, a paid PR campaign, censorship of social media content, and action against journalists and lawyers.
A 12-hour Arunachal bandh was called by local bodies and youth groups, including the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF), Adi Baane Kebang United and the Adi Galo Welfare Society, on October 23. The bandh was followed by large-scale arson in Pasighat, East Siang district, targeting an office of the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), a police station, and the homes of two MLAs and the BJP’s state president.
The proposed SUMP, with an estimated capacity of 11,200 megawatts, is planned on the Siang River across the Upper Siang and Siang districts. First proposed in 2008-09 by the UPA government, it was initially conceived as two smaller projects, with memorandums of understanding signed in 2013. On September 26, 2017, following a meeting between chief minister Pema Khandu, state delegates and NITI Aayog, the plan was changed to a single 250-metre-high dam, which would be the country’s largest in terms of installed capacity. However, stiff local resistance forced survey teams to withdraw, bringing the project to a temporary standstill.
The BJP-led governments at the Centre and in Arunachal Pradesh revived the project in 2020, following reports of China’s plan to build a dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, known as the Siang in India. In April 2022, the Centre directed the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) to conduct a pre-feasibility survey to assess the project’s technical, economic, social and environmental viability. The exercise involves geological investigations, including drilling, and identifying villages that may require relocation.
Chief minister Pema Khandu and other state representatives have maintained that the survey does not amount to a decision to build the dam. NHPC has said that preliminary topographical, geological and geophysical work is complete, but core drilling to assess rock characteristics remains on hold because of local opposition.
However, the manner in which the survey was pursued has fuelled distrust. In May 2025, Central Armed Police Forces were deployed at several locations. Police maintained that the deployment was necessary to maintain law and order and that the required clearance had been obtained months earlier.
In September 2026, the state Cabinet approved an empowered committee to oversee the survey, alongside a significant deployment of central forces. Villagers, however, fear that the survey is a precursor to the dam’s construction and have accused the government of using security forces to suppress their opposition.
Questions over consent have further deepened the mistrust. Activist and politician Tadak Nalo alleged that many consent forms cited by the government were false, with endorsements largely coming from villagers whose lives would not be directly affected by the project.
Several indigenous communities, including the Adi, Galo, Nyishi, Apatani and Idu Mishmi, inhabit the Siang valley and depend heavily on the river, not only for their agricultural practices but also for their cultural identities and religious beliefs. They call the river Ane Siang, or Mother Siang. According to independent fact-finding reports, the SUMP would completely submerge nearly 27 villages across the Upper Siang and Siang districts and displace an estimated 1.5 lakh people, almost 11% of Arunachal Pradesh’s population.
With their homes, livelihoods and cultural heritage at stake, people in the Siang valley have only intensified their resistance over the past two weeks. The BJP government’s response, however, has been one of force and intimidation rather than dialogue. It bears resemblance to the way dissent has been dealt with elsewhere under BJP rule — in Delhi, for example, against ongoing protests demanding accountability from chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Use of Force, Detentions and Internet Shutdown
One of the issues against which the October 23 bandh was called was the detention of anti-SUMP protesters since October 9. According to reports, The state government invoked the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (APUAPA) and detained at least 10 protesters. Four of them — Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, picked up from Pasighat — were reportedly held under APUAPA. Among those detained was the president of the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) Youth Wing, a vocal opponent of the mega project.
The crackdown intensified after the October 23 violence. A further 69 people were arrested and four detained in connection with the violence. A total of 55 cases were reportedly filed: 26 criminal cases in Upper Siang, 21 in Siang and six in East Siang district. Arrests and detentions were also carried out under the APUAPA. Those arrested reportedly face charges relating to rioting, the torching of vehicles and the vandalism of office buildings and residential houses.
The state has also significantly increased its security deployment in the region. At least 30 companies of Central Armed Police Forces and three companies of Assam Police have been deployed, in addition to Arunachal Pradesh Police personnel. The Centre also flew in two additional companies of the Rapid Action Force (RAF).
There were also reports of police using tear gas and batons against protesters on October 23. Five women were reportedly taken to hospital after experiencing breathing difficulties. The police, meanwhile, maintained that some protesters had allegedly attempted to breach barricades and attack security personnel.
The crackdown has not been confined to Arunachal Pradesh. On October 31, a solidarity protest against the SUMP outside Arunachal Bhavan in New Delhi, organised by Youth for Change (YFC) Arunachal and Himkhand, also ended in the detention and alleged manhandling of protesters by the Delhi Police.

The protesters alleged that the Delhi Police used brute force and even subjected some of them to sexual assault during the detention. As of November 2, internet services were suspended in Upper Siang as the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum (SIFF) and the SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA), with the support of various student unions and community-based organisations, enforced a 36-hour bandh in parts of the Siang and all Upper Siang districts from 5 am. Protesters demanded the release of the detainees under APUAPA.
Censorship of Social Media Content
The crackdown on the anti-SUMP movement has also extended to the online space, with social media accounts of activists, journalists and news outlets being restricted or taken down. The censorship is part of a wider pattern in India, where government orders and platform restrictions have increasingly curtailed the circulation of content critical of those in power.
Tadak Nalo, founder and president of the political party Arunachal Frontier Tribal Front (AFTF), released a video statement after his Facebook account was restricted. Describing the situation in Arunachal Pradesh as “emergency-like”, he said fundamental rights, including the right to freedom of speech and expression, were being suppressed.
“My Facebook page, ‘Tadak Nalo for Revolution’, has been misused under the Information Technology Act and restricted completely within India today. If you want to view my page, you will have to go outside India. That is how they have set it up,” he said in the video.
Nalo alleged that his commentary on the SUMP was among the reasons behind the restriction. “A project this big is being built in our Arunachal, and it will cause displacement and render the indigenous inhabitants here landless. I had made some commentary on this and written some posts,” he said.
Several journalists and news pages have also reported having their Facebook pages disabled. Shaan Jijong, managing director of Upper Siang News 24*7, released a video statement saying that the outlet’s official Facebook page had been disabled. He also named two others, Ebo Mili and Katon Moyong, whose Facebook pages had allegedly been taken down.
“We are journalists, and we have been covering the SUMP from the ground also. But our news channel was disabled. Is this okay? We are journalists; we are the fourth pillar of democracy,” Jijong said.

The Arunachal Press Club (APC) and the Arunachal Pradesh Union of Working Journalists (APUWJ) have condemned the restrictions on news reports and videos relating to the SUMP on social media platforms in India, and demanded transparency and their immediate restoration.
Targeting Arunachal Times Deputy Editor and Lawyer Defending Activists
Arunachal Pradesh Police have also moved against a journalist covering the anti-SUMP movement, seeking a search warrant against Tongam Rina, deputy editor of The Arunachal Times, in connection with the violence in Pasighat on October 23.
Police have also sought a search warrant against her lawyer, Sunny Tayeng, along with youth leader Otul Jerang, who has been arrested, and activist Tajong Talom, who was previously detained and allegedly harassed.
Rina took to X to assert that the police action would not deter her from her journalism or activism. “…I have seen enough intimidation in my life, so this isn’t something that will stop me from writing or my activism. More power to the people of Siang Valley and Arunachal. We owe it to Siang and her people…” she wrote.
She also criticised the move against Tayeng, pointing out that the lawyer was representing several activists, including Ebo Mili, Tajong Talom and Otul Jerang. Rina said she wanted Tayeng to be able to “focus on her practice rather than be burdened by extra work”.
The application for the search warrant, as reported by The Wire, describes Rina and the three other individuals as “accused persons”. It states that searches were “necessary to establish the individual roles of the accused, ascertain their alleged involvement in the offences and collect relevant material evidence”. However, the application does not specify how Rina or the other three individuals were linked to the violence.
The application states: “It is reasonably suspected on the basis of the facts and material collected during the investigation that certain articles and material connected with the commission of the alleged offences including clothing worn during the incident, mobile phones and digital devices containing relevant photographs or video recordings and other case-related articles may be found at the residences or premises…”
The Press Club of India also issued a statement expressing solidarity with Rina and condemning the Arunachal Pradesh Police’s move.
Paid PR Campaign
Actress Taba Reema, who has been vocal against SUMP, has posted a video alleging that PR firms were reaching out to content creators to speak about the construction of the dam in a positive light. “A few months ago, I also got an email from PR teams and agencies… they said they would pay this much for one reel and a list of pointers of advantages of building a dam. And now every reel or content like this I see… same to same…”
According to Reema, they tried to reach out to a lot of content creators from Arunachal, but they all declined. “And not that Arunachali creators have refused; they are using outsiders for this kind of content….”

According to an Indian Express report, Mumbai-based Concept Public Relations was awarded a one-year contract in July 2025, which was subsequently extended until November 2026, to build opinion in favour of the project, at a total cost of Rs 10.91 crore.
Asked about the agency’s appointment, an NHPC official told the newspaper that it had been hired to put forward “their side” and help supporters within the community speak out, despite “the pressure from violent elements”.
Alt News located several X posts which appear to be part of a concerted effort to delegitimise the protests by portraying protesters as Chinese stooges and calling for them to be “dealt with an iron fist”. While these posts do not, by themselves, establish any link with the PR campaign, they illustrate how opposition to the project was being framed in online discourse.
A short video on Instagram by user @creaatingchaaos has her saying, “You people in Arunachal, have you gone mad? China is making a dam of 60000 megawatts; India also has to do it…” In another video, she can be seen dancing while the text reads, “Arunachal does not have a problem with the dam; the convertereds do”. Several other reels show her making fun of anti-dam protesters, including their accent.

Helen Sharp, a 40-year-old PR professional and ceramicist, was flying with her husband, Adam Robinson; their children, Emma and Charlie; their friends, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr; and their children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, when their private jet crashed, killing all nine passengers.
Based on accounts from friends, family, and fellow artists who knew her, Sharp was a talented ceramics artist, a world traveler, a loving mother and wife, and a beloved friend.
"Helen embodied a life well lived," said a statement posted on her ceramics Instagram page on behalf of friends and family. "She embraced the world, made beautiful things, built lasting relationships, and loved her people fiercely. "
She graduated from the University of Arizona
"Helen was incredibly ambitious, talented, and a light to be around," Texas-based ceramic artist Rebeca Proctor commented on Instagram.
Proctor told Business Insider that she and Sharp were family friends growing up in Houston and became closer when Sharp began taking a class at the community pottery studio Proctor owned.
Sharp attended the University of Arizona. According to a tribute Facebook post from the University of Arizona School of Art, she graduated in 2009 with a BA in Interdisciplinary Studies, focusing on art history and anthropology.
Read more of our coverage on the Learjet crash
She traveled the world
Her LinkedIn showed that she spent time in Buenos Aires, Argentina, as an ESL teacher from 2008 to 2009 and in Taipei, Taiwan, as a writer and editor from 2013 to 2014.
"I left my family, friends, and everything I knew to be alone — to grow up away from society as I knew it," she wrote in an Instagram post in November 2025 about her time in Taiwan. "My isolation and regrowth were pivotal to my development as an adult."
According to her LinkedIn, she returned to Argentina in 2015, where she worked for several years, first as a business development manager and then as an account executive.
It was in Buenos Aires that she "met the love of her life, Adam," the Instagram statement said.
She made a career in public relations
In 2019, Sharp founded her own boutique public relations agency, Influential PR, which focused on sustainable and mission-driven brands.
She announced in May 2024 that her close friend of 20 years, Molly Ford Leibowitz, would be joining Influential PR as COO and partner.
She had a love for ceramics and opened her own studio
Sharp had a self-professed "lifelong love for clay" which started when she first touched clay in kindergarten.
Sharp posted on LinkedIn in February that she had started her own ceramics studio in Aspen, and that Leibowitz would continue to run Influential PR.
At the time, Proctor recalled, Sharp was in the third trimester of her pregnancy with her son Charlie, whom she called her "miracle baby."
"I remember her coming into the studio, very pregnant, just glowing and beaming with joy, working on this huge piece," Proctor recalled. "She was incredibly strong though, and determined, but also knew when to accept help. We were all amazed by her."
Sharp went on to pursue her goal of having a successful career as a ceramics artist, taking workshops with artists such as Austin Coudriet, Paul Briggs, and Bari Ziperstein.
Proctor remembered Sharp as being humble and ready to learn.
"I think in every part of her life, Helen had a vision, and she would always see it through, even through challenges — which, in ceramics, there are many!"
She was beloved in the ceramics community and beyond
After the tragedy, tributes to Sharp and her family flooded in.
"She was my ceramics sister," a fellow ceramics artist commented on Instagram. "I can't even say how much her just being her inspired me to be the woman I am today, and to believe in my own power and talent and the possibilities in front of me."
"She had this beautiful ability to turn any moment into something fun, to make people laugh, and to make even an ordinary day feel special," wrote another commenter, who said he'd met Sharp in Argentina and hired her.
Bari Ziperstein, one of the artists Sharp had learned from, commented, "I'm in total shock! What a loss for the ceramic community & all that she was building."
She loved her children and family
Sharp was remembered as having been deeply devoted to her family and husband.
"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever," the families' joint statement read.
The Instagram post on her ceramics account remembered her and Robinson having "built a life rooted in family, adventure and love."
"Her happiest place was next to Adam and their two beautiful children, along with their dog Bonnie, who was always by her side (and usually in her lap)," it continued.
"She was a wonderful mother and an incredible person who lived life to the fullest," Proctor told Business Insider.

Lamarre-Condon says Baird had “too much adrenaline” and lunged at him with the knife.
As police officers we are trained to shoot people at the centre of body mass … I had a split second moment where I said drop the knife … It was just police ,ode now
If I didn’t do that I was 110% going to have that knife driven into my throat.
And Jesse Baird was going to be sitting in my position today.
Lamarre-Condon ‘had an idea’ to dress up as an UberEats rider
Lamarre-Condon tells the court he had seen what he assumed to be someone’s delivery motorcycle:
As soon as I saw that I had an idea … I saw a hi-vis hooded jacket, waterproof long pants and gloves.
This moment here … I wish that I didn’t do this … But I had the thought process that if I was to put on this helmet and outfit I could knock on Jesse’s door I would look like an UberEats driver without any verbal interaction with Jesse.
And if he wasn’t home I could get the spare key and get my belongings.
Lamarre-Condon says he did not want to come into contact with Baird due to a risk the other man could take out an apprehended violence order against him as Baird had asked him to “please refrain from contacting me”.
At the very least I would have had an AVO out against me … police don’t hesitate to put another police on an AVO … I was worried if I knocked on the door it would be perceived as harassment.
‘It’s time to leave the police force’: Lamarre-Condon says he talked to his mother
Lamarre-Condon and his mother drove to Hertz to pick up a hire car as her vehicle had begun leaking and was dropped at a mechanic, he tells the jury.
The two had picked up the car the day before the alleged murders, and had a conversation. Lamarre-Condon’s voice begins to waver as he tells the court:
I put my phone on airplane mode, which I normally do when having private conversations. My mum could tell something wasn’t right.
I had told her that I just essentially wasn’t feeling OK because of work.
My mum understands this because she was a police officer. She’s been through similar experiences.
The conversation in the car on the way was just not feeling OK and she was just trying to tell me it was time to leave the police force.
Court hears Lamarre-Condon signed out his firearm for a shift three days before alleged murders
Lamarre-Condon tells the jury he signed out his firearm for a shift on 16 February 2024, three days before the alleged murders.
He had permission to do this, he told the court, and on the way to work had stopped at East Village in Zetland to get his car washed.
The former officer claimed in court that it was common for police to get coffee or stop off elsewhere on the way to work.
He says he was thinking of stopping at Paddington to get his belongings from Baird before the other man got home from work, which would have put him in the “exact same” position he was in today as his firearm was still in his backpack.
Lamarre-Condon says he shot his gun in the Royal national park to test the volume
Lamarre-Condon tells the jury about an occasion when he went to the Royal national park with a friend and shot his gun.
At this time he was thinking of taking his own life, and he wanted to test how loud his gun was, he told the jury.
He says he fired it at a tree:
I was very aware of making sure the bullet didn’t hit any innocent person.
Police normally wear eye protection when firing their gun, Lamarre-Condon told the court, so when particulate entered his eyes from the shot, he said: “Shit there’s stuff in my eyes” and began rubbing it.
He then retrieved a brown paper bag and put it over the firearm before firing a second shot, he told the jury.
A little paper bag like that would never change the sound of a gun shot.
