It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.
But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
Soares clung to the banister as, step by step, she climbed two flights of stairs to the polling booth under the watchful eye of her granddaughter’s husband, Marcio Marques.
Inside, the frail but jaunty centenarian keyed the number “13” – representing Bolsonaro’s leftwing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – into an electronic voting machine and pressed confirm.
“I like Lula. I really do!” enthused Soares, a retired bank employee who has lived in Rio de Janeiro most of her life.
“I don’t like Bolsonaro or his father. So the efficient thing to do was go out and vote,” Soares added, as her grandsons, Tito and Ravi, played on the balcony around her surrounded by pot plants and books.
Soares is one of more than 1 million elderly people who, having missed the election’s 4 October first round – which Lula lost – decided to vote in the second.
Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round loser bounced back, but Lula did just that. And after Lula’s shock revival, elderly voters have been hailed as the election’s unsung heroes – including by Lula himself.
At his 81st birthday party last week, the leftist veteran shed tears while describing his gratitude to the elderly people who helped him clinch a historic fourth term while clutching walking frames and sticks.
“I honestly think it was the most powerful and human image I’ve ever seen during an election,” Lula said of viral pictures showing voters in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried into polling centres by relatives or carers, some in stretchers or wheelchairs.
In north-east Brazil, where Lula was born into rural poverty in the 1940s, a 114-year-old retiree called Josefa Pereira da Conceição went to vote wearing a red T-shirt emblazoned with Lula’s face and the slogan “Strength of the people”.
Election experts are still crunching the numbers to fully understand how Lula pulled off his unprecedented fightback, finding 10.3m extra votes between the first and second rounds.
Explanations include a sharp increase in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote; an extraordinary digital mobilisation involving a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11m members in less than a month; and a student-led street rebellion in which millions of citizens protested across Brazil.
Some believe elderly people were also crucial, noting how 1.4 million of the 3 million extra voters who took part in the second round after skipping the first were over 70. Pre-election polls suggested such voters were more inclined to vote for Lula.
Speaking at Lula’s victory celebration, the former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph which sent a message to the democratic world. “It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” Tebet declared, claiming: “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”
The political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said there was concrete evidence of higher turnout among older voters in the runoff, particularly those aged 60 to 79. Voting is only mandatory in Brazil for those aged 18 to 69.
“The images [of elderly people voting] aren’t misleading: they reveal a phenomenon that isn’t just an isolated case. It’s not some made-up story or a staged example. It really happened – and it was a movement you can measure statistically,” Toledo said of the images suggesting an unusually large number of older voters.
That said, Toledo believed the swing to Lula was explained mostly by fear, not age. Voting data suggested many people who backed Lula in the runoff had previously voted for Bolsonaro’s rightwing adversaries, hoping to protest against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), which has governed for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.
In the runoff, faced with a straight choice between Lula, a familiar and predictable figure even for detractors, and Bolsonaro, who represented a leap into the unknown, many preferred the former.
“A protest vote in the first round [became] a safety vote or a lower-risk vote in the second – even if it wasn’t a happy vote,” said Toledo, who believed Bolsonaro alienated many voters with his “arrogant” behaviour after winning the first round.
Particularly damaging was the rightwinger’s authoritarian-sounding vow to “re-democratise” the already democratic country – something Toledo suspected stoked fears that Bolsonaro aspired to be “the emperor of Brazil”.
Even before those remarks, Soares fretted over the direction Brazil might take under Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.
“His father wanted to stage a coup … and stay on as president, just like Getúlio [Vargas did in 1937],” recalled the great-grandmother, who was 12 at the time and lived through the subsequent eight years of dictatorial rule.
Marques, a 51-year-old food entrepreneur, said his grandmother-in-law was also critical of how Jair Bolsonaro undermined vaccination efforts during the Covid pandemic, when 700,000 Brazilians died.
“She’s got three great-grandchildren … and she understands she’s nearing the end of her life. But she’s worried about the country, about her family and about future generations,” said Marques, becoming visibly emotional as he recalled watching Soares exercise her democratic right, perhaps for the last time.
“It was so moving to see her strength and desire [to vote] … We felt she had an intuition, or something telling her she needed to be part of this … She doesn’t know if she’ll get another chance,” added Marques, whose 85-year-old father, Helço Muniz, also voted Lula – in his case for the first time.
Sitting in her armchair overlooking Rio’s Guanabara Bay, five days after the election, Soares voiced excitement that Lula would soon start his fourth and final term. “I’ve been fond of him ever since he was poor,” she said of the lathe operator turned president, who first took office as president in 2003. “He was poor and he became rich, but he carried on being a simple man.”
Occasionally, Soares’s memory betrayed her and she needed reminding that Lula had pulled off one of modern history’s greatest democratic comebacks. “But that’s wonderful!” she beamed.
Reminded of Lula’s feat, Soares predicted Bolsonaro would flee abroad.
“He’s already gone!” her granddaughter, Poliana Soares Jordão, 46, told her. “His dad’s in prison and he’s fled.”
Soares, who has lived through four coups, 16 presidential elections and four Lula wins, was not surprised. “He must have gone to the US, then,” the centenarian guessed, correctly. “He’d been getting ready for that for a while, hadn’t he?”

A bitter end for Ronaldo - the icon who transformed Portugal
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.
The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.
The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.
It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.
His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.
A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.
Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.
So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.
Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.
When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.
He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.
The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.
A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.
It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.
Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.
In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.
That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad. He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.
Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.
The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.
In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.
Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.
Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.
The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.
Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.
After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.
At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.
In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.
Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.
And Eder did.
But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.
His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.
When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.
That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.
Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.
No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.
Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.
Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.
After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.
In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.
After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.
Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.
The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.
Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

Days after Republicans, led by US President Donald Trump, suffered a major setback in the midterm elections, media reports suggested that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was considering leaving the Trump administration as he weighed his next moves. A Bloomberg report on Thursday (local time), citing people familiar with the matter, said that Rubio and his advisers were weighing options for his future. The report added that he had not decided whether to step down as the country’s top diplomat and national security adviser, and that there was no timetable for his possible departure. Rubio has reportedly discussed the possibility of stepping down with White House officials, who have advised him to stay. However, the State Department has denied that he is considering resigning. While the White House did not comment on speculation surrounding Rubio's possible exit, Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of State for global public affairs, said, "This is complete and total fake news based on the word of anonymous sources, befitting a tabloid." He added, "The secretary has not discussed leaving his role, and he will continue to proudly serve in President Trump’s administration long after this fake news is revealed as yet another baseless hoax.” According to the report, Cabinet members and senior aides often consider leaving an administration as its term draws to a close, particularly following a significant setback in the midterm elections, such as the one suffered by Republicans this week. If Rubio steps down before January, Trump would have an opportunity to nominate his successor before Democrats assume control of the Senate. Once Democrats assume control of Congress, they plan to investigate a series of White House initiatives, including those in which the Secretary of State was directly involved, such as attacks on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and the administration’s Venezuela policy. Any nominee Trump puts forward to replace Rubio is also likely to face heightened scrutiny. One question is whether stepping down would allow Rubio to distance himself from the US-Iran war, which reportedly contributed to voter dissatisfaction ahead of the midterm elections. The Secretary of State has defended the administration's decision to launch attacks against Tehran, although he has also sought to distance himself from the conflict. Rubio, a former senator from Florida who once challenged Trump in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, has since become one of the US President’s most trusted aides. He and Vice President JD Vance have frequently been mentioned as potential contenders to succeed Trump as the Republican Party’s leader and seek its presidential nomination in 2028. Bloomberg added that those familiar with the matter believe Rubio could return to the private sector and consider a presidential bid after the 2028 US presidential election. People close to Rubio have indicated that he may prefer to avoid a potentially divisive contest within the Republican Party to determine Trump’s successor, particularly if Vance enters the race. Unlike several other members of Trump’s Cabinet, Rubio has spent decades in public service, earning a government salary, and has not accumulated significant wealth. He has also repeatedly backed Vance as the party’s strongest potential nominee while avoiding questions about his own political ambitions. During his 2016 campaign, Rubio jokingly floated the idea of one day taking over as commissioner of the National Football League (NFL). However, current commissioner Roger Goodell’s contract is set to run until 2031. According to The New York Times, Rubio dismissed reports suggesting that he was considering leaving the Trump administration, saying that working for President Trump until the end of his term had "always been my plan." Rubio further said, "I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you." He added, "I love the work I’m doing," and remarked, "And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. Ridley Scott’s 1982 film Blade Runner casts a long shadow. In some ways, literally.
It defined what noir sci-fi would look like for years to come: the rain, the dramatic lighting, the trenchcoats. Denis Villeneuve delivered a worthy sequel in 2017 with Blade Runner 2049, but for some fans nothing will ever touch the original.
Silka Luisa tries not to think about these things. “If I didn’t love Blade Runner this would’ve been way too hard,” the showrunner of Prime Video’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 said Wednesday during the WIRED World Fair event in Miami.
Luisa’s show differs quite a bit from its forebears. It still has the humanoids known as replicants, but in 2099’s future, they’re the ones calling the shots, giving humans the grunt work they used to do. Set 80 years after Blade Runner and 50 years after 2049, it focuses on a replicant Blade Runner, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), on the search for rogue agents. Along the way she gets teamed up with Cora, played by Hunter Schafer, a human pretending to be a replicant to survive. (We’d say more, but the show doesn’t premiere until November 25, and, you know, spoilers.)
If this vision of dystopia sounds too familiar for comfort, Luisa hears you. When asked about how she chose to tackle the franchise, she noted that in the last couple of decades, “the present caught up to the films” as megacorporations and environmental collapse became realities in ways they weren’t in 1982. The point of her Blade Runner is to show what happens in a post-revolution world and “not focus on the fears we’re living with right now.”
That doesn’t mean that Blade Runner 2099 is entirely a dystopian tale. For Luisa, it’s about showing the “silver linings” of a world run by replicants. To do that, she picks up on some of the environmental themes touched on in Villeneuve’s movie, which showed how Earth had been wrecked by human activity. Blade Runner 2099 depicts a world that replicants are trying to bring back from the brink of ecological collapse using the skills they gained when they were working for humans. “They’re able to rehabilitate the planet,” Luisa says.
Blade Runner 2099 also gave Schafer a chance to flex some action-hero muscles—something she’d never done before and something her costar, Yeoh, has been doing for decades. Schafer jumped right in, running and diving across the screen from the pilot onward. For the fight scenes, though, she got some help from Yeoh.
“It was really physically demanding,” Schafer said during WIRED’s conference. “I felt so lucky to have Michelle Yeoh, who is the fucking master, as a scene partner.”
But back to that shadow cast by Scott’s original adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? In addition to being a sci-fi classic, it also created a whole new template for what dystopian fiction could look like. It broods.
Luisa insists there’s a little more hope in hers—and hopes audiences see that, too. She also wants audiences to know that replicants aren’t the same as the AI bots humans are fixated on in 2026. “They’re more akin to us,” she said. “AI, I just don’t have that same sympathy for.” Hear that, Claude?

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”
Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.
The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.
Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.
Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.
“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”
Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.
Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.
“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.
Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.
“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

Trillions of bacteria living in the human gut may play a role in Parkinson’s disease, a brain disorder that causes tremors, stiffness, and slowed movement, according to a new study involving patients from Keralam.
Researchers from the Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT) and the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Thiruvananthapuram, found significant differences between the gut bacteria of Parkinson’s patients and those of healthy individuals. The findings were published online in npj Parkinson’s Disease, an international scientific journal.
Parkinson’s disease occurs when nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement, gradually die. Scientists have long suspected that the gut and brain communicate continuously, and that an imbalance in gut bacteria could contribute to inflammation affecting the brain. Studies have shown that non-motor symptoms, including constipation and other gastrointestinal problems, can appear years before the tremors begin in Parkinson’s patients.
The study involved 65 Parkinson’s patients attending SCTIMST’s Comprehensive Care Centre for Movement Disorders and 65 healthy individuals, most of whom were the patients’ spouses. Spouses were included as healthy individuals for comparison, as they were more likely to share similar diets and living conditions.
Metagenomic sequencing
Researchers analysed stool samples using metagenomic sequencing (16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing), a technique that identifies the bacteria present and helps assess their potential functions in the gut. They found higher levels of bacteria potentially associated with inflammation and lower levels of beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which help maintain the gut lining healthy and regulate the immune system, in Parkinson’s patients.
The researchers suggest that the shift in bacterial communities could weaken the gut barrier and allow inflammation to spread.
“The study found that differences in the abundances of these bacteria were strongly associated with disease severity and other clinical features of Parkinson’s disease,” said Baby Chakrapani P. S., director of the Centre for Neuroscience and assistant professor in the Department of Biotechnology at CUSAT. “The findings also suggest that gut bacteria may be linked to disease progression through their influence on processes involving dopamine, glutamate, and GABA, chemicals that play important roles in brain function.”
Funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the study was conducted by Aneesa P. A., a research associate at CUSAT, under the supervision of Mr. Chakrapani and Dr. Syam Krishnan of SCTIMST.
Gut bacterial composition is influenced by factors such as diet, age, sex, and lifestyle. Differences in these factors, as well as genetics, could explain why studies in different populations have reported inconsistent associations between particular bacteria and Parkinson’s disease.
According to the researchers, this is the first study in an Indian population to integrate gut microbiome composition with its functional role in Parkinson’s disease. The findings could help future research into simple tests for early diagnosis of the disease and treatments aimed at restoring gut health.

The drugmaker issued its own statement saying that since its treatment — called Zolgensma — was approved in 2019, it has received nine reports of tumors in previously treated patients. Of those, two cases to date showed evidence that the tumors may be linked to the treatment itself.

Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
- Published
Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in Eskişehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.
Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.
In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ryan Phillips, 47, the owner of Bearfoot Gardens, a farm in Seoul. His words have been edited for length and clarity.
I moved to Seoul in 2006, the same year my relationship with the girl I thought was the one ended.
One day, I came home from my accounting job to find she'd moved out. We'd only been living together for a couple of months.
I lost it: I remember breaking the phone after we talked. But then a friend who was about to go to Korea to teach English told me, "Man, just come to Korea. We'll find you a job." I thought: maybe that's what I need.
I was 27. And while I'm the son of a half-Korean adoptee, I didn't speak Korean. I had traveled widely, but I'd never been to Korea or even Asia.
The start of a Korean odyssey
My father was born in Korea and brought over to the US when he was 3. He and my mom were high school sweethearts and prom king and queen in the '70s. They've been together ever since.
Growing up, we moved around Texas a few times and eventually made our home north of Dallas.
I got a degree in international economics and finance from Austin College in 2000, but my career took an unexpected turn.
After trying accounting, I ran into the owners of a ranch where I'd done odd jobs as a teenager. They asked, "Can you cook? We need a chef." I thought, "Let me have a shot at that," and ended up spending about two years cooking mostly American barbecue before returning to accounting.
The first job I landed in Korea was teaching cooking classes to children at an expensive preschool.
I initially planned to do it for a year or two before returning to the US, but the department head valued my experience and persuaded me to teach in the culinary program at a small career-training college.
In 2015, I went back to school for a master's in hospitality at Le Cordon Bleu in Seoul.
Eventually, I thought: I've got to find some land
On the first plot of land I rented, I failed miserably. Four other guys and I wanted to farm organically, without herbicides, pesticides, or chemical fertilizers, and learned mostly from YouTube.
It took three years to see results. Curious local farmers would stop by, see our chilies, and shout, "Not like that! Single stalk!" in Korean. That's where the name of our hot sauce, Han-joolgi, or "single stalk," came from. Our hot sauces, which use ingredients from the farm, are now sold in three restaurants around Seoul.
I started renting and got set up on my present plot of land in Hwaseong, on the southwestern outskirts of Seoul, earlier this year. I named the farm Bearfoot Gardens. I don't live on the farm but hope to move very close next year
We're now growing 30 different varieties of chilies, as well as basil, thyme, oregano, corn, and more. Along with private catering, I hold farm-to-table events here, ranging from dozens to hundreds of people, charging between 50,000 and 150,000 Korean won, or $37 to $113 per person.
We serve American barbecue, Mexican food, and Korean food.
We try and do things you can't do in restaurants. For a recent event, we built a whole fire pit.
I do all the cooking, with support from temp workers and volunteers. International students and US military personnel also often visit the farm. In a separate kitchen, I smoke meats and bottle hot sauces. After seven tough years, the farm is doing well now.
There's been a lot of trial and error to get here.
No plans to return to the US
I've been living in Seoul for 20 years now. I wish my Korean was better, but considering how I use it for work, I think it's pretty darn good.
It took 10 years to feel at home here. There was the language barrier, and body language that I was less familiar with. It felt like "Don't touch me, you're a stranger. You're not in my world." But now I've learned to respect it as different.
I'm single again these days, and work is busy, so there's not much time for dating. I try to spend time with friends when I can. I like to visit new restaurants and support my friends' restaurants.
I've also watched the perspective on Korean food change abroad. Each year, when I go back to Texas to see family and friends, more people tell me how they are making kimchi at home or have tried a new Korean dish. It's a pretty beautiful way to relate.
Other than family and friends living elsewhere, I have zero reasons to leave Korea.

The ‘Chalo Delhi’ march led by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi concluded with a rally at Ramlila Maidan on 01 November 2026, protesting Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged voter roll anomalies. Amidst the demonstration, two videos (here & here) went viral on social media with claims that Delhi Police fired upon Congress workers, allegedly killing four people and injuring ten. Let’s verify the authenticity of these claims.
Claim: Visuals of Delhi Police opening fire on Congress workers during the ‘Delhi Chalo’ rally on 01 November 2026, allegedly killing four people and injuring ten.
Fact: These videos depict clashes between garment workers and security forces in Dhaka, Bangladesh. There were no credible reports of any such violence occurring at the Delhi rally. Delhi Police have officially refuted the rumours, warning of legal action against those spreading the misinformation. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we reviewed media reports to understand whether any such firing on Congress workers happened in Delhi during the rally, but we could not find any evidence. Furthermore, we found no statements or allegations from the Congress party on their official social media handles (here & here) regarding such an incident.
Next, we investigated the first video, which shows clashes between police and civilians, and observed that the language on the signboards is Bengali. A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version (here, here & here) uploaded by Bangladeshi media outlets. These reports identified the footage as an incident from the Mirpur-10 area of Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Furthermore, Google Street View confirms that the location seen in the viral video is in Dhaka, not Delhi.
According to Bangladeshi media reports (here, here & here), severe clashes erupted in Dhaka’s Mirpur area in early November 2026 as thousands of garment workers protested to demand a minimum wage increase from 12,500 to 30,000 BDT. The unrest saw workers blocking major roads, including the Mirpur-10 intersection, and vandalising police vehicles. In response to the vandalism and roadblocks, security forces deployed tear gas, sound grenades, and baton charges to disperse the crowds.
We then investigated the second video, which shows a group of people climbing on and vandalising a police vehicle. According to Bangladeshi media reports (here & here), this video also depicts the same garment workers’ protest, specifically showing individuals attacking a police vehicle under the Mirpur-11 metro station in Dhaka. Additionally, the Dhaka Metropolitan Police logo can be seen on the vehicle.
Moreover, the Delhi Police and PIB Fact Check issued a statement clarifying that these viral videos originate from Bangladesh and have no connection to Delhi. They also warned that appropriate legal action will be taken against those spreading this misinformation.
To sum it up, unrelated videos from a protest in Bangladesh are being shared as footage of Delhi Police firing on Congress workers.

A new UK law banning porn featuring choking and “fauxcest,” or simulated incest, may have unintended consequences for content creators and smut fans all over the world, some experts warn.
As of November 6, amendments to the Crime and Policing Act will outlaw the “possession or publication of pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation”—a law intended to curb violence against women and girls. Yet some experts warn that the legislation is written broadly enough that it could potentially criminalize far more innocuous content, including “breast smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” and even potentially oral sex, ostensibly because people could have their airways impeded during these activities.
“I would encourage both content creators and consumers to underscore the risks of this law,” says Myles Jackman, an obscenity lawyer in the UK. “Because to me, it genuinely seems like one of the greatest acts of suppression of free speech in global history.”
The new amendments were inspired by a lengthy pornography review authored by Baroness Gabby Bertin, a Conservative member of the UK House of Lords. The legislation bans various depictions of sex acts, including “pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation,” as well as content showing performers role-playing as minors under the age of 16.
It also takes aim at “fauxcest,” an extremely popular porn niche that depicts simulated sexual relations between family members who are not related by blood, such as stepsiblings or stepparents. In Bertin’s review recommending the ban on such content, she cites “anecdotal evidence” suggesting that fauxcest “can be used between an abuser and child to permit interfamily child sex abuse,” describing it as a “fig-leaf” of sorts for actual sexual abuse.
Under the new law, those caught distributing or in possession of such content face up to five years in prison and a fine.
The impending UK legislation has prompted panic among some adult creators, many of whom are currently combing through their content libraries and removing clips that could get swept up in the ban.
“The problem is always how broad [the legislation] is,” says Alexandra Snow, an adult content creator and educator. “And we won't know how they're going to interpret it until they start making people's lives hell.”
Snow says she is particularly concerned about how the aspect of the legislation pertaining to “suffocation or strangulation” will affect kink creators, who may make content related to collaring or leather fetishes. She’s also worried about AI image-recognition software, which is already in widespread use among the platforms, potentially flagging content that isn’t violative at all. “They use a very broad, heavy-handed approach,” she says.
Cami Strella, an OnlyFans creator in the US who estimates that 60 to 70 percent of her content depicts some form of role-play, including step-“fauxcest,” is also concerned about the legislation. She says that the content she makes is “just playing a fantasy,” and that more sex education and literacy is required to teach people about the risks of various behaviors.
“I don’t think banning it is going to do anything,” she says. “If anything, it’ll just push even worse content that is actually illegal or immoral underground, so you’ll have to access it away from these platforms. This is just a slippery slope we’re getting into.”
The new UK law is seemingly targeted at the trend of choking in porn, which has been linked to real-life instances of fatal choking during sex. Though the practice is highly risky, potentially leading to brain damage or death, it’s increasingly common among young adults, largely due to the prevalence of eroticized choking depictions in the media and in porn. The death of a 16-year-old Australian girl in August, who authorities say lost consciousness after she was choked consensually during sex, has led to renewed calls for legislation banning depictions of the practice in online porn, which has “absolutely sort of normalized this kind of sexual violence,” Bertin recently told the BBC.
The UK has a history of imposing stringent restrictions on internet pornography, particularly compared to the United States, where statutes like Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 largely exempt platforms from liability for hosting objectionable content. Long before many US states started requiring users to verify their ages before visiting porn sites, for instance, the UK communications regulation agency Ofcom has been slapping websites with fines of up to 10 percent of their worldwide revenue for failing to comply with age-verification requirements.
“The UK is really pushing for limits on free speech,” says Michael Fattorosi, an adult industry attorney based in Italy. “This is just something they're throwing on top of the heap of restrictions.”
In a statement to WIRED, Clara Coleman, a spokesperson for the UK’s Ministry of Justice, denied that the legislation was intended to curb sexual expression. “We’re committed to halving violence against women and girls in a decade, and that includes preventing harm before it starts,” Coleman says. “[These] laws aren’t about policing people’s sexual freedom, they’re about cracking down on content that normalizes violence against women, encourages unlawful behavior, and can cause real-world harm.”
Jackman, the lawyer, says that he has no issue with the provision banning strangulation, as its risks are proven and there are existing laws banning strangulation in the UK. He cautions, however, that the law is written broadly enough that relatively innocuous content could also potentially be penalized.
“It would be up to a court to decide this on a case-by-case basis, but given that it would appear that face-sitting by a vagina owner is now arguably suffocation, the insertion of a penis could equally be considered suffocation because it blocks the airways,” he says. In other words, “the UK could have just banned blow jobs” in online pornography.
Though the law currently applies only to consumers and creators in the United Kingdom, the stiff penalties for “possession” of such images—which the law defines as an image being stored on a phone, a hard drive, or in cloud storage—is of particular concern to Fattorosi.
“As far as creators are concerned, if you visit the UK, if you’re going there on holiday, if you’re going there for a conference, you should probably be careful about what you keep on your phone,” he says.
The subscription-based platform OnlyFans is particularly vulnerable, he adds. Though most American porn companies don’t have a substantial presence in the UK, making it difficult for Ofcom to go after them, that doesn’t apply to OnlyFans. The subscription-based platform’s parent company, Fenix International Limited, is based in the United Kingdom and has already faced steep fines from the agency for failure to adhere to age-disclosure requirements.
“If I were OnlyFans,” Fattorosi says, “I’d be very worried about this.” (In a statement, OnlyFans tells WIRED the platform “complies with applicable laws and regulations in all jurisdictions in which it operates and has longstanding, proactive safety measures in place that meet UK legal requirements.”)
In advance of the new legislation taking effect, adult content platforms have issued updated guidelines for creators. The platform IWantClips has already started complying, publishing a new set of guidelines for creators and fans based in the UK and removing clips that could potentially be swept up in the legislation. The laundry list of sexual niches and categories banned now includes “breast smothering,” “ass smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” “BBW facesitting,” “plastic fetish,” “scissorhold,” and “butt drops.”
Trans Princess Jezebel, a dominatrix and adult content creator in the UK, says she has already started going through her content library on IWantClips and OnlyFans, removing videos that may be seen as violative. She’s heavily reliant on clips to advertise her services as a dominatrix, and she’s concerned that once the law takes effect on November 6, she’ll take a huge financial hit.
“When the state starts regulating which types of pornography people are allowed to watch, a dangerous precedent is set,” she tells WIRED in an email. “Where will it end?”
But even though the UK is, for the time being, an outlier, Jackman warns it may not be for long. He says he has heard of lawmakers in Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain discussing similar legislation, as well as members of the evangelical lobby in the United States.
“In terms of free speech,” he says, “the lights are going out across the globe.”

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published5 days ago
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Why rugby league needs Tonga-Samoa World Cup final
- Published
With blow out wins and a convoluted format, the men's group stage at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup did little to dissuade cynics about the unhealthy state of the international game.
From Group A, Australia and New Zealand came through as expected and are widely tipped to face off in the final on 15 November.
But from the strange lands of Group B-C, two beacons of hope have emerged. Tonga will face New Zealand after winning all three group matches, before Samoa face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.
And if either goes all the way, it would be good for international rugby league, shaking up the game in the same way Wakefield's Grand Final win has for the Super League – proving there is still room for surprises in rugby league.
"Could this be a dress rehearsal for the final? I hope so," former Bradford Bulls head coach Matthew Elliott told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra after Tonga and Samoa's riveting Group B-C match, won 20-18 by the Tongans. "I shouldn't say that out loud as an Aussie but I hope so."
History suggests this scenario is unlikely, but not impossible.
The first semi-final, New Zealand v Tonga, is a match with a dramatic recent history. Tonga beat New Zealand 25-14 in an epic Pacific Championships match two years ago to reach their first-ever elite tournament final.
Last year, their meeting was overshadowed by a head injury to Tonga back-rower Eli Katoa, who needed emergency brain surgery after receiving three separate concussions and has not played since.
Tonga were semi-finalists in 2017, winning their group after stunning New Zealand 28-22 in the group stage. In the last four they were only narrowly defeated by England, 20-18, scoring three tries in the final seven minutes to give the English a huge fright in their best previous World Cup effort.
'It was an absolute cracker'
Samoa have gone one further of course and were surprise runners-up four years ago having not previously gone beyond the quarter-finals since first appearing at the World Cup in 1995.
They were beaten 60-6 by England in their opener but fought through to the semi-finals, where they stunned the hosts 27-26 in a golden point win at Emirates Stadium.
At Old Trafford they were overpowered by Australia but not overawed, losing 30-10. In doing so Samoa became only the sixth different team to reach a men's final after Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, England and France, in 16 editions.
Australia have won 10 of the last 11 World Cups, including the last three, with New Zealand winning the other.
Such dominance at the supposed peak of the sport, in a tournament reduced from 16 to 10 teams this year, indicates a gap growing between haves and have nots.
Of the outsiders, Samoa and Tonga can shake that up.
The teams met at the quarter-final stage of the last Rugby League World Cup, with Samoa winning a classic 20-18 in Warrington. Tonga won by the same scoreline three days ago, in similarly exhilarating fashion.
"The occasion was unbelievable," Samoa head coach Ben Gardiner said after the game. "I looked down at the start of the game and I've never seen so many people on the sidelines at a footy match in my life.
"It was a sensational occasion, and international rugby league is about that. It's about fanfare and it's about creating opportunities for our fans to come and watch our nations play. It was an absolute cracker."
'Five or 10 levels above NRL'
Not only are the Pacific islands bringing the colour and passion of their nations to the world stage, they are also bringing world-class quality.
Nine players featuring in the group game squads played some part in this year's State of Origin, an annual series between New South Wales and Queensland representative teams regarded as one of the pinnacles of world rugby league.
"I think that was about five or 10 levels above NRL tonight," Tonga half-back Isaiya Katoa told Premier Sports of the group match. "Every tackle felt like the first of the game. There are going to be some sore bodies out there.
"Something that goes so unnoticed is the impact Woolfy [Kristian Woolf] has as the coach. He cares about every single one of us. The reason you've got Jojo Fifita and Rob Toia [two of the State of Origin players] wanting to play for Tonga is because of the coach."
Both nations have Australians in charge. Gardiner has been in post since 2023, while Woolf has led Tonga since 2014 and overseen their remarkable rise in rugby league prominence.
Both have experience coaching in the NRL, and have brought the quality and professionalism of the world's best domestic league to bear fruit on their respective islands – with both talking about working on "emotional regulation" in big games.
They have also both been helped by an international eligibility system which is much more forgiving to smaller nations than in many other sports.
Since 2016, the IRL introduced a tier system for member nations: Australia, New Zealand and England are in tier one; all other full members are in tier two.
Under this system, players can elect to represent both a tier one and two nation but are permitted to represent only one nation in a calendar year or at a Rugby League World Cup.
This flexibility has allowed members of diaspora populations to represent their family heritage and national identities – particularly those with ancestors from Pacific islands, who may have had to move away in the past.
These connections mean that when those with Tongan and Samoan heritage do represent their historic countries, they do so with gusto.
'This is the pinnacle'
"I can't put it into words," Tonga prop Addin Fonua-Blake told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "This is the pinnacle for me. Representing my people is something special.
"I just want to thank from the bottom of my heart all the supporters. You could feel it this whole week, the amount of support that we had, that both teams had. And it's only going to keep growing. What the supporters have done for this game, it's unheard of.
"A few years ago, we wouldn't even sell out a game out of Campbelltown and now we're sitting here on one of the biggest stages selling out, and it's only going to get bigger."
Both countries have also benefited from generous financial deals the likes of which English rugby league supporters want introduced for their team.
Australia's government in July announced, external it was committing A$250m (£130m) over 10 years to the Pacific Rugby League Partnership, designed to help create opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and is being led by the Australian Rugby League Commission.
It is the kind of diversification rugby league badly needs, after a reduced and unbalanced World Cup which at times has struggled to live up to its name.
"The branding of the World Cup, I think that's wrong," former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is, it's a festival of the sport.
"I'm not saying Rugby League could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but certainly more than 10. It's meant to be a festival and showcasing to everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play, get it out there.
"I'll talk about Italy in 2013. Italy don't play Rugby League too much. They managed to get a team full of people who love their heritage, based in the NRL, a lot of Australians, and they managed to beat England in a warm-up game. So don't tell me there's no countries out there, such as Italy, who cannot live up to displaying well in the World Cup and putting on an event."
If rugby league is to grow and the World Cup is to survive, it needs new blood to thrive. A world title for Tonga and Samoa would certainly help.

India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs. In an advisory dated November 4, 2026, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified the threat actor behind the campaign as 'CRAFTY FALCON', describing it as an AI-assisted financial threat actor that uses machine intelligence to identify targets, execute attacks at machine speed and exploit victims' own payment and disbursement APIs to initiate unauthorised fund transfers. Banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), fintech companies and other financial services entities have been warned of the growing threat. CERT-In's Computer Security Incident Response Team-Finance (CSIRT-Fin) said the campaign has witnessed a significant escalation, with successful attacks continuing to be reported across the financial services ecosystem. The agency has urged all BFSI entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Repeat Attacks Despite Remediation A key concern highlighted in the advisory is the threat actor's continued targeting of financial entities that had already received earlier restricted advisories and undertaken remediation measures. According to CERT-In, some of these organisations have been deliberately targeted again, including cases where remediation was incomplete. The attacks have also been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other periods of reduced monitoring, potentially delaying detection and response. CERT-In's analysis identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools in the campaign. These include the ARTEX family of large language model (LLM)-based tools, PentAGI, an autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, and the Cairn attack search engine, alongside the CyberStrikeAI framework. These tools can execute complete attack chains autonomously, generate and refine large volumes of customised attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on responses from targeted systems. The supporting attack infrastructure also changes frequently, with IP addresses rotating within hours to days. CERT-In said infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with affected entities through restricted advisories. AI Agents Pose Growing Cybersecurity Risks The latest advisory follows another critical warning issued by CERT-In in October, when the agency flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools to conduct financially motivated intrusions into Indian organisations. The watchdog warned that autonomous AI agents, ostensibly deployed for research and evaluation, had accessed live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. Meanwhile, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has also warned banks, NBFCs and fintech startups about the growing use of AI agents by cybercriminals to perpetrate financial fraud. The agency said it had uncovered multiple individual cases in which malicious agentic AI systems exploited compromised financial systems to execute unauthorised transactions involving amounts running into crores of rupees. CERT-In Flags Vulnerabilities In Tata Motors' Connected Vehicle Apps Separately, CERT-In has flagged multiple vulnerabilities in select versions of Tata Motors' iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev connected vehicle applications, which could allow attackers to access sensitive credentials and vehicle-related information. The agency identified four vulnerabilities, including hardcoded service account credentials, API keys and authorisation tokens within the applications; inadequate validation of URLs and origins loaded through the apps' WebView component; authentication tokens being recorded in application logs; and improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. CERT-In has urged users to update their applications to the latest versions of iRA 2.0 (version 26.8.2) and iRA.ev (version 26.9.1). The applications provide access to connected vehicle functionalities, including vehicle status updates, health monitoring, trip details and remote vehicle commands.

Color us nostalgic.
Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.
Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.

Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?
- Published
"Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."
British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Instagram. Last week, World Triathlon announced it was partnering with Hyrox - the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations.
The agreement means Hyrox becomes a recognised discipline within World Triathlon. And now it sits under a recognised international federation, it could be eligible for inclusion at the Olympics and Paralympics.
It is too late for the Los Angeles 2028 Games but is there room for both hybrid racing and triathlon to feature at a future Olympics? Or could one replace the other?
For triathlon, a sport which has been in the Olympics since 2000, and has long-established professional circuits, its athletes are questioning whether they'll reap any rewards from this partnership - or even, whether it could "kill" the sport altogether.
'We were kind of blindsided'
Stapley, who spoke to BBC Sport from a training camp in Thailand, was having dinner with friends when his phone started pinging with news of the proposals and reaction to them.
"I was like, hold on a minute, what's this?", said Stapley.
"We don't even get an early notification, we found out on Instagram".
The post read, external: 'Hyrox x World Triathlon are officially introducing 'Hybrid Racing' as a new discipline within the World Triathlon family.'
Sophie Evans - who won gold as part of England's Commonwealth Games mixed relay team in Birmingham in 2022 - said she was "surprised" to receive the news like that.
"I'm not actually against it being part of World Triathlon. It's more the fact we were blindsided, it's just like it's here," she added.
Stapley accused World Triathlon of not caring about its athletes because he did not receive any communication from his sport's governing body prior to and after the announcement was made.
"They have no respect for us," he said. "They don't even contact us like 'hey, do you guys actually care about this, or what do you think?'"
In response, a World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The World Triathlon Executive Board approved the partnership. The board includes representatives of the World Triathlon Athletes' Committee elected by their peers.
"Athlete representatives are involved in every executive board discussion, and their voice is always heard.
"The announcement was communicated through the same procedures followed for all World Triathlon releases."
'An attack on our existence'
World Triathlon says the partnership is designed to "benefit the entire World Triathlon movement",, external with new opportunities to engage athletes and audiences, and a stronger platform to grow triathlon and multisport from grassroots to elite level.
The question for athletes is, how?
European champion Roksana Slupek, of Poland, said she was "not against the idea", but wanted more information.
"What's the benefit for us, for triathlon? It's nothing against Hyrox," said Slupek.
However, Stapley called the move an "attack on our whole existence" and is concerned that World Triathlon could direct attention and resources towards Hyrox's Olympic ambition - at the expense of his own sport.
"How does Hyrox grow triathlon? If anything they've killed triathlon," he said, while also suggesting brands would rather get in early with Hyrox athletes before they potentially appear at an Olympics.
"Sponsorships have reduced because there's no visibility on TV, you have to pay to watch us.
"We are triathletes that do the short distance, which is the Olympic distance, and we've trained all our lives for it.
"There's no swimming, there's no biking, it's indoors. [Hyrox] has got nothing to do [with triathlon]".
"It seems like our sport's gone, 'no worries, come along, use our structure, use our access to the International Olympic Committee, and perhaps take our space'.
"We've got an opportunity to win medals in Los Angeles [at the 2028 Olympics], but will we have it further down the track?"
Evans said that while triathlon was an "established" Olympic sport, that has provided high quality racing since its introduction to the Games 26 years ago, this new partnership has introduced a "level of uncertainty".
"A lot of the resistance has come from athletes, because you don't know," she added.
A World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport, it is continuing to "increase its focus and involvement in the Olympic and Paralympic families" and that it is in the "planning phase" for Brisbane 2032, adding that "triathlon is, and will remain, at the heart of everything we do".
BBC Sport approached Hyrox for comment, but they referred us to the statements made by World Triathlon.
Can triathlon and Hybrid racing co-exist?
Sam Dickinson - who won an Olympic triathlon bronze in Paris as part Team GB's relay quartet - can see why the move makes sense but wants more clarity.
"It's trying to get people active not from an elite side but from a participation side," Dickinson told BBC Sport.
"So in that sense it does make sense that as a multi-sport it comes under the World Triathlon umbrella.
"But it's early days, we don't have any of the bread and butter of exactly what's going on."
And there lies the crux of the problem - the lack of clarity has fuelled speculation about what the future holds.
World Triathlon does have other disciplines in its remit, such as Aquathlon and duathlon.
BBC Sport has been told that 'Fitness Racing' was first included as a discipline in the World Triathlon Constitution in October 2025, a move supported by the majority of the governing body's National Federations.
A World Triathlon spokesperson added that the partnership provides opportunities to 'reach new audiences' through collaborating with global partners.
Founded in 2017, Hyrox's popularity has continued to grow rapidly. A total of 1.5m athletes took part during the 2025/26 season - up from 650,000 the year before - with participation projected to surpass 2m in the current season.
British Triathlon, one of World Triathlon's national federations, told BBC Sport it recognises "World Triathlon's work to grow, develop and strengthen the sport of triathlon, multi-sport and its community", but is waiting to hear the "full operational, governance and commercial framework" for the partnership.

India successfully test-fires indigenously developed quasi-ballistic missile Pralay | Watch
Pralay, developed by the DRDO, is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg.
India on Thursday successfully test-fired quasi-ballistic missile Pralay from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the coast of Odisha. The missile, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), is capable of carrying conventional warheads, the defence ministry said in a statement.
Pralay is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg. "With this successful test, the induction of the system has become imminent," the ministry said.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh also complimented DRDO, Defence Forces and industry partners on the successful flight-test and said the missile equipped with advanced technologies will further enhance the technological capabilities and operational preparedness of the military against emerging threats.

The defence ministry said that all the test objectives were fully met as confirmed by the test data captured by various range instruments deployed by Integrated Test Range, Chandipur.
Research Centre Imarat, Hyderabad, along with other DRDO laboratories, indigenously developed the missile, it said.
Bharat Dynamics Limited, one of the development-cum-production-partners, has produced the system.
The flight-test was conducted in the presence of senior officials from DRDO, representatives from the industry and the defence forces, as part of user evaluation trials, the ministry said in a statement.
