Disney tech employees are pushing management for answers after several major rounds of layoffs this year and reports that more cuts are coming.
Several staffers told Business Insider they're struggling with morale and are putting in extra effort to look busy — and some of their colleagues sounded off in a company meeting Thursday.
"Do we know when the cost cutting is targeted to happen?" a Disney software engineer asked in a town hall on Thursday afternoon.
The question was submitted in writing during the Q&A portion of the meeting. Business Insider viewed screenshots of some of the questions.
The uncertainty came days after Bloomberg reported that Disney is planning to lay off thousands of employees, citing sources familiar with the matter. It said some managers were asked to aim for 20% in annual cost savings. Disney declined to comment to Bloomberg. Disney didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
"Would it [be] better for employee morale to first hear from mgmt about future employee benefit changes and layoffs, instead of hearing about these from the media?" a veteran tech employee asked.
A third tech staffer asked: "How do you anticipate these cost cuts will impact MPA?" (MPA refers to Disney's "Media Platform Alliance," which includes the streaming distribution, infrastructure, and metadata teams.)
A fourth employee asked leadership if they had "any insight into what motivated the early retirement package offers" that the Mouse House offered certain higher-ups, which were first reported by Deadline in late August. Dana Walden, Disney's creative chief, said at a Bloomberg event on October 1 that the company had offered "an extremely generous" early retirement program.
During the town hall, Disney streaming leaders didn't give specific answers to questions about whether cuts were coming or when they could happen, two streaming employees who attended the meeting said.
A fifth employee asked what Disney's "plans are for these new c.ai folks," referring to the 66 staffers the company is paying $60 million to hire from Character.AI, an AI chatbot startup that filed for bankruptcy in mid-October. Disney's new tech chief, Karandeep Anand, had been Character.AI's CEO before joining in early October.
"What will they be working on?" this tech staffer asked, in reference to the Character.AI members moving to Disney.
After the meeting, several Disney staffers expressed their frustration on Blind, an anonymous forum that verifies work email addresses before allowing users to view a specific company's page.
"Their answers in the Q&A make my blood boil," one Blind user said.
Another Blind user said that the town hall was "forced positivity" and that leadership was "completely ignoring all the actual changes and issues destroying morale."
'Very demotivating'
Layoffs — and reports of possible layoffs — are affecting morale inside Disney, four employees said this week ahead of Thursday's town hall.
Reports of coming cuts are "very demotivating," a high-level engineer said, adding that it weighed down on their mood — even after a positive annual review.
"I've been through enough of these to know that doesn't mean safety," this person said.
Another software engineer said Disney staffers are on edge, antsy to prove that they're pulling their weight.
"Everyone's looking more 'busy,'" this person said, noting that some high-ranking tech employees are "attending meetings they'd otherwise skip."
Disney had three rounds of cuts in CEO Josh D'Amaro's first seven months and filed a WARN notice in California in late October, signaling that it's planning to let go of 159 park employees.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
- Published
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.
"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.
In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.
"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
A diplomatic dilemma
Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.
Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.
Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.
Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".
The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.
"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.
To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.
But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.
"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
Waiting for winds to change
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.
Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.
In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.
And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. What Changes For Operators? The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. Connecting Phones To Satellites TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

Rumors that the U.S. Department of Defense gave a high-value contract to a foreign pharmaceutical company to produce "ketamine wafers" for the military circulated in October.
People on social media alleged the product was being developed by Singapore-based iX Biopharma and was called Wafermine, described as a "small ketamine wafer that dissolves under the tongue and delivers the drug through the mucous membrane without injection."
The claim gained enough popularity that Snopes readers reached out to us via email and asked us to investigate.
The claim was true, according to multiple documents from iX Biopharma. The company did not respond to Snopes' request for comment, but we will update this article if we hear back.
An official for the Defense Health Agency, a federal agency that describes itself as a "combat support agency," emailed a statement to Snopes that called the development of "pain management solutions for warfighters" a priority.
The official said of their partnership with iX Biopharma:
The potential solution suits the Department's requirements on a suitable timetable. The potential solution has a track record of pre-hospital analgesic use in Australia for 10 years.
The agency learned of iX Biopharma and Wafermine as part of standard market research on analgesic ketamine products. The agency requested additional information from the company to determine the suitability of Wafermine for pre-hospital pain management.
DHA is confident our government and industry partners will work through each step of the regulatory process to deliver appropriately approved and manufactured products that support the health and readiness of our warfighters. Questions about the regulatory process should be addressed to the manufacturer and the FDA.
FDA, DOW, and iX Biopharma continue to discuss the best methods to deliver safe and efficacious pain management products with a strong preference for domestic manufacturing to strengthen supply chain and distribution in support of our Joint Force.
Safe and efficacious drug development and manufacturing is, rightfully, a regulated process. DHA is committed to working with our government and industry partners through each step of the process to deliver products to support the health and readiness of our warfighters.
On Feb. 12, iX Biopharma issued a news release and announcement from the board of directors about the contract with the Department of Defense. "The U.S. government will provide $40,954,914 in funding to support the development of Wafermine," the announcement read.
IX Biopharma described Wafermine as the "world's first patented sublingual racemic ketamine wafer being developed for acute moderate to severe pain" which can be administered without an injection. The news of the announcement was added to the company's newsroom website on Feb. 12.
The announcement added that the "contract was awarded to the Company under a sole-source procurement process, meaning the U.S. government determined that the Company was uniquely capable of delivering the required product within the required timelines."
The contract was celebrated in the company's 2026 annual report, released in September, which called the DOD's investment its "defining event of the year" and said it "anchored" the company's entry into the U.S. healthcare market.
The report clarified that the development of Wafermine is intended for the U.S. military "to deploy on the battlefield and include in its standard issue medical sets, kits and outfits."
A 2019 study showed that as the use of ketamine in U.S. combat operations increased from 2010-19, use of opiates decreased.
Deployment of a new product like Wafermine would usually be subject to full approval by the Food and Drug Administration before release, but on Sept. 3, the Department of Health and Human Services made an Emergency Use Authorization declaration, available to read on the Federal Register.
The declaration cited a determination made by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July which declared a current or "significant potential" of a military emergency.
The HHS declaration read, in part:
On July 15, 2026 the Secretary of War determined, pursuant to sec. 564(b)(1)(B) of the FD&C Act, that there is a military emergency, or a significant potential for a military emergency, involving a heightened risk to U.S. military forces of an attack with a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear agent or agents; or an attack by an agent or agents that may cause, or are otherwise associated with, an imminently life-threatening and specific risk to U.S. military forces (including agents of military combat such as firearms, projectiles, and explosive devices). Injuries arising from these attacks may cause U.S. military forces to experience moderate to severe acute pain and place them at risk of developing life-threatening hemodynamic instability, including shock or respiratory distress.
In sum, an EUA would allow Wafermine to be expedited for use on the battlefield despite not yet having full approval from the FDA.
IX Biopharma announced the move toward an EUA in September, writing that "circumstances exist for the FDA to consider Wafermine for EUA. Before the Declaration, supply of Wafermine to US military personnel would have required full FDA approval. With the statutory precondition under section 564 now satisfied, a regulatory route exists, subject to the FDA granting an EUA."
The company said it planned on filing its EUA before the end of the year.
In October, Politico reported that iX Biopharma's Nevada-based manufacturing partner, Orion Specialty Labs, was not yet licensed by the state pharmacy board to operate.
IX Biopharma's annual report stated Orion had "ordered specialised manufacturing equipment" and that it "relocated our manufacturing equipment from Australia to Orion's facility to accelerate the production readiness."

Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.
“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.
Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”
He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.
Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.
But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
A new Northstar
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

- The Xbox PC app has received a major overhaul, available to Xbox Insiders starting November 5, 2026.
- The updated app launches 60% faster, with easier navigation, improved search, and better ways to connect with friends.
- Xbox is also rolling out the refreshed design and navigation to cloud gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets.
Following reports of a new Xbox PC app update with console-like features in early October 2026, Microsoft has officially announced the overhaul, bringing faster launch times, simpler navigation, and a cleaner interface. The updated app is now available to Xbox Insiders, starting November 5, 2026.
According to Xbox Wire’s latest blog, the updated Xbox PC app launches up to 60% faster, with Home, Store, and Xbox Game Pass pages loading up to 50% faster and in-app windows opening up to 65% faster. Not just that, Microsoft has made it a lot simpler to navigate the app for PC users.
The new Xbox PC app makes it easier to find the best Xbox games with simpler library navigation, updated filters, and more ways to organize your collection. Microsoft has also brought friends and social features into the main navigation, making it easier to see what friends are playing, chat, and join parties.
Furthermore, the improved search brings together results for games, installed titles, add-ons, and people in one place, so you can find games on the Xbox Store or on Xbox Game Pass more quickly. Lastly, Microsoft has also given a cleaner look with the Xbox PC app overhaul, with refreshed game cards, Home, Settings, and animations.
The updates don’t end here, as Microsoft is bringing a refreshed Xbox Cloud Gaming experience with the Xbox PC app overhaul, which introduces a new Library tab that brings together owned and Game Pass cloud games, with options to browse, sort, and filter by recently played titles, genre, and input type.
Additionally, desktop mode uses larger screens better, while new dark and light themes and five high-contrast options let players customize the experience to their preferences. After Xbox revealed new cloud gaming prices, it is now rolling out the updated design and navigation to cloud gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets.

NC will never split: Farooq Abdullah assures unity after meeting disgruntled MLAs
Fifteen disgruntled National Conference legislators met Farooq Abdullah in Srinagar to present their demands. The rebellion over the Cabinet expansion and governance has put Omar Abdullah's majority under scrutiny.
National Conference (NC) president Farooq Abdullah on Friday dismissed reports of a possible split in the party as “baseless”, asserting that the organisation would remain united after meeting disgruntled legislators in Srinagar.
“These are baseless reports. The NC will never be split. I have heard their grievances, and we will work on them,” Abdullah said after the meeting at his residence, where 15 party MLAs had gathered amid growing discontent over the recent Cabinet expansion and the functioning of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah-led government.
The meeting, which also involved Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, was called to address the concerns of the dissident legislators and resolve the growing internal tensions.
According to sources, the Chief Minister had refused to meet the lone Independent MLA who is part of the dissident group, conveying that he was willing to hold talks only with legislators belonging to the NC.
The legislators who arrived for the meeting included Javed Mirchal, Sajad Shafi Uri, Ghulam Mohiuddin Mir, Farooq Jan, Bashir Ahmad Veeri, Abdul Majid Bhat alias Larmi, Farooq Ahmad Shah, Mubarak Gul, Justice (Retd.) Hasnain Masoodi, Nazir Ahmad Gurezi, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Javed Iqbal Choudhary, Saif-ud-Din Bhat and Qaisar Jamshaid Lone.
The disgruntled MLAs are expected to formally submit their resolution to the party high command, placing their demands before the leadership amid the ongoing internal crisis.
The meeting comes amid mounting discontent over the recent Cabinet expansion and the functioning of the Omar Abdullah-led government.
DISGRUNTLED MLAs REFUSE TO BACK DOWN
Ahead of the meeting, 15 disgruntled NC MLAs and one Independent MLA held another closed-door meeting in Srinagar on Thursday evening to finalise their collective strategy. This was reportedly their fourth such meeting since the recent Cabinet reshuffle.
Sources in the dissident camp said the legislators remained united and were unwilling to dilute their demands.
They have maintained that their actions are aimed at addressing internal grievances and saving the party.
The rebel MLAs have also alleged that they have faced continued humiliation and public disrespect from the Chief Minister and his close aides since the NC government came to power in October 2024.
WHAT ARE THE MLAs DEMANDING?
The group has stuck to three key demands:
Reshuffle the entire Cabinet: The MLAs want Omar Abdullah to relieve all ministers of their portfolios and constitute a new Cabinet after proper consultations with the NC legislature party.
Remove CM's adviser: They are demanding the removal of Nasir Aslam Wani from his position as adviser to the Chief Minister.
Address legislators' grievances: They want an assurance that MLAs will be treated with respect and an internal party mechanism will be established to address their genuine concerns.
The MLAs have indicated that they have been patient for long enough and are now seeking concrete action from the party leadership.
NUMBER GAME PUTS OMAR GOVT UNDER PRESSURE
The rebellion has also brought the numbers in the 90-member Jammu and Kashmir Assembly into focus.
The ruling alliance currently has 54 MLAs, comprising 41 from the National Conference, six Congress legislators, six Independents and one CPM member. The majority mark stands at 46.
The Opposition has 29 BJP MLAs, four from the PDP, one each from the Jammu and Kashmir People's Conference and AAP, and one Independent.
According to the scenario being discussed, if 20 disgruntled NC MLAs resign together and one Independent MLA withdraws support, the Assembly's effective strength would fall to 70, bringing the majority mark down to 36.
In that situation, the ruling alliance's strength could fall to 33, comprising 21 NC MLAs, four Independents, six Congress MLAs and one CPM member — potentially putting the Omar Abdullah government below the majority mark.

A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.
On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast. Its remote location and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” said Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.”
Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.

A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch early Friday morning, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.
Just before midnight, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia.
She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion, in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.
"The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.
Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.
The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.
A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.
Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.
Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.
The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.
Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.
Among their many concerns, critics said the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.
Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.
"Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."
Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.
Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.
"[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.
As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.
The commission started deliberating just before 10 p.m. The discussion lasted less than an hour.
The commissioners who spoke first were Trump allies and appointees. They thanked the speakers for taking the time to share their views, but — in brief comments — expressed their support for moving forward. They continued to cast the arch as a tribute to the nation and those who served, despite the broad pushback from individual veterans and veterans' groups.
The Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws. They maintained that Congress authorized the project when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle in 1925, which were never built.
And they pointed to recent claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the monument will enhance national security — even though officials at the meeting confirmed that no such analysis or details were included in the final submission. In fact, Interior Department official Greg Wischer said "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court but that the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."
The most vocal criticism of the arch came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the council. He asked questions about the arch's purpose — military and otherwise — earlier in the meeting and said, during deliberations, that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.
"We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.
Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, expressed concerns about delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wants to "commence building very quickly."
Within minutes, the commission had given the arch its green light. The Trump administration notified the court within half an hour. By Friday, that light had turned red — at least temporarily.
"While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project," Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said in a statement.
Arch critics look to the courts and Congress for relief
Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome.
Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, called the night's vote a "sham."
"It undermines the democratic process, violates federal statute, and insults our nation's veterans who have made the ultimate sacrifice," he said in a statement. "From the start, this Arch project has been driven by an artificial sense of urgency, while public opposition has been brushed aside."
Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement that the organization is disappointed but not surprised. He vowed to "bring this to members of Congress, to ensure this arch is never built. Not here. Not ever."
Many Democratic lawmakers have vowed to stop — and investigate — the arch after they regain a Congressional majority in January.
Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen — the consumer rights nonprofit representing the veterans in their lawsuit — told NPR on Thursday that Congress doesn't need to act to stop the arch, since it never actively approved it. That decision, he said, will be up to the courts.
But, he added: "It would be fine if Congress takes additional measures to block construction, since we've seen this lawless administration circumvent the law and court orders so frequently."
Virginia Rep. Don Beyer has introduced a bill that would prohibit and defund the arch, and said Thursday he expects the number of co-sponsors to grow from 80 to at least 200 in the new year.
And Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners that companies and "officials working to advance a project not authorized by Congress will put themselves at legal risk."
He argued that the project violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws, which fall within the jurisdiction of the House committee he expects to soon lead.
"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," Huffman said.

Claim: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries.

Further, we conducted a search using the ‘M World’ logo visible at the top of the viral clip. This led us to the M World News Instagram page, where we found the original video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. To sum up, this Video of Sergey Lavrov making derogatory remarks about India is digitally manipulated.

Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine.
The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."
Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.
The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.
The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.
"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.
"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."
The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.
President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.
Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.
"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."
Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.
"In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."

CAPFs debated merit, ex-Agniveer postings before Union Cabinet’s Agnipath overhaul approval
The Cabinet approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial service an option to remain in service
The central armed police forces (CAPFs) debated how to assess Agniveer merit for induction and where to post these highly trained soldiers to ensure smooth integration with existing personnel without friction, before all of the short-term military recruits were given a retention option.
Seventy-five per cent of the first Agniveer batch were set to be released under the Agnipath scheme before the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial four-year service an option to remain in service for two more years. Agniveers were offered a route to enrol as regular soldiers at the end of the extended period.
In March 2023, the government announced a 10% Agniveer quota in CAPFs and exemption from the Physical Efficiency Test when the scheme was first notified. They had to take the written test, and ex-Agniveers could join as constables (general duty), the junior-most functional rank. “The quota increased from 10 to 50% in CAPFs, a substantial increase. More than that, the issue concerned 50% of former soldiers being inducted directly while the other 50% had to clear all tests. It was a challenge to ensure this would not affect the morale of those who had to clear all tests to get inducted,” said an officer.
Deep Dive
The CAPFs were awaiting clarity on how merit was to be established for the 50% ex-Agniveers because there was to be no test, written or physical, during their induction until the Union Cabinet’s retention approval.
Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, who on Wednesday announced the Cabinet’s decision, said there would be no reservation for ex-Agniveers. “The reservation in the paramilitary forces and states was announced when 75% of soldiers were to be released back into society.”
He said the defence forces are offering all 75% Agniveers a chance to join back and also enrol as regular soldiers after completing their tenure. “This is why, after this, no reservation, whether in paramilitary forces or state government, will exist because the Indian defence forces are providing them all an opportunity to rejoin for a second engagement period of two years and after that to become regular soldiers in the armed forces.”
Merit assessment and integration within CAPFs gained urgency after the government made changes to the Agnipath scheme over the last year. The first two Agniveer batches from the Navy and Air Force were due to complete their tenure in November and December, making them eligible for reemployment in the CAPFs.
People aware of the matter said Union home ministry officials held meetings on how to decide merit among the Agniveers and avoid friction between regular CAPF personnel, who have to pass three tests.
In November 2025, the government exempted ex-Agniveers from all written, physical efficiency, or physical standard tests for enrolment in the CAPFs.
Officials said the ministry also formed an ex-Agniveer cell this year. The cell was taking feedback and inputs from all CAPFs regarding the induction and career progression of the ex-Agniveers.
The Central Reserve Police Force was appointed the nodal agency for their induction and career progression across all CAPFs.
A second officer said all CAPF chiefs were holding internal discussions with their senior officers on ways to induct the former soldiers into the force in the weeks leading up to Wednesday’s announcement. “This looked like an easy transition, but it is a challenging one. Soldiers are highly trained and motivated.”
The second officer said the Agniveer job is proactive, while it is reactive in CAPFs, barring counter-insurgency or counter-militancy operations. “All chiefs were taking inputs to find the best place to post highly trained soldiers and reorient them. ...this would not have been the first time such a transition happened. There are hundreds and thousands of cases, especially in the early years of BSF [Border Security Force] when the force took army personnel on deputation.”
The officer added that many officers enjoyed the work culture and decided to continue their service in the CAPFs. “There are also many cases of army officers joining state police forces too.”
Brigadier (Retd) Rohit Nautiyal joined the CRPF as a deputy inspector general and was posted in Srinagar in 2022 after serving the Army for 32 years. He retired from the CRPF last week after a three-year tenure post-reemployment.
Decorated Colonel (retired) Nectar Sanjebam of the 21 Para Special Forces, who led the 2015 surgical strikes in Myanmar, was inducted into the Manipur Police as a senior superintendent (combat).

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
- Published
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
- LIVE: Follow latest updates
- BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
- THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results
- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
- 'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.
The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.
The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

Australia turn to Hussey ahead of Ashes after batting slump
Nov 6 : Australia roped in Mike Hussey as a long-term consultant coach on Friday to tackle their batting vulnerabilities ahead of next year's Ashes series in England.
Hussey's new stint will also include next year's 50-over World Cup and an advisory role for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and the subsequent Twenty20 World Cup.
The appointment comes as Australia seek to halt a worrying slide in red-ball form ahead of a packed test calendar that includes the Ashes, which England will host in June, July and August next year.
Pat Cummins' side have faced mounting scrutiny over their batting after slumping to a 2-1 series defeat by South Africa, capped by a humiliating final-day collapse in the third test.
The setback followed a shock nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh, their first test defeat against the South Asian team, in Darwin in August.
"I am extremely excited about being a part of the team in a more formal and meaningful role in the coming years," Hussey said in a statement.
"This team has achieved so much in recent times, to which I hope I can add value to the coaching and playing groups ahead of what will be an exciting and challenging period."
The 51-year-old, who played 302 matches for Australia across all formats, will also assist during its upcoming T20 series against England and preparations for the home test series against New Zealand.
"Mike has been a highly valued part of our staff in the past and brings a considerable skill set which is complementary to the coaches and players," Australia coach Andrew McDonald said.
"Not only is his expertise as a player and coach across multiple formats, competitions, countries invaluable, so are his qualities as a person."
Hussey, known as "Mr. Cricket", was part of England's coaching staff when they won the T20 World Cup in 2022 and has also worked in franchise competitions including the Indian Premier League and The Hundred.
He will begin his role during Australia's T20 series against England, which starts on November 21.
