- The claim that the U.S. and Israel would carry out a nuclear strike on Iran after the 2026 midterm elections is unproven.
- The rumor stems from an X post by the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson, who claimed on Nov. 1 that Trump could decide to carry out the alleged strike as early as next Nov. 7. Carlson claimed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was attempting to push Trump and his administration to use nuclear weaponry in the war in Iran.
- At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed whether the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran. Experts warned that doing so would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region and could start a global nuclear arms race.
- A White House spokesperson told Snopes that Carlson had "no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking" but that Trump would "do what is right to keep the American people safe."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Sunday.
On Nov. 1, two days before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson posted (archived) on X that "the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran."
In a more than 700-word post, Carlson claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was seeking to pressure U.S. President Donald Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and U.S. Central Command head Brad Cooper to take out Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected key location in Iran's nuclear program, using a nuclear bomb.
According to Carlson's "informed observer," Trump could make a decision on whether to carry out a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain as soon as Nov. 7.
Carlson's post also circulated on Facebook and Bluesky (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about Carlson's claim.
At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed that the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran.
The U.S. has not used nuclear power in warfare since dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, a move that forced a Japanese surrender and led to the end of World War II. Over the past month, Trump has given mixed signals in media interviews about his plans for ending the war in Iran, but has not suggested he was considering using nuclear force.
Experts warned that using nuclear force against Iran would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region, could inspire existing nuclear powers like Russia or China to use their arsenal in conflicts in Ukraine and elsewhere and would lead to a nuclear arms race.
A White House spokesperson said in an email to Snopes on Nov. 5:
President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe. Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking.
We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Nov. 1. We await replies to our queries.
Why is Pickaxe Mountain important?
Though there was no proof that the Trump administration would use nuclear power to do so, Trump has been considering striking Pickaxe Mountain — the target Carlson claimed would require nuclear force — since at least July. For example, on July 21, Trump told reporters at the White House (time code 26:34), "We'll be hitting that area pretty soon and very heavily."
In September, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, wrote that Israeli intelligence reportedly indicated that Iranian authorities moved "uranium centrifuges and centrifuge parts," which are necessary to enrich uranium for commercial or combat use, to Pickaxe Mountain, which is near the Natanz nuclear facility.
At the time, the think tank wrote that Pickaxe Mountain would be "difficult" to destroy "even with the heaviest non-nuclear U.S. munitions." The facility is reportedly buried deep in a granite mountain and the U.S. does not have access to blueprints that would give away its size and shape, or whether it has weak points like the ventilation shafts the U.S. targeted at the Fordo nuclear facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025.
Trump has repeatedly said since the start of the war in Iran that his and Netanyahu's primary goal is that Iran does not get access to enough enriched uranium to obtain a nuclear weapon. To achieve this aim, the U.S. and Israel would need to curtail Iran's nuclear material and capabilities like the site at Pickaxe Mountain through either force or diplomacy.
Carlson's post suggested without proof that the Trump administration was weighing up using its ultimate military power to achieve its aims in Iran.
Mixed signals about Trump's next steps in Iran
Trump has given mixed signals about how he wants to approach his and Netanyahu's goals in Iran. By October, Trump was still saying that he wanted to strike Pickaxe Mountain, though no reports suggested such a strike had taken place.
For example, Trump told Newsmax on Oct. 15, "We're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Starting after Oct. 20, several U.S. news outlets reported that the Trump administration was drawing up plans for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. These reports did not say that Trump was considering using nuclear force.
In fact, Trump said on Oct. 15, in response to a question about whether he would use tactical nuclear weapons in Iran, "No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to."
This remark could suggest that the U.S. had non-nuclear ways of destroying Pickaxe Mountain or that Trump wanted to allow time for diplomatic negotiations to take place.
However, by the start of November, PBS reported that negotiations between Washington and Tehran on a deal to end the war were "tense." According to the report, Washington wanted early assurances that Iran would not develop a nuclear weapon, while Tehran wanted to defer the issue for later talks.
On Nov. 2, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi appeared to signal that the ball was in the U.S.'s court. He reportedly said:
We have put forward our conditions and proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political judgement. If it opts for sincere diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if it intends to resort to deception or military action, it will face a response more bitter and more severe than before.
Carlson published his post alleging that the U.S. was considering a nuclear resolution to the war in Iran that same day.
By Nov. 3, despite the October reports that the U.S. was planning strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, Trump reportedly told the Financial Times that the U.S. seemed to be "getting everything we want" in diplomatic negotiations and had no plans for immediate strikes.
However, that same day, Trump also told Fox News (time code 13:57) the U.S. had to "do something large" in the war with Iran. He did not specify whether "something large" was in reference to diplomacy or military attacks, but did add, "A lot of people would like to do the heavy hitting."
Trump must balance input from Tel Aviv and Washington
It was unclear from Trump's Election Day interview with Fox News who "a lot of people" were, or who exactly the president was taking advice from on the war in Iran.
On Oct. 28, news broke that U.S. Vice President JD Vance reportedly sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's top security body, in a bid to restart peace talks. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance sent the letter at Trump's request, though Trump himself appeared to suggest it was Vance's idea. Either way, the letter suggested the U.S. had not given up on the idea of a diplomatic solution to the war in Iran.
On Nov. 1, Carlson claimed that Netanyahu had pressured both Trump and other officials, including Hegseth, to use nuclear power in Iran. PBS reported that there had been "growing fears" that Netanyahu could be pushing Trump to escalate the conflict in Iran.
Netanyahu, whose coalition failed to secure a majority in Israel's October elections, will lose his position as prime minister if he cannot form a 61-seat majority in the Knesset. PBS reported that Netanyahu could be, "pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war." Snopes has not independently verified this claim.
Trump reportedly spoke to Netanyahu on Oct. 31, the day before Carlson's post, though the details of that call were unclear. However, the Telegraph newspaper reported it was unlikely Netanyahu would have pushed for a nuclear strike on Iran, writing that if Israel "were seen to be involved in any way in breaking the taboo on the use of nuclear weapons, it could rebound horribly. It would take only one strike on Israel to make it unliveable, given that it is such a tiny country."
Therefore, while Netanyahu might have reason to encourage refreshed strikes on Iran, it's unlikely he would push for those strikes to use nuclear weapons.
Ultimately, the mixed reporting throughout October and November and Araghchi's statement on Nov. 2 suggested the U.S. and Iran were preparing for both a diplomatic and a military resolution to the war, potentially developing at the same time. The available evidence did not suggest that the Trump administration, regardless of input from Netanyahu or anyone else, was planning a U.S. nuclear strike on Iran, something that could set off further strikes in the Middle East and Europe and lead to a nuclear arms race.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the war in Iran.

Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.
Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.
"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."
In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."
"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.
During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.
The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.
Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.
"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."
Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.
In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.
Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.
The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.
In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.
"I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."
For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.
"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."
"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Married at First Sight UK cancelled after review, sexual assault allegations
Channel 4 says show will not return after 3 female contestants alleged misconduct
Britain's Channel 4 says it will not bring back Married at First Sight UK, following the results of an external review into contributor welfare.
It was commissioned after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on set.
The show follows strangers matched by relationship experts who meet for the first time at the altar, take part in a mock wedding ceremony and move in together as newlyweds.
The U.K. version of the program was considered to be a massive ratings juggernaut for Channel 4, and ran for 10 seasons.
In May, BBC's current affairs program Panorama spoke to two women who said they were raped by their on-screen husbands, and a third who alleged her on-screen husband subjected her to a non-consensual sexual act.
The men denied the allegations. In June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.
Channel 4 commissioned a review tasked with examining whether the show's welfare protocols met its duty of care obligations — and whether those protocols needed to be changed.
The results of that review, released Thursday, found the show's welfare protocols were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard — though in some isolated incidents, not fully implemented.
Measures to improve welfare
The final report also included recommendations to improve the welfare of Married at First Sight UK cast members — including putting couples in separate bedrooms on wedding night and honeymoon, reviewing the frequency with which couples are asked about the physical side of their relationship, and removing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.
It also suggested installing CCTV and sound recording equipment in all areas of the apartments to be monitored 24/7 by a welfare-trained team, and providing two lockable ensuite bedrooms for cast members.
Channel 4 headquarters in London, U.K. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
"MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production," said Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra in a statement.
She thanked the team for its efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, but said "the series will not return to Channel 4, with the show’s budget reinvested in distinctive new programming."
Dogra also repeated her apology to the female cast members who came forward with their allegations.
"This review did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama program, but I would like to repeat that I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt."
She said she hopes Channel 4's swift action demonstrates "our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards."
The show is part of an international reality-TV franchise with editions in countries including the U.S. and Australia.
CBC News has not had any response to questions about whether those shows will continue.

AI startup Thinking Machines Lab is set to close a fresh round of funding as soon as this week.
The startup is raising $5 billion at a $40 billion pre-money valuation, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Accel is leading the round, according to the sources.
Previously, Thinking Machines Lab, which was founded by Mira Murati, was valued at more than $10 billion and raised a $2 billion seed round last year before launching a product.
This round would more than triple Thinking Machines' valuation from its last public round last year, showing that investors are still willing to place enormous bets on AI labs even as the industry's talent war intensifies. Last year, the company was seeking a new round at a $50 billion valuation, but talks were abandoned.
A representative for TML declined to comment. Accel did not respond to a request for comment.
It emerged from stealth last year as one of the highest-profile AI labs thanks to its leadership's deep ties to OpenAI. CEO Mira Murati previously served as OpenAI's chief technology officer, while other key figures helped train the early versions of ChatGPT.
The company's first tool, Tinker, is a system that enables users to more easily fine-tune large language AI models. TML released a new version of Tinker on Thursday, stating that the model has seen gains in AI coding.
The startup has attracted top talent like competitive coder Neal Wu. At the same time, the battle for AI talent has intensified, and Thinking Machines has lost many of its founding members, including Barret Zoph, Luke Metz, and Andrew Tulloch, to rival companies.
As Business Insider reported in May, about a third of its founding team has left Thinking Machines, driven by a mix of factors including huge pay packages offered by rival AI labs like Meta and OpenAI.
In September, The Information reported that Thinking Machines Lab was in talks to raise a new round of funding.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
B – BALANCE loss
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
E – EYE changes
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
F – FACE drooping
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
A – ARM weakness
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
S – SPEECH difficulty
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
T – TIME to call 911
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
- Published
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week
- Published
At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats in the second such incident this week, with the UK calling it a "malicious hoax".
Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair's Helsinki-Rome flight.
EasyJet said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. London Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.
No explosives have been found during searches, and it is not clear if the incidents, some claimed by a little known group, are related.
The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.
The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".
They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.
These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.
"Fighters of the Male State" likely refers to the Russian group "Muzhskoi Legion" ( "Male Legion") - an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."
She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".
A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.
Heathrow later said in a statement it had received a threat earlier in the day which was "deemed not credible", adding there was "no risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft".
"There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to assess and safely manage these types of situations," the statement said.
Meanwhile, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".
The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:
- Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible".
- Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria
- Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft
- Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found
- Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets
- No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said
- Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports"
- A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported
- Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight
- Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded"
Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.
Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.
On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."
Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing and saw one touch down behind the aircraft.
After landing at the Évreux-Fauville air base in Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat.
Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs.
The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome.
Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents.
A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said.
He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".
Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real".
He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel.
Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion".
Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
- Published
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.
The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.
Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.
A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".
"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.
Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.
The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.
The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.
These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.
Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.
The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.
Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.
Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

The best smart ring does a lot without asking much of you, passively tracking your activity, health, and sleep. Some models go even further, with meal logging, AI coaching, and cycle tracking. No distracting screens. No bulky smartwatch banging you in the face while you're deep in REM sleep.
Once the preserve of wealthy wellness buffs, top-of-the-line smart rings are becoming increasingly affordable and available. Although our top pick is still Finnish pioneer Oura's Ring 5 (from $399), the company is no longer the only fish in the smart-ring sea, thanks to upstarts like Ultrahuman and RingConn, established fitness-tracking brands like Amazfit, and even tech giants like Samsung. I expect to see more entrants in the coming months, but for now, these are the best smart rings we’ve tried.
For more wearable recommendations, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Smartwatches, the Best Fitness Trackers, and the Best Fitbits.

How I Test Smart Rings
WIRED has been testing smart rings since the NFC Ring and the first-ever Oura Ring. I wear each smart ring 24/7, for at least a month, to assess how it performs in everyday life. Every ring is worn during activities like commuting, exercising, and sleeping to see how comfortable it feels over extended use and whether the design causes irritation, scratches easily, or gets in the way of everyday tasks.
- Sleep tracking: Sleep tracking is one of the biggest reasons people buy smart rings, so I wear each device overnight for several weeks and compare data trends against other trackers I regularly use, including wearables and sleep-tracking mats. I also evaluate whether the personalized insights (readiness metrics, sleep apnea detection, and coaching recommendations) are useful.
- Fitness tracking: I wear each ring during a range of workouts—including walks, runs, and high-intensity training—to evaluate how accurately it tracks movement, heart rate variability (HRV), and other exertion metrics. I compare data trends against other fitness trackers I regularly use.
- Durability: I expose all smart rings to daily handwashing, temperature fluctuations, and bumps. I check for scratches, coating wear, and water resistance performance.
- Companion app: Since most smart rings lack screens, companion apps need to be user-friendly. I evaluate how easy the apps are to navigate, how clearly they present health data, and whether paywalled subscriptions lock away essential features.
- Battery life: Battery life claims are tested. I track how long each ring lasts with all available features, such as continuous heart-rate monitoring, workout recognition, and sleep tracking. I also look at how quickly each ring charges and whether its charging accessories are practical to use.
- Sizing: Because fit is critical for accurate readings and usability, I take note of sizing ranges and kits. I test multiple finger placements when possible and track performance to determine how dependable the readings are.
- Value: Some smart rings cost as much as a premium smartwatch, and many also require monthly subscriptions. To determine whether a ring is worth buying, I consider its build quality, the accuracy of its features, the app experience, and any ongoing fees.

Best Smart Ring Overall
The original Oura Ring unilaterally created the health smart ring category. This stylish, unobtrusive ring, popularized by biohacking billionaires, soon brought miniaturized fitness tracking to the masses.
Why WIRED recommends: The latest Oura Ring 5 is 40 percent smaller than its predecessor, making it one of the comfiest wearables to keep on all day and night. The titanium exterior has a new coating applied with physical vapor deposition (PVD) to improve scratch resistance, and the ring itself features redesigned sensors, stronger signal detection, and consequently, better accuracy. It also has improved battery life, lasting up to nine days of use.
The biggest upgrade is Oura's push toward AI-powered health guidance. Similar to Google Health Coach, the Oura Advisor can answer wellness questions, provide personalized recommendations, and help identify patterns across your long-term data. New health features, including blood pressure signals and nighttime breathing insights, expand Oura's focus beyond basic fitness tracking.
The trade-offs: While it now supports live activity tracking through the app and can work with compatible heart rate monitors, the Ring 5 isn't the best choice for athletes who need live workout stats or a built-in GPS. If you already own a Ring 4, I'd probably wait another generation, considering that most software additions are coming to older hardware anyway. Finally, you'll need an Oura membership ($6 per month or $70 annually) to unlock most of its insights. (Without it, you can only view your Readiness, Activity, and Sleep Scores.)
Is There a Class-Action Lawsuit Against Oura?
Last August, San Francisco’s Clarkson Law Firm filed a class-action lawsuit alleging that Oura rings cannot measure one’s sleep stages and rely on the company’s AI models to do the guesswork. The complaint argues that sleep is “defined by brain electrical activity, eye movements, muscle tone, and other signals measured through electrodes placed on the scalp, leads on the eyes, and sensors on the chin. [Oura] doesn’t measure any of these parameters.”
In an email statement to WIRED responding to the lawsuit, an Oura spokesperson wrote, “Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature.”
According to Oura, its sleep-staging algorithm is informed by research based on more than 1,200 nights of collected data. “We published a peer-reviewed paper that describes how the sleep-staging algorithm was developed and how it uses the signals collected by the ring,” wrote the spokesperson. “Multiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy, and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”
As of November 2, the court has yet to rule on Oura’s response to the complaint. I’ll continue to monitor the lawsuit and report back on any significant developments. For now, though, nothing has surfaced that changes my judgment of Oura as my top pick.
TL;DR: Though still subscription-based, the Oura Ring 5 is the best sleep tracker, one of the best fitness trackers, and the best smart ring for most folks. Read my full review.

Best Subscription-Free Smart Ring
I'm currently testing the RingConn Gen 3, but the Gen 2 Air remains one of our budget picks thanks to its affordable price and subscription-free model.
Why WIRED recommends: The RingConn Gen 2 Air is slimmer, lighter, and much more comfortable than previous models. It tracks your steps, calories burned, heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep. It can prompt you to get up when you’ve been sedentary for too long and nudge you to take a breather if your stress levels spike. It's also compatible with colored ring protectors to swap out with your outfits if you're someone who likes to color-coordinate.
RingConn added an AI assistant to the app that generates a plan for you, adjusting your targets weekly based on your activity and feedback. This feature is fine. You can ask questions and get tips, but it doesn't dramatically change the overall user experience or make me more motivated to use the ring.
The trade-offs: Compared to the Gen 2, it's made from cheaper steel, has a slightly shorter battery life (still up to 10 days), can’t detect sleep apnea, and comes with a basic charger instead of a nifty charging case. Workout tracking is limited and does not work well when your heart rate is elevated. It also consistently overestimated reviewer Simon Hill's sleep and underestimated his steps and activity compared to the Oura and Apple Watch.
TL;DR: The RingConn Gen 2 Air is worth considering given that it's comparatively affordable and subscription-free.

Best for Samsung Users
The Samsung Galaxy Ring works seamlessly with the Galaxy Watch8 series and Galaxy Watch Ultra, extending each device's battery life by trading tasks and keeping tabs on your activity while the other is charging.
Why WIRED recommends: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So found this ring's accuracy similar to the Apple Watch Ultra. It accurately auto-detected workouts—even pool workouts—and the heart rate tracking is also reliable. Its cycle-tracking feature, powered by the fertility-tracking app Natural Cycles, uses skin-temperature sensing to track when your period will come—and it works.
It comes in an attractive, clear charging case with an LED that shows you how much battery life you have left.
The trade-offs: While you can use the Galaxy Ring with most Android phones, it costs about as much as the Oura Ring 5 upfront and doesn’t require a subscription. The most useful features, like your daily Energy Score and wellness tips (what the company calls Booster Cards), also rely on Galaxy AI, which means you'll only be able to see them if you are using the ring with an Android phone and the Samsung Health app. Lastly, Adrienne found the Galaxy Ring to be a bit too generous with its sleep tracking, which makes sense since it lacks a gyroscope.
